第三幕：Fed、Warsh 与 Jackson Hole

All right, let us move on to something else that constantly gets yelled about — and people who are constantly attacked — which is the Federal Reserve.

Warsh 的鹰派演讲

Warsh gave his first Jackson Hole keynote as chair on August 28th, speaking hawkishly about inflation without committing to a September hike. He opened the speech with an extended literal riff on Jackson Hole, using the word "hike" three times in his first paragraphs. Some might say he was deliberately toying with some algorithms that pay attention to these things.

But the actual important quote was: "We must be confident that underlying inflation is moving towards our objective clearly and at sufficient speed. Otherwise, we have some work to do."

This is with a backdrop of 12-month PCE inflation being 3.7%. And reminder, the technical Fed target is 2%. And September rate hike odds jumped from 35 to the mid-50s on this one.

And he said, quote: "I stand here today committed to a discipline, not to a decision. You can call it an outline. You can call it a trail map. Just don't call it forward guidance."

The press conference needed to be a cleanup of the muddled July one. Stocks have kind of not really paid any attention to this whole thing happening. Bitcoin's trading roughly around where it was.

Ram：Warsh 不想颠覆船

But the question I have for you guys is what do you make of this thing?

Ram: I think he was just staying primarily to his prior messaging. He's not trying to rock the boat. There was de-risking ahead of it, I think some de-risking after it. I think a lot of markets focus on midterms, and it's quite possible that a lot of that midterm risk has been pulled forward now to where we are today.

I don't expect that there's going to be any rate hikes in September, even though there's a 60%-plus probability on these various betting markets right now. I'd want to look at the other side of that.

Austin: Not betting — not betting, prediction, prediction markets.

Ram: Right — prediction markets. There you go. Prediction markets.

Austin: I'm looking at Kalshi. Ram was referring to the traditional volatility surface when he said there. Yeah, it looks like Kalshi's saying 77% chance of a hike before '27, Andy.

Andy：概率的正确解读

Andy: Yeah, we've got a 57% chance of a 25 basis point hike currently priced in for the September meeting. What was interesting in the August meeting is we only had an 18% probability. And the FedWatch numbers there — sort of the traditional finance — have like a 45% probability. And what's again interesting about that is you can sell one and buy the other and lock in risk-free arbitrage. So we've seen a huge number of hedge funds and individuals looking at, "How do you do those trades?"

But yeah — look, I think the value you get from these markets — I talked about that quality of the value earlier on, how well calibrated they are. But just because something's got a 57% chance, what that means is that 57 times out of 100, it'll hike. That doesn't mean that it's definitely going to hike. It's just because there's 43 times out of 100 that it's not going to hike.

And even if something is at a 5% chance, that just means that one time in 20 the 5% odds is going to come out. And what our markets are saying is not that the percentage point is guaranteed to be right — it's saying that the market's really well-calibrated. The 5% thing occurs 5% of the time — it doesn't occur 10% and it doesn't occur 0%. So it's an accurate calibration.

And perhaps as Mr. Warsh is going to do less forward guidance, the Kalshi dates — or the prediction markets that Ram was talking about there — across the board where you have these prices, I think it's a great way of having a vision of the value of the comments. And we've seen to date that that's been highly valuable.

In fact, Morgan Stanley put a research piece out last week highlighting the fact that the Kalshi data was as good as anything on the street. And in some of the things like payrolls and GDP, and others where there isn't really a market, it's more accurate than surveys and better than surveys. So we are finding people want to get hold of that data, as Ram would know, to be able to express their views through both the prediction markets and in traditional assets, given that is a powerful information source.

Chris：如果 Warsh 加息呢？

Chris: Horse markets would be more exciting though. What would happen, do you think, if Warsh comes in and he raises rates — I mean, wink wink, nod nod? What's the President going to do? Because he has been obsessed about lower interest rates. Is this just another case of him talking a big talk and not taking action and hoping for the best? Talk, talk, talk as hawkish as possible, hope that the Iran war abates, inflation comes down, oil comes down, things look much better. What do you think, Ram? Like, what's your take?

Ram: I still think it's going to be very hard for him politically to raise rates, particularly going into midterms.

Chris: Yeah, no, I agree. They're not going to change rates going into midterms. I don't think it makes any sense at all. And Warsh knows why he was appointed by Trump. So I think he's just going to talk hawkish and be soft on policy.

Austin: I mean, do they even have the votes? Like, he's not the only guy voting here. People forget the Federal Reserve is not a centralized entity. In many ways, like crypto, it is quite decentralized. So Warsh could vote to hike and other people don't go along with him.

Austin：Fed 的两难困境

I feel like the Fed right now is caught a little bit between a rock and a hard place from two different angles, Chris.

One is, do you hike or do you cut based on the short-term concerns, right? Labor market's doing OK. It's not historically great. If you look at what's going on, although unemployment headline is looking pretty good, employment headline is looking pretty good, labor market participation is going this way. So you're probably pretty cautious about hiking into that because that tells you you're on a pretty narrow margin. On the other hand, inflation is higher than you would like, but it's not critical — right, it's at 3.7. It's not at like six. We're not looking at the 1970s, but we're not at two. And so both of these kind of are uncertain and pulling in opposite directions. On that hand, from a traditional standpoint, you kind of do nothing.

On the other hand, we also have a much larger debt-to-GDP than we normally have. We're living in a world where, very specifically because so much debt is outstanding, the dynamics of raising rates work a little bit differently than they have in the past. Because if you have short-term debt that you're rolling and you raise rates, you're actually reducing credit but increasing free cash flow to the private sector in a way that is not true if you have like a 10% debt-to-GDP.

So we may also be in a world where the answer to solving these problems is not within the control of the Federal Reserve. Like, this may be a Congress problem. I'm curious as to what you think of that pushback.

Chris：Bessent、Fed-Treasury Accord

Chris: You're going to continue to see Bessent have a very strong role in this new era. It's a new Fed-Treasury Accord. They both rode on the plane recently to, I think, somewhere in North Carolina, somewhere down south, where they're meeting with other ministers. It's an era of coordination. I think Bessent's going to use more and more tools at his disposal, similar to what we saw at the end of intervention, with an idea of keeping rates low as possible for as long as possible. More to follow.

Andy：三个来自 Kalshi 数据的洞察

Andy: I'll make maybe three interesting points from our markets.

The first one is that we put a research piece out relatively recently which showed the oil price correlation — the at-pump oil price correlation with Republican success. As the oil price went up, Republican success went down in terms of the Kalshi markets.

Now, we have an index called KPOW (K-P-O-W), and it aggregates all of the prediction markets. We have millions trade on these markets, and we have multiple markets that are next president, midterms, Congress, etc. And we bring all those together for a reductive story, and we're seeing that the Republicans have trended down slightly over the last couple of months in that sort of aggregate market. And that's super correlated to oil.

And you see that again — the final part of that is we have a "when will traffic at the Strait of Hormuz return to normal," which is a proxy for sort of oil prices at the pump. Not a total proxy, I get that, but it's an interesting one to evaluate. And you look at that, and it says that there's a 62% chance that it occurs before July '27. But before Jan '27, there's only a 28% chance of it occurring. So there's a view that it's going to take a while to get things going in terms of ships going back through the Strait of Hormuz for insurance and other reasons and problems with Iran that are going to play out.

So you can see these market factors all, I think, working together in terms of inflation, popularity, polls. But I think there's a lot of similarity, in my view, around the "it'd be striking to raise the month before midterms" in terms of the Fed. I think that would be very challenging.

Austin：真正的问题在国会

Austin: So I'm going to wrap back around to a question that raises then, which is: if we've got this dynamic where the Fed is not able to do anything, if we agree that the Treasury is the one who probably has the stronger hand from a presidential perspective — at what point do we get to a framework where Congress actually sits up and pays attention? Or are we years away from that?

I know we have the rate hike question going, but all of this fundamentally is still against the backdrop of ever-growing debt-to-GDP. Or do we think real productivity is going to pick up enough that that starts shrinking? But I'll be honest, I find that hard at the rate at which we continue to spend.

And I'm curious at what point the group spending most of the money starts paying attention — or, because I saw the letter from Druckenmiller pointing out that Bessent could do whatever he wants, he knows this isn't going to work, it's ultimately a Congress problem, and as we know, those two know each other pretty well — at what point are we starting to see this actually as shadow messaging starting: that Congress needs to spend less money, before we start hearing from the Fed and Treasury that Congress needs to spend less money?

Ram：不会很快，除非债市崩

Ram: Not going to happen anytime soon. You've got to cut entitlements, which is what Druck was pointing out. That means Social Security, Medicare, Medicaid. It turns out those people vote a lot. When have you seen a government program pull back and have benefit cuts? It's extremely rare. You'd have to have a breakdown in the bond market — that's not going to happen either. So there's no clear path to Congress doing much here. But productivity growth is a real story. Growth is a real story also. So it's unfortunate that debt-to-GDP is so high, but I don't think it's as concerning as people think.

Austin：2030 年代早期的社会保障悬崖

Austin: So, Ram, I'll answer your question by saying, the times you see that are when sort of the party stops because the cuts are already coming. I guess your prediction then would be the early 2030s, because that's about when Social Security is going to start running into problems where the trust is no longer sufficient to pay out all the benefits.

Ram: That's a good point. I mean, yeah, there's a forcing mechanism there. And there have been points in the time in the past where Social Security benefits have been amended — you know, ages raised, inflation indexing has been introduced. So they'll find a way to kick the can down the road without fully addressing their obligations.

Austin: I mean, the easiest way to fix it right now is get rid of the inflation indexing, right? Like, here you go — we're just going to pay you the same amount of money over time and let inflation take care of it.

Chris: Yeah, or means testing.

Austin: Yeah, there's a lot they could do. I will say, I think the means testing is going to be pretty damned ugly because part of why Social Security has persisted so long is that it's not means tested, so everybody supports it. The moment you put it on there, it looks like another welfare program, and then you start getting into the exact same political fights that you don't currently have.

I can see the inflation pull first. But to your earlier point, if you're going to see the bond market freak out, it's if they get to the Social Security cliff and they kick that can by being like, "Oh, we're just going to issue more debt and keep paying people full benefits anyways" — because then the market can look at that forward path and be like, "I'm out." That's when you see it.

Chris：新兴市场化的信号

Chris: Again, look to the emerging markets path. We're seeing the problem of short-term rates and long-term rates no longer behaving in the normal way in the U.S., and behaving like Brazil. That's when you'd see that.

Austin: Chris, am I crazy on that front?

Chris: No. I'm still thinking about these divorce markets. We need one for the divorce of the people from the party. The volatility in those markets would be extremely high depending on the day of the week.

Austin: Exactly. That was extraordinary. Blue Monday.

结语：还有哪些市场值得期待？

Austin: Any markets you guys seriously think that should be out there that we haven't seen yet when it comes to a company like Kalshi?

Andy：稳定币与 AI 市场

Andy: Before I answer that, I'll give a point from someone who's in the UK. First of all, on your last point — the first point is that stablecoin issuance is enormous. Yeah, the amount of development of stablecoins and the amount of money that's coming out of banks around the world into stablecoins through emerging markets, whatever, is, I think, phenomenal.

And I think there's two things that that does: 1. It dollarizes deposits effectively into emerging markets, but as well as dollarizing deposits, 2. It supports the front end of the curve tremendously for the US, which I think is an enormous advantage that you just don't get in the UK.

And so this concept of forcing function and flight to quality, etc., I think is just going to be in places like the UK, Europe, as examples — and I think maybe Canada, etc. — I think is going to be much less in the US, or the timescale is going to be a lot less.

And then in terms of markets — we're focused on developing AI, so we're going to take this conversation back into a full loop. AI markets are enormous. - We've got forward compute markets where we're looking at the price of a forward chip based on whether it will be above or below things. - We've got technical markets. - We've got markets on what's going to be the best AI model.

And so you start to then layer in some of the minerals around that and some of the power around that, and you're actually starting to get a proper big ecosystem to manage and hedge and run the risk around a lot of this AI stuff.

And we talked about it being scary at the start — well, some people think it's scary. I'm kind of like, this is quite exciting now in terms of the ability to hedge all of that together and run a better society. Again, I think hedging, free market forward pricing, risk reduction is hugely beneficial for the development of those markets. And I think it just plays to American exceptionalism over and above classic economies that are kind of prescriptive around it.

Austin：对税率的远期市场

Austin: All right, I'll throw one final dart out there. Forward markets on tax rates. That is another thing that actually would be an excellent hedging market for people.

Now, we're going to run out of time here — speaking of things you cannot hedge. So, Andy, in particular, I want to say thank you to joining us for this episode. It was really enjoyable. Appreciate your thoughts.

And for everybody else, thank you as always for joining us for Bits and Bips. We'll be back in one week to discuss more about how the worlds of crypto and macro are colliding.

Until then, everyone —

Thank you for watching and hope you enjoyed this episode of Bits and Bips. Just remember, nothing we say here is investment advice, and please check unchainedcrypto.com/bitsandbips for more disclosures.

item.description:
## 一、真正的"监管套利"是反向的：守规矩者才是最好的靶子
节目末尾 Andy 那句关于 Coinbase 与 Binance 诉讼数量对比的观察，其实是整期最锋利的一刀，值得被单独拎出来放大。**合规者被诉讼的频率远高于不合规者**——这不是巧合，而是一个系统性反常识：一旦你把自己嵌进规则里，你就获得了"可被起诉的地址"；而彻底站在规则之外的人，反而处在一种"法律真空态"，谁都够不到。这个逻辑同样解释了 Kalshi 为什么在第九巡回法庭吃了瘪，而海外的体育博彩网站在同一天照常运营——**合法性本身是一种诉讼负债**。
这里有一个跨领域的隐藏映射：这与生物学里的"驯化悖论"惊人相似——被驯化的物种（牛、鸡、狗）在数量上取得爆炸性成功，但个体承受了远超野生同类的疾病、繁殖控制与屠宰风险。Kalshi、Coinbase 是"被驯化"的金融物种，它们换来的是规模与合法进入主流的门票，但代价是把自己的脖子伸进了每一个州总检察长办公室的套索里。
## 二、Ninth Circuit 判决的真正战场不是体育博彩，而是"什么算 Swap"这个 20 年未解之谜
大多数听众听完这集会记住"

item.title: [YC Root Access] Building AI That Optimizes AI
item.dc:creator: YC Root Access
item.content:encoded:
💡 创造性洞见

一、令人意外的观察：他们卖的不是"速度"，而是"用户耐心的延展"

表面上 Wafer 是一家推理云公司，卖 tokens per second。但真正让 YC 决定切换的关键数据，不是延迟数字，而是"用户在切换到 GLM 5.2 之后停留时间显著变长"。

这里藏着一个反直觉的系统性真相：当延迟低于某个阈值，产品的"品类"就发生了跃迁——从"AI 工具"变成"对话伙伴"。Jared 那句"before GLM 5.2 it was too slow or too stupid"透露的其实是：智能与速度在用户体验中不是加法关系，而是乘法关系。慢的智能等于愚蠢，快的中等模型反而超越顶级慢模型。这解释了为什么 OpenAI 和 Anthropic 的"更聪明"叙事，在特定场景中会被彻底击穿。

二、跨领域连接：HFT 的"纳秒竞赛"正在殖民 AI 推理

注意 Stephen 的背景——他来自 Two Sigma，来自那个"以纳秒决胜负"的高频交易世界。Yaka 最初的设计动机（让 AI 自动优化 C++ 代码）本质上是把 HFT 行业的执念（微秒即金钱）迁移到通用计算。

这里有一个巨大的暗流：过去 30 年，最激进的性能优化方法论一直被囚禁在金融行业内部。因为只有 HFT 的商业模式能证明"多榨 5 纳秒"的 ROI。而 AI 推理的爆发第一次让"极致性能"在金融业之外找到了同等甚至更大的经济合理性——一次 voice agent 响应快 200ms，可能意味着一个真实客户不挂电话。Wafer 本质上是 HFT 文化向消费/企业软件的第一次成功溢出。这也预示着未来会有更多"前 quant"进入 infra 领域，把那种病态的性能洁癖带进来。

三、隐藏的系统性真相："AI 优化 AI"是一种新的复利结构

大多数人把 Wafer 的技术叙事当作一个 marketing 口号，但其中藏着一个真正独特的递归复利机制：

  • 传统 infra 公司：每支持一个新硬件/新模型，需要线性投入人力工程师
  • Wafer：每支持一个新模型，让 agent 跑一晚，得到 kernel + speculative decoding + quantization 的组合优化

这意味着他们的边际成本曲线不是线性下降，而是加速下降。更关键的是——他们优化的对象（LLM）和他们优化的工具（LLM agent）是同一件东西。每一次 GLM、DeepSeek 变强，Wafer 的"内部工程师"也自动变强。

这在商业史上极为罕见。类比来说，这像是一家钢铁厂的效率随着全球钢材质量的提升而自动提升——一种奇怪的正反馈闭环。这可能才是他们愿意"烧掉 GPU 抢客户"的真正底气：他们赌的不是当下的速度优势，而是优化速度本身的复利。

一个附加洞察：为什么"过热到断货"是最好的融资策略

Jared 那句"launch and run out of money"的建议看似鲁莽，实际上暴露了 VC 定价的信息不对称结构。融资估值不是由"你有多好"决定，而是由"投资人对你未来能有多好的不确定性"决定。当你先展示需求压垮供给，再去融资，你把叙事从"我们能长多快"变成了"我们必须马上有钱否则错过窗口"——这是把认知不确定性转化为时间紧迫性。这个心理转换，比任何 pitch deck 都值钱。

📝 转录文本

开场介绍

[music] Stephen and Ameilio, welcome back to YC. Thank you so much for coming back to join us today.

Thank you for having us. Thank you. Thank you.

Yeah. So, you guys just graduated from the University of Chicago about one year ago. You are 23 years old and today you are announcing that you just raised a $40 million series A for your company. Uh congratulations.

Thank you. Thank you so much, Jared.

Um that is a pretty wild story. Even by like the standards of Silicon Valley and the AI revolution that we are living in right now. Um, and so I'm excited for you guys to tell everyone the story of how you guys went from being University of Chicago undergrads to running this company that's on fire in basically a year.

Wafer 是什么

Why don't you start by just telling everyone like what is Wafer? What are you guys doing?

So Wafer is a fast AI inference cloud. We run AI models at the best speeds in the market and the way we do this is by having agents optimize GPUs.

What kind of companies are using wafer? What would I use it for?

Yeah, totally. So, we have a lot of customers that use us for um voice agents because it happens to be that when you're running a voice agent in production, you want the lowest latency possible because I'm speaking to an agent over the phone and it takes two to five seconds to respond. It kind of like breaks the — it's a bad customer experience. So, it ends up being a lot of what we do like low latency applications.

The other side of what we do is high throughput applications. You can think of like coding as one example of this where we um work with a lot of customers like Verscell to make sure their coding agents go as fast as humanly possible on on the GPUs they're using.

$40M Series A 融资

Let's talk a little bit about the series A that you guys are announcing today. Can you guys tell us about it?

Yeah, so we raised $40 million. Um and this was co-led by um Marathon and Chemistry. There were a bunch of like awesome angels followed on with like Jeff Dean as existing investors, obviously YC. Yeah, I mean we're super excited about it.

One reason why you guys raised this crazy oversubscribed series A is that Wafer in the last four months has really blown up. You went from essentially zero to 8 million ARR in four months which is like bananas and as a result you like ran out of GPUs and had to like immediately raise money in order to like keep scaling. Um that's insane. Can you guys talk about what happened? Like what caused you guys to blow up like this?

转折点：从卖优化到自己做推理云

Basically around 4 months ago, we decided to shift from selling the AI that optimized GPUs to other companies to just use the agent internally to grab open source LLMs and make them run really fast.

So we did this for example like most famously when we began with GLM 5.2. It was a huge announcement when it came out and we basically grabbed our agent, we rewrote some kernels, we optimized all levels of the stack of the GPU and we made it run two to 3x the performance that everybody else in the market was running it at.

This caused like a huge spike in demand cuz suddenly you didn't need to go to cerebras to get these massive speeds. You can just get them on open router. And that was the moment where we sort of projected where our GPU spend and our where our GPU costs were going and we were like okay we cannot sustain this demand [laughter] if it continues — and it indeed has continued. So that was the moment where we were like okay it's time to go for the next funding round to grow faster.

Office Hours 中的融资建议

And I remember we actually did office hours — I don't know if you guys remember this — but we actually did office hours about 2 weeks before you launched your like fastest GLM 5.2 on the market. And I remembered you were like, "Jared, I think when we launch this thing, it might take off really fast and we might run out of money really quickly." And your question was like, "Should we raise money now?" And I was like,

no, you should probably like launch and let it take off and run out of money and like that's a great story to go to investors and be like, "our thing is growing so fast, we're like running out of money cuz like we can't we can't onboard compute fast enough." And I I remember being like, "Wow, I really hope that that's what happens." But, you know, who knows? Because like launches are unpredictable — and then it was pretty wild because you like a few days after you launched you were like it literally played out exactly the way we we like we thought it was going to play out.

Yeah. Yeah. I think the demand for fast inferences is just extremely high. [laughter] Um and if you can actually — it's kind of like revenue will take care of itself if you can actually achieve the best speed in the market. That's kind of like something we follow internally. It's just the technical difficulty of being the number one is just very high. And um yeah, that's the thing we focus on.

混乱的扩张期：Santa Cruz "度假" onboarding Blackwell

I feel like this experience of like having customers signing up for your product so fast you can't keep up with them and having to like scrounge around to find GPUs any place that you can find them — like this is kind of the promised land for a startup. And like Stephen, you were the guy in charge of like finding the GPUs and like keeping the site up while it was like melting. What was the experience of the last few months like for you?

It's been very chaotic. I think back to a team offsite we took to Santa Cruz, which was supposed to be a fun weekend on the beach. Uh we got a nice hotel right next to the beach. Everybody had rooms. However, what it turned out to be was actually constant onboarding new Blackwell nodes. Um everybody just packed in the same hotel room uh trying to onboard these nodes, also ensure they're reliable and then also ensure that you know they're performant. We're trying to debug, you know, networking issues and so on. So, this specific instance is maybe a taste of how chaotic it's been, but at the very least, I look back and think that this time was very worth it. And also, you know, with the team also some pretty fun as well. So, we're, you know, bonding along the way.

客户案例：Neon Health

Tell us about some of the customers — like you guys went 0 to 8 million ARR. There must be like some big customers paying you all this money. Who's uh who's using it? How are they using it?

Yeah. So one of the best examples is a company called Neon Health. So they do um automation for hospitals. So for example, let's say a customer calls and they want to process um some sort of medicine and they want to get the medicine. Usually there would be another human on the line which fills out a form for these humans. What they have done is they basically do this entire process with AI agents and they really really care about having low latency.

So Neon Health was previously on another larger inference provider, but they decided to switch to us because we were able to give them 30 to 50% better performance on a per call basis. So that's a good example of like the sort of latency improvements that you can achieve with with Wafer.

YC 也是客户：Office Hour Simulator

Yeah, I have direct experience with these latency improvements because YC is not just an investor in Wafer, we are also a customer. So perhaps we can talk about how YC is actually using you guys.

A while back, I built this product that we call the office hour simulator. It's this pretty crazy idea. It kind of looks like an arcade machine. It's designed to look like that. And you walk into it and you hit go and you can talk to an AI clone of a YC partner. Unlike Neon Health, which does voice agents over the phone, this is more like a Zoom call where it's like a full video experience. You're talking to this AI version of a YC partner and you can both see and hear them. But similar to Neon Health, we care a lot about the latency because the whole point is you're supposed to feel like you're actually talking to a YC partner. And so shaving off milliseconds of latency is really important.

Um, and I ran this benchmark to try to find the lowest latency LLM in the market that's actually smart enough to still do a good job with the conversation. And you guys actually beat the benchmark in like a clean head-to-head against basically like every model and every inference provider I could find like I could get my hands on.

Yeah. No, we're super proud of that. And I think the coolest thing about that is that even for the comparisons that you were doing for other providers, we are using a model that's like 20 times larger. So the fact that we can actually get that model to be much much faster than the ones you were trying out is super awesome to us. And that came from just like deep work with like the agents we built to enable that latency for you.

A/B 测试：速度改变用户行为

Yeah. Before Wafer, I was experimenting with Gemini models and OpenAI models. They both have like pretty light like mini models that are good for voice agents. But since you guys got GLM 5.2 running super fast, I switched to your GLM 5.2 like super fast mode. And it's like both smarter and better than the commercial models, which is pretty wild.

And I can actually share another cool stat. I — we haven't released this publicly before — but when we made the switch, we were actually able to A/B test it. And so I actually ran a three-way A/B test between your model and the two proprietary models. We could not only measure a decrease in the like latency of the LLM, we were actually able to see that the users changed their behavior when the calls got faster. And the users who got the wafer GLM model actually stayed and talked to the avatar significantly longer than the ones who had the commercial models.

This is pretty awesome. This is pretty awesome. Yeah, I think having — we have all these examples too of like where people can ditch other parts of sort of like their scaffolding around the LLMs because it's so fast now that it can just do more things live. Um this is an example where it's like literally affecting user behavior. So yeah, speed speed is the moat as we like to say.

Yeah. [laughter] Yeah. I mean it super matters for real-time conversation. Like you know even with the fastest LLMs, no LLM voice agent is quite at human level yet in terms of like latency. And so you really feel it when you're talking to a voice agent that it's just like a little slow to respond compared to a human. And so until we can get it to like absolutely human level, which is probably not like imminent — I think it's like really hard to get it like fully human level — like there's going to be so much gains to anyone who can shave off some milliseconds.

秘诀揭秘：AI 优化 AI

When I saw these benchmark results, I was like pretty stunned, guys. I was like, "Holy — what magic are they cooking up in the lab that was like able to make this the fastest provider?" And so, I don't know how much of your secret sauce you can share, but like I'd love for you to talk a bit about the technology behind it and how you made it faster.

You know, the headline here is AI that optimizes AI, but what does this really mean? I mean when we went through our benchmarking period with Y Combinator you know we asked for some information on our end — you know like the specifics on the specific workload that YC was running. This is all very valuable information for performance engineers.

Um and that being said, the general flow at which we use AI that optimizes AI is: we take the workload characteristics of any given customer, throw this into you know let's say an AI blackbox and this AI blackbox does a ton of things — whether it's goes and writes custom kernels, goes and trains a speculative decoding model, quantizes the model and so on. In the end of this whole process comes out with let's say a engine or a runtime that is hyper optimized for a specific user allowing us to get 2x, 3x and so on speed ups over other inference runtimes.

Um I think some cool examples in this specific situation are you know maybe looking back to — or you know let's say this YC example — um we also have examples of our agent going off and writing custom kernels, bringing up AMD hardware to find perf per dollar parity with Nvidia hardware and so on.

一年蓄力，四个月爆发

So even though this new product that you guys launched — the inference cloud — took off just four months ago when you launched it, this is a little bit of like an overnight giant success like a year in the making because all the technology that you just talked about, you'd basically been working on that for like a while, and the reason that he was able to take off so quickly is that you'd spent months doing all of this like very hard deep technical work, right?

Yeah. I think back to our time in YC and you know not not a ton of let's say progress was really made on the revenue side but on the tech side — I mean I can give a flashback. We started as "cursor for CUDA." From the very beginning, we're using agents to optimize kernels themselves. Um, as we progressed more in the ML performance space, we moved up the stack. We were able to do contracts with folks like AWS writing kernels for them. Uh, do work with Digital Ocean, optimizing models for them.

And so we let's say developed this muscle — you know, or just develop agents for doing performance engineering. And so when we made the switch to become the cloud, it was very easy to get AI to optimize AI because this is something that we'd been doing right since the start of our YC batch last year.

商业模式的顿悟时刻

Interesting. So the first idea was basically customers would give you their proprietary model and you would use agents to optimize their model, and then the big unlock was just switching to like open source models that you could just optimize and then just give the optimized version like for anyone.

Yeah. So there's a funny story that's fun to talk about here where Stephen — basically we had a big demo with one of the inference providers, one of the large inference providers that has broken out in the last like two years, and we were getting the agent to get results on like what performance improvements it could get over like base LLMs to show them the next day.

And basically Steven stays up all night cuz he just often does that [laughter], and he — just running the agent, like orchestrating. And then he shows me the results in the morning and he's like, "we beat like some of these core NVIDIA libraries with just like the agent running overnight and me just like making sure that we're just coordinating these agents at very high level." And I was like, "what?" And he just shows me these results and I'm like — there was this moment where we're just like, "okay let's cancel this meeting and let's just meet and talk about this more because it just seems that there's so much value in these optimizations that I don't even know if we want to give them away."

Interesting.

And that was kind of like the start basically 4 months ago that we talked about where we were like, "Oh, wow. We really have something here that we might just verticalize and just compete with the inference clouds directly instead of selling them these optimizations."

开源模型崛起的浪潮

Was another unlock just that the open source models like got really good — like last summer when you guys started the open source models weren't that good.

Yeah, this is true. I think GLM 5.2 was a big moment. Yeah, I think GLM 5.2 um brought out a ton of use cases. Many folks started to really use open source models for their coding workflows. Um and this of course brought a ton of traffic to our platform and to my understanding, brought a ton of traffic to just serverless business as a whole for selling tokens.

We were talking with the Ollama and open code founders recently and the sense that I get from them is that with the new wave of open source models that came out in the last few months, the adoption of open source models is just like on an insane exponential right now. I'm curious what you guys are seeing when you talk to like large companies — is there like a huge push across the board to switch from commercial to open source models?

Yeah, personally from the GTM side we've seen like these massive companies start doing inbound to us and I think there's like a very special moment going on where people are realizing that they can actually run the same workloads that they run with OpenAI and Anthropic and save let's say like 80% of the cost.

So on the cost axis there's just like whatever like lands on the CFO desk and big big enterprises want to cut those costs and they're seeing the token cost rise. And then on the other front they're seeing how much is possible when you can actually get like 5x the speed with open source models. So if you can actually have an opus-level model that will respond five times faster, that's a huge value add for some products.

Like think of your usage of like Granola. They're not one of our customers, but when I'm in a sales meeting and I ask Granola something, I want it to respond as fast as humanly possible because it's like something that the customer is asking me for, right? I would pay a lot of money — I would pay an extra per token money to get a faster response. There's many applications of like the performance sensitive applications that we really are seeing um trickle down.

速度作为一种全新的产品维度

So, I think this is a really insightful point because I think a lot of people think that the reason to switch to open source models is that they are cheaper — and like fair enough, that's a good reason to adopt a thing. But I think a lot of people think that's the only reason to switch to open source models is sort of like, "ah it's like almost as good as Anthropic and OpenAI but it's a lot cheaper," and that's probably driving some of the demand.

What I didn't realize until a couple months ago when I started using Wafer is that there's a whole other reason to switch to them, which is: they are actually the best models if you have a latency sensitive use case. They are actually the fastest models. Like for my office hour simulator I was not price sensitive — like YC is in a fortunate position where we don't care about the LLM cost at all. And so I was actually happy to pay a huge premium for the fastest model that money could buy. And it turns out that the fastest model that money could buy was GLM 5.2 running on Wafer.

Yeah. And there's many situations where people's core product depends on how fast they can deliver the actual response. So we're very excited about all the applications that would just like — the core product depends on how fast you can generate a response.

Totally. I actually think for my office hour simulator that basically switching to GLM 5.2 — that was actually the key turning point where it found product market fit. Like I actually think before GLM 5.2 it was just a little too slow or a little too stupid and so users would churn. GLM 5.2 and Wafer is like just fast enough that people are like, "oh actually this is great. I'm just going to like talk to it all day."

Have you seen people talk to it all day?

Yes.

Wow. [laughter] That's great for us. Please do — the start. Having folks schedule [laughter] time block —

That's awesome though. I mean having access to infinite Jared is obviously very valuable for the world. [laughter]

But it was cool because I feel like because you're sort of like building at the cutting edge and sort of getting access to these products before the rest of the world, that I had like a little peek into the future that other people didn't have.

创业起源：从芝加哥大学到 Yaka

Yeah. Maybe let's rewind back to the very beginning and talk about how you guys ended up starting this company. I actually met you guys before you had started Wafer when you were undergrads at the University of Chicago. Maybe you guys can tell us the story of how you guys met each other in school and what you were doing at the University of Chicago and how you ended up deciding to start a company together.

Yeah, I mean there was a point where Steven showed me a tool he was building and it was called Yaka, um which was actually what we demoed uh YC sometime later like an expanded version of Yaka. And this was a thing that basically grabbed some piece of C++ code and asked an LLM to just optimize the code and just loop through it like, "hey optimize it, measure if it's better, then do it again, do it again, do it again."

And I just thought that it was very interesting to think of this new idea of having the AI as a sort of maybe as a sort of compiler where you can just grab some piece of code and through the LLM you are able to find how to map it to the hardware so that it runs more efficiently, right?

So basically there was one point where we were like, "okay you were going to go to New York, you're going to do your job as um you engineering at Two Sigma — obviously like really good job. I was going to come to a series A startup to do like AI research." First of all it would be way more fun to just like keep working together in something. So there's like one reason for that where it's just like very fun.

And also this exact problem — like the thing that we've been sort of working on here, the Yaka that you showed me — it has the like thing that if you do solve this problem it's like obviously very impactful cuz like a bunch of energy is being wasted on just not running GPUs as efficiently as they should just because the software is not optimized. And the other aspect was like we're both uniquely suited and very interested in this challenge. Like it's something that we see ourselves working like for the next hopefully like 20 years on, right?

So we were like, "Yeah, why not?" And we applied to YC, moved to San Francisco and that was kind of like the start of Wafer.

Yaka 的灵感：来自 Quant 世界

What made you decide to build Yaka in the first place?

When you think about a lot of folks in finance space, they really care about how good or how fast their code is. Um, you know, HFT is a very very competitive field and most often times you win at let's say the nanosecond, right?

And so I was really curious on — at least during my time in these experiences, it seemed that folks really cared about really fast C++, really fast Python, so on. How can I get an AI to solve this problem of generating this really fast code, because it seemed relatively automatable.

So it really did come out of your quant experience because like — yeah, like quant firms are obsessed with squeezing microseconds of performance out of code. But it wasn't initially it wasn't to be a startup, right? It was like — it sounds like it was just like you were just building it just to see if it was possible to build just cuz like you were interested in exploring it, right?

Yeah. When we talk to college students who are interested in starting companies, one of the pieces of advice that we often give them is that they should just build projects just for fun that aren't like trying to be startups just because they find them technically interesting just to explore like, "oh I wonder what the models are capable of." And it sounds like that pretty much perfectly describes what happened here where you had this side project that you were working on just cuz it was interesting and then you guys began talking about it, you're like, "wait the side project — this could be an actual startup."

决定创业：从"好工作"到"火箭飞船"

Let's talk quickly about the decision to do the startup though because when I met you guys at the University of Chicago it was your senior spring and you both had great jobs lined up to do after you graduate and you were not planning to do a startup. You were planning to go do these jobs at great companies. Um, and then something changed in your mind in the next couple of months where you're like, "actually maybe this project that Stephen built before, maybe we should just go do that as a startup." Like I'm curious like what that decision process was like for you guys. Like was it a difficult decision where you went back and forth? Did your parents and your friends try to talk you out of it? Was it emotional or was it just like, "yeah sure why not?"

My thing was very simple. It was like when YC came and gave the talk — I think we've talked about this before but you guys had a line that I still remember which is like, "you don't need a business co-founder." Stephen and I like — just we were both engineers. Um I've never had a real job. [laughter]

So it was kind of shocking to hear that directly from you guys. And I think on my side, this is what started conversations more seriously. But yeah, curious on Stephen.

Yeah, I think personally that held a lot of — how to say — weight also in my decision primarily from a perspective of, now it flipped the switch of, all I have to do is look around at many of my peers and many of the folks who I hang out on a daily basis and really just ask, "should we do this?"

Um I personally, you know, throughout life have always wanted to start a company or at least have a lot of ownership in something that I was to pursue. Um and it seemed that the opportunity was definitely there to one, pursue something worth a lot of let's say value to society, while also maintaining this let's say ownership and being able to do it on my own.

给未来创业者的建议

Do you guys have advice for other people who are interested in starting companies in a similar space or people maybe with similar backgrounds to yourselves? Like imagine rewinding back to a year or a year and a half ago. Like what is advice that you wish other people had told you?

If you're interested in startups at all and you're sort of looking into what startups are the best, there's a lot of people that I've talked to recently that tell me a lot about the role, but I'm a very big believer on — if you're offered a seat in a rocket ship, you just don't ask what exactly you're going to do within the rocket ship.

What you should be evaluating in a company as more and more people are evaluating joining startups in YC and many others after grad or starting one — but specifically for the people that are evaluating joining one, what you should really ask is like, "how could this company go from where it is today to like a thousand x?" And I would specifically focus on the founders and the founding engineers — like what is the culture of the company and will that enable us to grow massively? Because the job itself is going to change super fast. We've never hired for specific roles because the roles just change super fast.

So that's kind of something I've been thinking about — just like make sure that you're investing in the right company and founders instead of your specific role within that company.

招聘中：Member of Technical Staff

Feel like that's a great segue. Um, speaking of joining rocket ships, you guys just raised $40 million. Are you hiring? Can you tell us a bit about who's on the team now and who you're planning to add?

Yeah. Um, I can talk about — we're definitely hiring. Um, we're hiring across the board. The engineering role that we hire for is Member of Technical Staff. This is a person that doesn't need to have any GPU experience. What we really care about is, has this person been exceptional at anything before? This is basically our recruiting guideline that has worked us super well in the past and that we're doubling down on. So if you've done anything exceptional in the past, doesn't have to be computer related, doesn't have to be anything — please reach out because we're hiring as quickly as we can the best people at ML systems performance stuff.

And can you tell us a little bit about — I don't know, like a day in the life as a Member of Technical Staff at Wafer?

You know, it's variable from day to day [laughter]. You know what we did last month is very different than what we do this month, but at the end of the day I think I want to put that word "problem solvers" first. Most often, whether it's a customer or a specific issue we're having with GPUs we're operating with, we're being fed like technical problems from the top and most often times it's just a matter of solving these problems.

You know, what this actually looks like could be things from, "how do we get an agent to write this specific kernel" or "how do we solve this specific reliability issue we're seeing with these GPUs." Um there's a lot of variance. Um but at the end of the day, I very much so view it as solving problems within the domain of ML performance or ML systems.

结尾

Yeah, I feel like that's a great note to end on. Um, thank you guys so much for joining us today and huge congratulations on the Series A.

Thank you so much, Sharon. Yeah, thanks for having us.

[music]
