item.description:
## 一、真正的商业模式不是"卖球赛"，而是"填补空档期"
Ultimate 7s 最颠覆性的洞察其实藏在一个不起眼的时间缝隙里：HSBC 世界系列赛从 12 月打到 6 月，之后就是长达半年的"精英级空档"。Barney 没有去挑战 15 人制的市场，也没有和世界系列赛正面竞争，而是**把"日历空缺"本身当成产品定义**。
这其实是一个被严重低估的商业逻辑——**基础设施套利（infrastructure arbitrage）**。世界上最好的 132 名球员，在 6-11 月这段时间基本处于"闲置资产"状态；各国联盟没钱养他们做高强度赛事，球员却仍需保持竞技状态。Ultimate 7s 本质上做的是**运动员的"共享经济"**——不是拥有球员，而是租用他们的空闲时间。
这跟 Airbnb 早期的逻辑惊人相似：不建酒店，而是唤醒沉睡的房源。差别在于，Ultimate 7s 唤醒的是"沉睡的顶级人力资本"。
## 二、令人意外的观察：他们赢的不是球迷，而是"迁徙路径"
大多数人以为新联赛的核心挑战是"建立部落归属感"（tribalism），但 Barney 反复强调一个更微妙

item.title: [Invest Like The Best] She Knows the 250 People Building AI. Here's What They Actually Believe.
item.dc:creator: Invest Like The Best
item.content:encoded:
💡 创造性洞见

一个反直觉的观察：规模正在杀死大实验室的"主体感"

访谈中最令人意外的一段藏在中间——Sarah 指出，OpenAI 从 200 人扩张、Anthropic 迈向数千人、单次训练需要 7500 亿美元资本时，研究员正在集体失去"我在推动历史"的感觉。两种情绪在顶级实验室的走廊里蔓延："反正模型会自己搞定"、"反正只有算力才重要"。

这里有一个诡异的悖论：AI 越强大，实验室越庞大，个体研究者的能动感越低。这不是 Jevons 悖论——这是它的镜像双胞胎。当访谈末尾她乐观地援引 Jensen 的 Jevons 论断（更高效意味着更多就业）时，其实无意间揭示了一个隐藏张力：在应用侧，AI 会创造无限杠杆感；但在前沿侧，AI 正在制造前所未有的"齿轮化"体验。这也解释了为什么她的整个投资策略成立——顶尖研究员流出前沿实验室、加入小团队，恰恰是"规模的诅咒"在为她供货。她的基金不是在与大实验室竞争，而是在收割它们的"心理副产品"。

跨领域连接：她其实在复刻 20 世纪的"哥本哈根学派"模型

Sarah 和 Mike 反复提到的 "250 个人在推动前沿" ——这个数字远小于任何主流社群理论的估算，却几乎精确对应科学史上"革命性时期的核心节点数"。玻尔的哥本哈根研究所鼎盛期的核心圈约 200 人；曼哈顿计划里真正做核心决策的科学家约 150 人；甚至 Xerox PARC 的黄金年代也只有约 100 名主要研究者。

每一次范式革命，都是由一个"超越 Dunbar 数、但小于 500 人的紧密网络"完成的。Conviction 的整个方法论——不追求管理规模、不铺开搜索面（每周只见 4–6 家公司）、痴迷于关系密度而非交易密度——本质上是把 20 世纪科学革命的"小圈子拓扑"移植到风险资本的架构上。这与传统 VC 追求"deal flow 广度"的模式完全相反。她不是在做一家更好的 A16z，她是在做一个"资本化的哥本哈根"。

隐藏的系统性真相：她的"直觉先行、反向补齐"其实是贝叶斯狩猎

她自述的决策模式极具启发：从 8/9 分开始，然后花几周时间搜寻"能把我拉下来的证据"。这看起来像是过度自信，但在信息论意义上，这是一种更高效的搜索策略——它假设你的先验是丰富的（高年龄段的人脉、多年的模式识别），然后主动寻找反证而非累积正证。

这与访谈中另一个隐藏主题共振：她两次强调"我不想告诉别人他们想听的话"（无论对 LP 还是对被投企业）。当你已经在 8 分，你才有资格不粉饰真相——因为你的下行是"降到 3 分放弃"，而不是"从 0 分挤到 8 分"。这解释了为什么大多数机构投资者难以复制她：他们的整个组织结构都是"climb to conviction"型的（层层评审、逐步加码），而她的模型是"start high, hunt for exits"型的。前者产生共识，后者产生 alpha。

一个尚未被讨论的暗线：她所有的判断都在"押注反循环性"

从生物学（"你不能在药厂只卖软件"——她说错了）到半导体（"venture 支持的半导体是烂生意"——她说过时了）到机器人（"数据永远不够"——她说创造性收集就够了）——她每一个具有回报意义的赌注，都是在赌"陈规已死"。

这里有一个跨领域的联想：这与 Renaissance 大奖章基金对"市场教条"的态度完全同构。Simons 团队的核心信念是"任何被普遍接受的市场规律都在被自身的接受度所侵蚀"。Sarah 在做的是同类型的工作——她在寻找"共识信念的半衰期"，并在信念崩塌前 12–24 个月介入。所以她不是"AI 投资者"，她本质上是一个"共识失效检测器"，只不过这个时代最富集失效共识的领域碰巧叫 AI。

📝 转录文本

She Knows the 250 People Building AI. Here's What They Actually Believe.

Invest Like The Best · 访谈：Sarah Guo (Conviction)

开场：一个疾速旋转、无法回测的时代

It is a violently competitive landscape. I think people are very concerned that it is a globally competitive landscape. There's insecurity in that because I think it's a bit narrative breaking as well. The belief is like with recursive self-improvement of AI research models that can improve the models themselves, we are a year, two years away from some sort of exponential intelligence.

Sarah, where to begin? Uh, what will hopefully be a really fun conversation, I guess, because you and I are interested in so many of the same things. I'm just curious what's on your mind today.

I think we're both feeling a little frenzied and it's been going for a while and it kind of feels like if anything it might get more frenzied and more chaotic — both for what you do but also the world around what you do. So just in this moment, like what — yeah, what does it feel like? What's on your mind?

An obvious thing for anyone thinking about how to navigate this period as an investor is just like: well, how does it unfurl and how's it different from the past, and what do I do if I can't back test? Right? I was talking to an investor friend last night and the analogy he gave me was like: "I keep saying I want to press the brakes as hard as I can but I'm not doing it — I'm going 90 miles an hour." And I do think the question is like, do you miss the opportunity on one side, or do you make the mistake of every boom-bust cycle in technology history? I think it's a complex question.

Do you think that we got it right in the profile that we wrote — that you're sort of making a specific, I think we called it a wager, a bet, a positioning, whatever you want to call it.

Yes. I'm along. Yeah.

That there is a really important fundamental thing happening between a couple of labs in AI and kind of everybody else, and that we need to sort of take up arms to make sure we don't end up in a very monolithic outcome. Do you think about it that way?

I would answer in a maybe different way, which is: I believe in the great man and great woman theories of history. I just believe that if you have very high agency people in all of these places, and they have the correct risk capital or support in the network or environment, like — yeah, you change outcomes.

And so you look at very important questions of what happens to open-source models and US industrial policy. You know, if you think about the opportunity for the ecosystem in the future — is there going to be a competitive Western open-source model? It actually leads to: did anybody make one? Could they raise the money, or were they willing to commit the capital and gather the talent base and build all the infrastructure and fight for the frontier or not?

And so I definitely think that individual people and entrepreneurs can affect the outcome. I don't necessarily think of it as a war. I am working closely with and co-invested with and have many friends at the labs, the big labs and small. But I think it's fair to say the extreme point of view that some folks may have — in and outside of those big labs — of the owner of one, two, three frontier models consumes the economy: I do not want that future very clearly, and I don't think we are going to end up there.

关于"伟大女性"：她为何选择不做主角

Do you actively want to be a great woman in this sense of the theory?

No. And I I don't mean that from a personal humility perspective. It was just — it's not in my set of goals, right? I want to be the best investor in the things that I try to do. So it's not out of a lack of ambition or even confidence. It's — I think some people are driven by "I want to be the person that made this happen."

And my realization — I thought I was going to be a software entrepreneur for the longest time. My decision that from an identity perspective I was going to be an investor actually had a lot to do with the idea of: I'm deeply curious. I like to understand things. I like to be right. And then I care — I'm very motivated by working with extraordinary people, and if I have a set of skills, using those to make them more successful. That looks like a pretty good fit for early-stage investing.

If I want to work with the very best people, and I want the companies to have impact, the firm can support a movement and support change we want to see — but I don't think it has to be me.

If that's the goal, what does it take, do you think, right now to be the best in a very competitive environment?

I think it's been pretty simple so far, actually. My read of the environment was: the growth of firms and generational transitions that were happening meant that it wasn't the most competitive landscape in early — that it has been. And you had this massive technology transition happening. If you took the bet on understanding the technology and the community and approached it from first principles, you might have better access and make better decisions than others who are less focused.

So all you have to do is take the risk and be focused, and then it's an execution play. That's one of those things that I think is pretty simple and it's just hard. It's effort.

250 个人：一张覆盖前沿的关系网

Your partner Mike said something interesting to me a couple weeks ago, which was: there's sort of 250-ish people that he thinks about — some combination of entrepreneurs and researchers doing the most interesting things on the frontier. Just like the people that are actually showing up in the morning and pushing this whole thing forward. And one of your goals as a firm is to be as close to those people, know them all, and support them in as many ways as possible.

I really like that idea. So it just feels like, from the outside looking in, there's more unique stuff going on than just "the competition set was low and we focused more."

To the point of perhaps making a bet that others wouldn't — we thought very carefully about what markets are going to matter, and what might be different about the founders that we look at in this era, if we are right about capability growth and the breadth of impact. That would just be non-obvious to other people.

I'll give you two examples. One of the things we were really looking for in the first year was application areas — like workflows and professions, tasks that we thought were a good fit for purpose for the models. Which is a very technology-forward approach. Lots of people would say: this is nonsense, you got to think about the customer problem, working from the customer back is the only way. I think we want to do both.

If you look at Harvey and the function of the law: rationally, if you think that we can do next-token prediction with language, and you knew that in late 2022 — then law is structured language. I'm not a lawyer, but from the outside I'm like, okay, you need to read a lot of documents, and we had retrieval, and you need to generate text. There's a lot of precedent text both inside firms and in common law and history. That feels like a really good match.

When I say focus, we also took a very specific view of what is now possible, and then what is valuable within what is possible, and then who's aligned with us. Winston and Gabe believed AI would transform the practice of law — in a very, it's like now even cringey to say it, but in a very AI-pilled way. They're like: we will do enormously complex work with lawyers. I don't know when — could be next year or five years from now. But from the kernel of "I can look at a landlord-tenant agreement in California and answer a question" — somewhat trivial — to "I can project to doing an Activision Blizzard M&A and doing 85% of the work" — that's a leap.

The thing that appealed to me in that moment was the ambition of what was possible then, and the technical logic of why it would work.

[Sponsor break — Ramp / Felix by Rogo / WorkOS]

RAMP is the only platform built to make your finance team leaner, faster, and better — saving businesses 5% annually on average so you can stay focused on growth. Ramp customers grow revenue 3.2 times faster than the average American business. Visa, Vercel, Cursor, Stripe, Notion, 11 Labs, Shopify, and 70,000 other businesses all now run on Ramp. Learn more at ramp.com/invest.

Felix by Rogo is a personal finance agent that turns a single prompt into finished client-ready work using your firm's own templates, context, and standards. Send Felix an email like: "Take these comments and turn them for me," or "Update my tracker with the context of these emails." Felix sends back finished PowerPoint decks, Excel models, and sourced research. Learn more at rogo.ai/felix.

OpenAI, Cursor, Anthropic, Perplexity, and Vercel all use WorkOS. To achieve enterprise adoption at scale, you have to deliver on core capabilities like SSO, SCIM, RBAC, and audit logs. Instead of spending months building these yourself, you can just use WorkOS APIs. Visit workos.com to get started.

前沿实验室里的气氛：递归自我改进与"我不再重要"的感觉

What is that group of 250 researchers talking about today? What's the most interesting thing, and the most notable difference between today and 6 months ago or 12 months ago?

It is a violently competitive landscape. That was true 12 months ago, but even more true than it was 24 and 36 months ago. People are very concerned that it is a globally competitive landscape, and there's insecurity in that because it's a bit narrative-breaking as well.

I'm going to describe a belief and then question the belief. The belief is: with recursive self-improvement of AI research models that can improve the models themselves, we are a year, two years away from some sort of exponential intelligence.

I think that belief is new within the last 12 months for a lot of researchers. Smarter people than me — Andrej Karpathy — will actually in a very self-aware way say: I've thought it was two years away for about 10 years. And he thinks it again, to be fair. But who can say?

I do think that the major labs are so compute-intensive and so large from a headcount perspective now, that the sense of contribution — "I can move the needle" — you know, if OpenAI is 200 people and there's not that many researchers, then the question of how do we get there is really up to every single person. Now if the question is: I need 750 billion dollars of compute spend, and we have many thousands of people working on this problem — I think people feel less ownership of the outcome.

Oh that's interesting. So it's just a function of getting compute — like that's the thing that's going to push this over the line, not our own human efforts.

I definitely think there's a large contingent of researchers who would feel one of two things is now true: (1) what I do doesn't matter anyway because the model is going to do it, or (2) the only thing that matters is compute scale. Both of those are somewhat disempowering.

So then what are they doing? If I believe both of those and I'm a top-five researcher?

That says something about your psychology — because you want to do something that matters. I think there's also a set of scientists who like the thing whether or not it matters that they're working on it.

An entrepreneur asked me yesterday: "Would any of the companies you backed not have been backed without you at that round? Would people have just said no?" A couple of them, 5% 10% max. They're resourceful, really talented people; they find other investors. But you know, maybe they wouldn't have gone the next hundred million dollars of compute.

I don't think every researcher doing frontier work at these top couple labs right now feels like they're essential to the machine.

最让她担心的：不是技术，是许可与对齐

What worries you most?

Compute is one — people understand that very well. The version of us having enough compute over the next 5 to 10 years. People are very much thinking about 2032 at this point at scale. I was talking to the leader for infrastructure at one of the hyperscalers earlier in the week, and he's like: there was nothing that is going to move the needle for us at sufficient scale before 2030. I was like — oh, that's depressing. It's just: where can we get sufficient natural gas?

Americans and entrepreneurs have been able to build new technologies and new capabilities very, very quickly in the past, and I don't think it is a technology or capability or capitalism problem. I think it is a regulatory problem and an alignment problem — and I don't mean AI alignment. If you want to build data centers in New York, you need to convince the people of New York they should want data centers there. If you want to make the price of nuclear competitive as baseload power, you need to convince people it's safe, and you need to allow enough construction — in order for the price to come down.

I don't think we lack the technical and entrepreneurial capability to build abundant cheap energy for the data centers.

The physical supply chain — that's a tough reality. It makes me worried that the learning to build things, the tacit knowledge and the labor and the raw materials — that can't go as fast as software or even decision-making. But the only way through that is through. We just have to invest in it.

On the investing side — what worries me: I was talking to several of our founders who are researchers, and explaining that the quality of their storytelling and their ability to make the company's bets legible to investors is obviously very important to their success, if it's going to be a capex-intensive play up front. The reality of the financial landscape for all of these people is: I'm not a research scientist, you're not a research scientist, and all of the capital is not research scientists.

There's a lot of proxying of judgment to pedigree or to other legible signals — like who's invested, what the references are, who are the referral sources. So the decision-making is less fundamental.

I asked an extraordinarily good investor friend — we had a debate — like: I don't understand, what is this company going to be that would be big? Explain it to me. And his explanation was essentially: "Do you know the quality of this person?" I'm like: yes, I've known the quality of the person for eight years. But the technical theory in the business doesn't make sense to me.

People are making large-scale research bets without any intuition for them or without any opinion on them. And I'm like: it's not all going to work. I may not be any better at deciding, but we want to get to that intuition. Not having a point of view on the business besides the pedigree of the person is very dangerous.

一位让她眼前一亮的研究者：Tony Zhao 与 Sunday Robotics

Who is a researcher that has most kind of blown you away, and how did they do so?

My partner Pranav and I were introduced to Tony Zhao and Cheng Chi at Sunday Robotics when they were PhD students at Stanford. They had worked at Toyota Research and DeepMind and Tesla, so they weren't just academics by any means. They were young PhD students — I think they're like 25. I think one of them didn't finish; they just started the company.

What I thought was impressive about them then and now — I remember looking at their body of work, and I was just like: I think, took me a while to get oriented, but I think that they have contributed dual-handedly more, most of the interesting ideas in robotics AI over the last four years. That's a pretty weird thing for two very young people to do.

If I try to characterize the type of ideas: it is "how can I use modern AI to solve the robotics generalization and robustness problem in a very practical way." It is believed in robotics that if we just had the internet of robotics data, we'd have fully general robots everywhere. So one of the big research and practical problems is: where do you get that data?

Some of the ideas Tony and Cheng have worked on: how can you be clever about collecting the data in the cheapest way possible, in a way that supports the distribution of real-world environments and tasks? The creativity of thinking about the actual constraints — we don't have the data, we don't have infinite dollars to spend on the data, and we're going to treat it as a technical problem: what is the shape of the data and the collection, how does it interact with the model, how much of this cheap data collection can we transfer to model learning — that's super interesting, very outcomes-driven.

I was blown away in the first meeting. We said yes immediately, thankfully. Just under two years that the company has been around. Nothing is true until it is shipped, but this entire team believes that we are going to have general semi-humanoid robot thoughts doing things in people's homes — first, in beta, end of this year.

That is not something that any of us believed. It blows me away that you can move that quickly from a bunch of cardboard in a Stanford basement to: we built the full-stack thing. It is manufactured here. We have done hundreds of iterations of hardware on model data collection, and translated it into tasks, and tested in all these real-world environments — and it's going to work.

房间里的决策过程：从"8分或9分"往回倒推

I'm very curious about the moments of your investment decisions. Is it always like that — first meeting, we're in — or are there examples where you hem and haw?

I'm very instinctive on people. I often know I want to do something immediately. If I know what somebody has worked on, then I interact with them and I hear the idea and I have some basis in the idea, then — we have a rating scale of 1 to 10, and I'm immediately an 8 or a 9.

What I'm then doing between that and a real decision is often figuring out: what are the holes in my understanding? Where's my judgment of their premise or of them incomplete or wrong? Because if you're an investor looking for the most ambitious, impactful companies, you can't know every domain. We have biology and defense and robotics and law. So I'm spending the next day to few weeks desperately trying to ground myself and asking: what does everybody else believe about this space? And are they the people I think they are?

That's what my process looks like. Then I want to get feedback. I want to get second reads on people. I want to understand what the core questions are. I'm a memo person — even at the very beginning of the firm, when it was just me, I would write the full memo, perhaps Greylock style, and ship it off to a friend who was an investor and whom I trusted, for their perspective outside of the fund.

Other people are more even in their decision-making. They're thinking about it and thinking about it, and then they climb to conviction — versus I kind of start there and then work backwards.

A similarity between both Mike and I: we'll start at a point and explain what will move us. I met a really interesting company earlier this week with my partner Bella, and — instinctively I'm positive on it, but I don't know enough about the science here, and I have to go make sure this makes sense. Can you really be an 8 or a 9 if you don't get it? No. So that's what I'm — I could get there.

If Brett Taylor wanted to dig in volcanoes or do dog streaming or something, I'd be like: yeah, of course, man. But — he wouldn't do that. These things are so inextricably intertwined in my mind. Part of what makes people great — I was trying to help one of my companies with a candidate yesterday, and they're like: "Oh, what did you see in these people?" I'm like: they're just so right. He's right all the time. Their industrial logic is impeccable. They have all these great character traits too. They're amazing at recruiting. But they have a point of view that I think is going to be right in the world, and I've seen them just make repeatedly correct decisions, including when I am wrong. I have a lot of respect for that.

So if I don't understand what they're doing, I can't have an opinion on their judgment.

时间的饼图：2/3 在陪投后公司

If I were to build a pie chart of your time now, what is it?

I spend two-thirds of my time working on portfolio company stuff — recruiting, helping people think through things, trying to influence the outside ecosystem in some way. Then raising money. The next largest piece is looking at companies. I probably see four to six new companies a week — it's not a very high volume. My first couple months at my old firm I saw 500 companies, and so now I feel more calibration — I have much more confidence, I can tell.

Then the balance of my time I am doing a combination of: helping one of my partners look at something; meeting people that might teach me something about the world (that can be a researcher, or — if you are purely early-stage in a larger firm, you can be very myopic because your ecosystem is big enough; we are a very small firm, we're very ecosystem-oriented, and so I've learned so much from just getting to know investors who think differently than I do, including different asset classes). I never spent that much time with public-markets people before, and it is very educational how they think about the world.

I spend time with companies — right now with a pharma company who is thinking about how AI is going to transform their business. This is very interesting to me because I've learned a lot about what they believe about the future. I'm doing a lot, but I'm leaving room in my calendar for just learning, feeding curiosity, and then — external communication, bridges to DC.

关于募资：不要告诉 LP 他们想听的话

What have you learned about raising money?

I stand with the belief that I advise entrepreneurs with — you should understand people's objections to what you are doing and their questions, but you should not tell them what they want to hear.

When I started the fund raise for fund one, I knew a lot of LPs over a long period of time already, so it was not very complicated. But I had one of my friends who is a private equity investor state: "You have to have a very differentiated story for LPs, and every part of the funnel should be the specific thing you're going to do." And I'm like: let's be honest, I don't know yet, but I need to raise some money so I can go experiment and figure it out.

So I never made slides and told a specific story about all the things that we attempt to do now — because I think you don't know until you make contact with reality. There were definitely LPs who did not like that. I gave people a two-pager on my background and investing history and claimed that I was good at identifying extraordinary people and then good at being useful to that set of people and being a genuine supporter. If you combine that with investment judgment and ability to recruit, you've got a starting point. I mostly said: here's some things I imagine about firm culture, and then we'll go execute like hell and figure it out.

I can see how this is tough from an LP perspective, and I deeply value the people who bet on us early — because they go write a memo for their investment committee, and they're like: "She's going to execute like hell. We'll find out." Sometimes the cleanliness of the story is what people are looking for.

For me as an investor, when somebody can convince me that the world works differently than I thought, I'm immediately incredibly excited. So maybe I can convince people that this is just how it actually works.

I've met a lot more investment managers over the last four years than — I knew a lot of VCs, but people who are doing creative things — I really like entrepreneurial investment managers, as you do. Not that I want to build the firms that they've built, but the creativity with which Philippe and Thomas Cotto, or Josh at Thrive, approach their business — and the encouragement they have for others to approach their business with "well, you can do new things and you should go express your opinions in the form of your investment management firm" — I think is amazing.

父母的印记：独立思考是道德问题

What was imprinted on you watching your parents, who were both entrepreneurs?

This is very helpful to me — because there was no moment of my childhood or being a teenager where I felt like they were not there for me, even though they worked all the time, both of them. If you try to resolve these things: one is like, well, I was a pretty independent kid, that helps.

It helps me to think: your family can make you feel like you are the center of their world, but they're whole people with other interests and they want to spend time doing other things too.

Our family values are very similar to theirs. There's integrity, thinking for yourself, independence of thought, and then there's focus and family, team spirit. The independence of thought is probably the least generic one of those. A lot of people want to be good and kind and work hard and whatever else. But for both my parents, it was a moral issue. They were like: you cannot ever worry about what other people think.

I'm probably far too that side of the spectrum, but I do think about it sometimes.

You do sometimes worry what other people think. What do you worry they think that you don't want them to?

I worry about raising people's competitive hackles in the ecosystem.

Why?

Because I'm a friendly person. I want to be friends with everybody. I don't mind competition, but the sometimes pure zero-sum competition stance of traditional Series A / Series B firms that says "I'm going to own 18 to 25% of this company and take the board and you're going to own none of it" — is not conducive to a lot of collaboration. There are issues with that from an incentives perspective.

The public-markets-like orientation is: people love to tell you about their best ideas so you'll pile in after them. And I'm like — this is an extraordinary situation. I would love to talk about why gaming and entertainment is going to be totally different and people are super underexed on it. There's part of that orientation that just appeals to me as a very positive-sum person.

灵感的来源与那种"愤世嫉俗的毒药"

Overall in your life, who has inspired you the most? And right now in this moment, who is inspiring you the most, and why?

I saw my parents build a company. I was like: this is so cool. It's us against the man, and the man is very big companies. The man's trying to kill us, and we can still do it just because the technology is better, the product is better, the customer will want it. My love and ethos goes to entrepreneurs, because — okay, you can make something out of nothing because you see a better future, and you can do it really fast. These things appeal to me in terms of what I want to try. There's so much courage in that, and optimism.

There is something poisonous that bothers me today, where — especially the post-Gen-Z entrepreneurial crowd — think it's all marketing, and brand is real, and building a network is totally real. No one denies that. But when folks are very cynical about how the world works, how entrepreneurship works — like that it's just nepotism, and Twitter is useful — I think that's nonsense.

If you focus on value and treating people well, and you work with extraordinary people and the vision is worthwhile, that works more times than you'd think. There's so much cynicism about playing the game, be it marketing or fundraising, and I hate that.

I'm inspired by — Pat is like this, I find him very inspiring. And Tuhin is like this, I find him very inspiring — where he's just like: if we just do the right thing by the customer, we will win. And I'm like: feels a lot more complicated than that. But he's right. That seems to be working.

关于开源模型与中国：猫已出袋

One of the huge debates right now is what to do about the fact that there are open-source models — not American-made — which are competitive at the frontier of performance, and seem to clearly have been at least to some degree based on the work of American models. What to do about this?

There's my point of view on what is healthy for businesses, America, the ecosystem, individuals — and then there's what's already actually happened.

The reality: we have over the last three years increasingly competitive open-source models from all fronts, largely China, but also the US and Europe. Most recently, ThinkyMachines, Poolside, people waiting for Reflection, Nvidia's models. We will have very powerful — and already do have very powerful — open-source models from Western countries.

So the cat is out of the bag, and these are in use everywhere. Even if you have no economic point of view on the labs — how is the diffusion of capability going to happen in the economy? There are a huge number of instances where it is too expensive, too sensitive, or too slow to use the model from the frontier providers today. And I think that's going to increase as we learn how to do more things with AI, because it's actually quite expensive. So it's objectively true that if the capabilities are more democratized, you will see them used in more ways. And I want to see that happen.

It would be irresponsible not to understand the safety profile of models as they progress — you just draw the line. We have companies that use frontier model capability for defensive cybersecurity and for biology work. If it works for those use cases, it obviously also should work in similar ways for the offensive use cases or the bioweapons / biosecurity use cases. We just need to look at that reality and think about what are the other ways in which you control this. But attempting to stop technological progress and openness around it — if you did restrict use of open-source models in the United States, you'd basically just restrict law-abiding American businesses and slow them down or move profits to different pockets, prevent certain uses of them, because the actual attackers or people who have adversarial uses of these things are not affected by your restrictions.

My view: there should be testing and understanding of these models at the frontier. People are very worried about backdoor-like behaviors in Chinese models — well, the thing to do would be to have a very rigorous set of safety testing on that. Let's go find out as much as we can, instead of talking about how there might be this issue in a speculative way. We can do it — it's not trivial, but we can do it.

The future where there is broad access to intelligence too cheap to meter, as Sam put it — that is coming. It will be supported by open source. Businesses want it to control their own destiny, for economics, for capacity. Given those models and the increasing democratization of the skills to post-train these models, build harnesses, use tasks — that's how you're going to get it into the economy. The economy is so big; every individual has these use cases that are not going to be imagined by a researcher in a frontier lab. You can't imagine the diversity of reality. Even if you trusted the models to go figure out what to do, they have to get there. And I think the best way for that to happen is an ecosystem of businesses, as we've always had in the economy, and cheap infrastructure.

计算的独立性：智能的能源政策

Do you ever worry that there's an alternate version of US history where energy was too cheap to meter because we built a thousand AP1000s, much like China is doing now in nuclear, and just a set of circumstances happened such that we didn't get that? Do you ever worry about that as it relates to intelligence?

Yes, absolutely. I can imagine very easily a world where we don't have that in a competitive way — because it is essential to economic competitiveness and national security.

Let me posit: there is not a version of the world where we rebuild our industrial base without automation in the United States. If we don't import people and our people are expensive and we lack some of the skills but want to produce a lot more goods and have a more resilient supply chain — it just doesn't add up. People in the United States do not want to work — and should not want to work — for $13 an hour doing a very inhuman job.

I don't think it is inevitable that we are competitive, and I think we need to actively make that decision. The version of it that I think is very possible is that people are very rationally afraid of the impact of AI on jobs, or dislike the capture of rent by a small number of technology firms, and rejecting the idea of being in the permanent underclass — and then connecting that to an anti-capitalist orientation. That contingent of thought can slow down build of energy and infrastructure and industrial capacity. And one of the most important inputs is compute. If we don't have it, we're naturally not competitive, or we're at least not independent. I think we're going to start talking much more about compute independence.

[Sponsor break — Vanta / Ridgeline]

Vanta automates security and compliance for over 16,000 fast-moving companies like Ramp, Cursor, and Harvey, keeping them audit-ready around the clock. It's the number one Agentic Trust platform. The Vanta agent works like a 24/7 GRC engineer in the background, finding issues, drafting fixes for you, and cutting vendor assessment time by up to 50%. Invest Like the Best listeners get a special offer for $1,000 off at vanta.com/invest.

Ridgeline is the first end-to-end system of record with embedded AI for investment management firms — running portfolio accounting, reconciliation, reporting, trading, and compliance on one unified platform. Firms are moving off legacy technology and onto Ridgeline because of how far ahead Ridgeline's AI features are compared to anything else in investment management software. Request a demo at ridgeline.ai.

拆解"计算独立"：它像能源独立

What are the missing pieces of compute independence?

If you just work backwards from a data center full of GPUs — cooling, powering, training, and inference so we can support the use cases — all of those inputs. It actually looks a great deal like energy independence. There is a global supply chain. There are parts of it — I've got my TSMC mug with me — parts of that supply chain that are like a very thin sieve, in a place that is not necessarily stable or accessible to the US and allies.

A different version of the world — that will take a bunch of investment and national security and energy policy — for example, Jacob Helberg is working on something called PACIA: for every part of the supply chain, can we invest in more capacity and figure out what the independent paths are? I don't think it all has to be created in the United States — comparative advantage is real. But having more than one source is a position that everybody wants to be in.

When we think about the components we've invested in: we've invested in the labor gap for data centers and robotics, we've invested in nuclear energy, we've invested in alternative chip architectures. We keep looking at people who are essentially data center builders, solar and battery installers of some kind — because part of this is the actual capacity buildup. But that's a very operational business, somewhere between operations, some technology, and real estate, and financing. Financing is probably the dominant thing.

We have not invested in it yet, despite looking very closely. I'm not opposed to it, but fundamentally I'm a technology investor — I want to understand what is the durable product asset people are building.

团队内部的辩论：市场是否配得上风险资本？

What are the biggest debates inside of Conviction?

A lot. I have a podcast called No Priors, and this premise of "some of the things you believed, especially about markets as a past, are no longer true" is an interesting one.

Regularly we look at companies in domains that are not traditional software domains — like: can you make money in this market at all? Venture investing in semis companies — Lip-Bu Tan aside — was a god-awful business for the longest time. The returns were really bad. But now I think we have arrived at the conclusion — that others are as well — which is: the market is different today. We are seeing consolidated at-scale demand for accelerators, or supply chain independence, because the big buyers of it want it too. We can't all be stuck on one line at TSMC. All of that is very, very valuable, and that changes the risk equation for these companies.

So we start with pretty aligned beliefs about the direction of travel or the problems that are worth working on. Then a lot of the debates are: is the market friendly to a venture-backed company or not? Space is not a friendly market to a venture-backed company, but is possible — and is the distribution of outcomes worth betting on? That could be true in solar and batteries and nuclear, in turbine manufacturing, in robotics and biology. These are not your favorite software markets from 10 years ago.

Biology is an interesting one where, by virtue of seeing the data empirically, I have now strongly moved to one side of the debate.

What side is that?

You can create and capture enormous value with models in biology.

There could be different AI software in biology. We're the first check in a company called Chai Discovery. Chai is working with a number of top-10 pharma companies in really significant ways to accelerate some part of the R&D process. The conventional wisdom when we invested in this company — and I'd been looking at computational biology companies for five-plus years at that point — was: the only way you make money in biotech, or serving pharma, is by making a drug. Get bio deals and then decide how far along that risk path you want to take. What that means for the capital structure is: the great traditional biotech firms find these principal investigators and own 40% of the company, and are assembling these things into candidates. But most of it doesn't work. So it's a very different distribution of outcomes and structure and way to invest in businesses. Dumb software investors — "you can't make money selling software to pharma, or build platform businesses in pharma."

The debate is: does it change with models? I'm a strong yes now. We still have a question to solve on regulatory, and the speed of the physical world — safety is not something you can overcome easily. But I think we should see a massive acceleration in cures, and part of the value creation will come from young companies. We are excited to invest in them.

What flipped that for you?

We invested when we didn't know yet.

Understood.

That's part of the fun adventure. We were like: it is possible and it is worth trying. There's no genius here. That's a $10 million contract, you know. The other piece: you just talk to the scientist at the customer, or somebody who leads a tool, a user of the tool. Or you see they're also enduser-adopted tools — product-led-growth tools that are working in the space. The customer knows if it's valuable or not.

The light-bulb moment for the industry is when we will have a new indication or a new drug that clearly the trajectory of the thing was changed, created by AI. Then I think we should see a huge wave of investment — and rightfully so. But it's going to happen. I'm very impressed by the speed with which pharma and healthcare overall has said: yes, this is going to make a difference, and we actually think it's going to change the business.

为什么叫 "Conviction"（信念）

Why'd you call it Conviction?

It's aspirational. The most traditional form of early-stage investing is: you start early with a company, you have a significant position, you never sell the position, and you work on the company until it works or a soldier dies. There's wonderful alignment and simplicity to that.

Mike and I have both had the benefit of being part of the journey for some companies where it took a minute to begin to work, or it's not obvious at the beginning. Figma, Notion, Rippling — you wouldn't bet on a company hoping that it's going to take four or five years to find the thing. Everybody is a product of their own experiences, including investing experiences. The first couple years at Base10 were very non-obvious as well.

So the ability to take a point of view that is not obvious in the market — because of the market, or people's backgrounds, or whatever reason — and then just suspend doubt and act with full belief until it's true or not: I feel like that's a great way to be a partner to somebody building a business. I'm trying to build a partnership.

I deeply believe in this as a team sport, but — I was talking to a friend who runs another investing firm, and he's like: "We don't have individual ownership of our investments." And I'm like: that is nonsense to me. How could you run a business that way? Because somebody has to own the decision. I don't know if this is right or wrong, but I don't know any other way to invest by saying: "Patrick, you must make the decision. Do you believe? Convince us. How can we help you make that decision?" All inputs to a single person.

承担风险与"寻找真相"

What have you learned about risk-taking and behind conviction? Is there always a leap of faith?

Unlike my good friends at Founders Fund, I don't have an instinct to be contrarian. But I do think it is so fundamental to decide what you think, and not worry too much about what other people think — "other people" being the dominant narratives of the period, or even different players in the ecosystem that are really important, declaring one way or another.

I think you just need to find the truth. If you find the truth, and it is wrongly priced, and you hold on to that — you're in a good position. You want asymmetric information and then the confidence to hold the opinion when other people haven't come around to it yet. I think a lot about how to make sure we have the information that is better than other people's, and then protect ourselves from noise.

What are the keys to doing those two things?

I want to spend my time — when I'm learning about the world — with somebody who is making it happen. Our portfolio founders, or the many founders who are doing amazing things outside of the portfolio, who are doing something that surprises me or advances their frontier, or really smart people who believe something I don't. Three different categories.

An example: Mikey Shulman at Suno is building an amazing business doing music generation. And shame on me — I knew Mikey; a mutual friend of ours, who was an investor, asked me to invest, and I stupidly said no. I was just like: ah, I don't think that many people want to make music. I make music. Can you turn it into a social network? How much consumption is there going to be? A lot of questions. My intuition has been actually somewhat wrong, because I have underestimated the amount of expression or entertainment and creation for a lot of AI tools. I'm like: oh, I've learned something here, by talking to Mikey about his business and what people are trying to do.

If it is founders who have companies creating a behavior you don't understand, somebody working on research in an interesting direction, businesses that are like "here's my plan for AI" — all that is super educational.

The circular logic sometimes of "what do people believe about the big-lab strategy today, and how can any of the applications live" — it's actually not that instructive for your decision-making. Any organization has a couple of key priorities. Let's assume the priority for OpenAI and Anthropic and DeepMind is AGI, or ASI in a safe way, where they capture a lot of profit. The priorities that ladder into that probably look like ChatGPT, ads, coding — and then maybe there's an expansion after that. Co-work, the ability to get different types of users to do richer tasks in more interfaces.

I think you have to judge the actual competitiveness of any of those efforts, the reasonable scope of them, and then look at them relative to each of our companies or opportunities we're looking at. But coming up with some grand strategic framework for "what layer is going to win here" — I think is not useful to me. People spend so much of their investing energy thinking about that. Versus I want to spend my energy figuring out: if we're 1% of the way in, what is the next 99% of diffusion?

一年后的世界：Jevons 悖论遍地开花

A year from now, what do you think is notably different about the world of technology?

I'm hopeful that a year from now we see Jevons paradox in practice, as we have agents and products that do more of the mundane more effectively in all the domains of our lives. It should look like the transformation that has happened in software engineering. You have companies — I have companies — where they're like: we are just going way faster. And I expect that some analogy like that will happen everywhere else.

We see it in our companies. In one of our portfolio companies, the marketing department is like a person in a house. This is a company that serves lots of customers, and they need to do very traditional things like sales enablement content. What happened was: the guy in charge of marketing is very interested in creating leverage for himself, and he's like — I made an autonomous marketing department for us, the company.

In every function, as you learn faster, do less of the mundane, you will repurpose that time somehow.

Do you work less now that you are more productive with AI?

I work more. This is a core wisdom of Jensen's — we're all going to be more employed. We need to make sure that people are given access and education to the tooling that will allow that to happen.

结尾：最善意的事

What is the kindest thing that anyone's ever done for you?

I love this question. I'm going to give a collective answer. There are so many people who are extraordinarily accomplished in Silicon Valley who care very little for pedigree as soon as they have a conversation with you, and they're like — maybe you can help me, or you have an interesting idea, or maybe I just think you're promising. And the dominant factor in their own willingness to invest in a relationship or a person is just their assessment of the idea in the person. I think that's amazing. That is not how most ecosystems work.

Aashim Chandran, and Anil Buster, and Joseph Ansanelli, and Reid Hoffman, who hired me at Greylock — I started when I was 23. People love to make fun of young VCs where they're like: "Ah, what a barnacle on the ecosystem. This is a terrible experience for entrepreneurs. They don't know anything. They're trying to advise people. Who gave this kid money?" And I'm like: well, one, my job was just to make other people successful at the time. Learn — and you can take any task in any job and just try to be great at that task, with mimicry and first-principles thinking.

We hire earlier-career people at my firm. But — oh my goodness — thank you for taking a shot on some random person, and then investing the time to teach me how to be an investor.

There were a few people who gave me advice starting the firm, who I think would think of this as entirely trivial — because they're like, I'm just giving you my opinion. But Ravi Gupta, who's now co-CEO of a new thing called Ithaca; Dylan Field and Elena Natalinsky; John Lily, who's been a longtime partner and friend — there were a few folks who were just like: you can definitely do it. I was going to do it either way, but having the encouragement of people who believed that there was room to be great — and including some of our first LPs — I will be forever grateful to the people who took risk with me.

It's beautiful. The world runs on faith — belief without evidence yet — and still, conviction in someone's ability to do something. Pretty cool.

And I think it's faith in people. We talked a lot about how people's ideas and our opinions of them are intertwined — but I think that's a beautiful thing, because you don't need any particular advantage to have an idea. So the fact that folks will evaluate that and put faith in us — I could not be more grateful.

I've learned a lot watching you operate and talking to you. This has been really fun.

Thanks for having me. Thanks.

[Closing sponsor reads]

Ramp — see how at ramp.com/invest. Vanta — vanta.com/invest. WorkOS — workos.com. Ridgeline — ridgelineapps.com. Rogo — rogo.ai/invest.

item.description:
## 一个反直觉的观察：规模正在杀死大实验室的"主体感"
访谈中最令人意外的一段藏在中间——Sarah 指出，OpenAI 从 200 人扩张、Anthropic 迈向数千人、单次训练需要 7500 亿美元资本时，**研究员正在集体失去"我在推动历史"的感觉**。两种情绪在顶级实验室的走廊里蔓延："反正模型会自己搞定"、"反正只有算力才重要"。
这里有一个诡异的悖论：**AI 越强大，实验室越庞大，个体研究者的能动感越低**。这不是 Jevons 悖论——这是它的镜像双胞胎。当访谈末尾她乐观地援引 Jensen 的 Jevons 论断（更高效意味着更多就业）时，其实无意间揭示了一个隐藏张力：**在应用侧，AI 会创造无限杠杆感；但在前沿侧，AI 正在制造前所未有的"齿轮化"体验**。这也解释了为什么她的整个投资策略成立——顶尖研究员流出前沿实验室、加入小团队，恰恰是"规模的诅咒"在为她供货。她的基金不是在与大实验室竞争，而是在收割它们的"心理副产品"。
## 跨领域连接：她其实在复刻 20 世纪的"哥本哈根学派"模型
Sarah 和 Mike 反复提到的 "250 个人在推动前

item.content:encoded:
💡 创造性洞见

一、反网络效应的悖论：Peragrine 是一家"故意反规模"的规模化公司

大多数数据公司的护城河建立在"数据越多越值钱"的飞轮上——Flock、Axon 都是如此。但 Peragrine 走的是一条几乎在商业教科书上被判死刑的路径：他们明确不拥有数据、不聚合数据、不让数据跨客户流动。Nick 甚至发明了一个我在硅谷从未听过的说法——"anti-network effects business"（反网络效应型企业）。

真正让人意外的是：这种"反网络效应"本身反而构成了一种更高维度的网络效应。因为城市之间会互相打电话咨询，警长会问同行"你们用什么"，正是"数据不出本地"这种自我克制的姿态，成了 Peragrine 在保守型公共机构之间口碑传播的加速器。信任本身成了他们的分布式协议。

这与比特币的哲学惊人相似：主权在边缘、共识在中心。Peragrine 本质上是在为美国的公共安全部门搭建一个"去中心化的智能层"，其内在结构比它自我描述的"平台公司"更接近一个联邦制协议。

二、"洞穴与绳索"的组织隐喻：他们把 FDE 当作生物神经的末梢，而非成本中心

Nick 用了一个非常生动的比喻——"我们把人送进黑暗的洞穴里，给他一个工具带，洞口有条绳子拴着一个朋友"。这不只是管理风格，这是神经系统的架构选择。

大多数公司把 Forward Deployed Engineer 当作"实施顾问"或"成本中心"，Peragrine 把 FDE 当作公司的感觉神经元：产品的所有 primitives 都从最远端的"疼痛信号"倒推回来。有个例子极具象征意义——某个 FDE 因为平台不能编辑字段，就用"评论"字段 hack 出了编辑功能。管理层看到后不是骂他"绕过流程"，而是把这个"绕路"作为下一版产品的路标。

这里藏着一个跨领域的深刻连接：这与章鱼的神经系统结构惊人相似。章鱼三分之二的神经元不在大脑里，而在八条腕足上——每条腕足都能自主决策、局部感知、独立行动，中央大脑只负责协调。Peragrine 的 FDE 组织模式就是"章鱼式公司"：最重要的智能不在总部，而在客户现场。这解释了为什么他们能在 Palantir 都嫌小的市场里活下来——传统"脊椎动物公司"的信号传导太慢、太贵。

三、最出人意料的洞察：他们真正在贩卖的不是 AI，而是"官僚系统的谦卑"

表面上看，Peragrine 是一家把 AI 卖给市政厅的公司。但如果你仔细听 Nick 反复强调的东西——"放下自我"、"悬置聪明"、"当安静的专业人士"、"不抢功劳"、"这是客户的胜利不是我们的"——你会发现他们真正的产品是一种稀缺的组织气质。

在 AI 泡沫最狂热的时刻，硅谷所有人都在争夺"技术叙事的所有权"，Peragrine 却把自己定义为"institutional memory layer"（机构记忆层）——一个明确愿意消失在客户功劳簿背后的基础设施。这是一种反向的品牌策略：通过刻意不发光来发光。

更深一层的悖论是：AI 越强大，谦卑就越是稀缺资源。当模型可以自动完成 90% 的数据集成、可以运行数小时的自主 agent、可以颠覆整个冷案侦查流程时——真正决定一个 AI 公司能否长期活下去的，反而是它是否愿意主动放弃技术给予它的话语权。

这与日本茶道中"侘寂"（wabi-sabi）美学、以及禅宗"减法"哲学有惊人的同构性：在一个所有人都在加乘的时代，敢于做减法本身就是一种战略护城河。Peragrine 用"减法"换来了那些不信任 Palantir、也不信任 Flock 的城市——而这些城市恰好是美国的绝大多数。这可能是硅谷十年内第一个真正"东方式"的公司结构。

Now we're using this in a in a few departments across uh the US. We recently were working in a county in Wisconsin where uh this again similar type of case 300 gigabytes of data and they were able to identify and place a a the suspect at not just the scene of the crime but where the body was found. And this was a single there's about a few cell records cell call detail records kind of ping of a phone that was scattered amongst

Yeah.

a lot of data. And so this this I this was really interesting to me and I think points to this area where we could really uplevel and help our our you know public servants unburden them with all this administrative watching hours and hours and hours of video and listening to hours and hours of audio.

十、"安静的专业者"与 AI 信任危机

As a quick comment this this example Ben brought up is so impactful to the organization as a culture for our business. We have the way that we maintain trust is not actually taking credit and shouting from the rooftops about the awesomeness of of of what happened here. Um I think that is one of the fastest ways to break trust frankly with these organizations.

The idea that you know we're going to scoop up the work and trumpet our skill and the way that we impacted the world. Uh so I think being the quiet professionals in a context like this um and empowering the the customer is why we have access to the next problem.

I wish you would talk about it more though because I think that we're in this moment where public distrust in AI is so high.

Yeah.

And this is a wonderful story, right? I think that coming back to an earlier example of um uh you know trying to identify threats to a synagogue um uh I think about network effects and I think about um what motivates us to tell our story.

Um I um I think the convergence of this idea of a kind of a a centralized authoritarian like AI capability and surveillance uh in American uh or or you know national society. The convergence of these forces has created this immense pressure and and I think distrust um in in many of the the the organizations and and frankly the communities that that we work with.

Um I that can't be ignored first of all.

反网络效应命题

Um and I I think if we look at the the organizations we work with and also the data landscape, the network effects are there and they are unbelievably strong.

Like for example, it would be very easy for an organization that's trying to kind of hack their way to building something useful to go and hit open source and pull in data that they might not — there might be a gray zone on whether they can or should access that based on laws, regulations, ordinances, standard operating procedures of of the department.

And for us, like we have to protect against those moments where the it's not like we don't need to we don't need to break the rules, nor obviously should any organization break the rules in order to find a way to like introduce AI or technology into these complex environments. The opposite is true.

We have to protect the data, right? And we have to protect these organizations that by virtue of their structure have astounding network effects, right? It's almost like the anti-network effect proposition. Like you how do you preserve the sanctity of the data and the ownership of the data and the ways of working for every individual agency, every individual organization — and then building the connective tissue, building the interoperability is going to happen.

But and this is where things that might sometimes seem mundane but we find really fascinating like how do you think through data governance? How do you think through permissioning logic in the context of AI become unbelievably important?

Um so I'm feel really motivated uh to talk about that in particular.

Peragrine the anti-network effects business.

Um, I think it's important, especially given the heat now around AI is so powerful and so a lot of this data that used to exist, I think people now fear what what happens when it's all swooped up into a central panopticon. That's deeply unamerican.

Yeah. Yeah. Yeah.

Um, yeah. Yeah. And I think that as a business, it's like I find that our business is a big practice in letting go. It's how do we build high integrity, transparent solutions for our customers? How do we make that transparent to our customers and their constituents?

Um and then how do we effectively let let go and not try to um grow too fast?

十一、道德抉择：面部识别与"客户即北极星"

Are there technology decisions that you have to make that are morally nuanced? So, for example, facial recognition. I'm curious your stance on that. And then more generally, what what is your north star for hard decisions?

Yeah, quickly on facial recognition. Um I I think the idea of like a Silicon Valley company imposing um a decision uh that is kind of general purpose for an industry is fundamentally wrong.

I think the idea that we as an institution would assert whether it be you know the utilization of a technology or a retention policy I mean it's um it's it's very much not how we we think.

Um for instead uh the idea is to to help a customer understand the context in which they're operating and actually bring to light all of the considerations they may or may not know and then help them — and this requires patience — help usher in the right way of doing business, the right way of thinking about deploying these technologies on facial rec.

Most public safety agencies in America and their communities choose not to implement facial recognition. Um some take a very strong stand and and some are are uh uh it's it's just a you know a matter of like subjective preference that they'll assert.

Um but uh um the idea of creating you know a technological um red line uh without understanding the texture and context is is not not a boundary line that we think that we can assert on top of our customer.

So follow the customer, follow the law.

Yeah.

And and expose it and and and create clarity around, you know, what leftright limits and and what what the institutional norms may be.

What I mean it's astounding how cities call each other, right? They call each other for advice. And so if you really just listen to the way that people learn inside of the industries that we serve, what we realize is um helping them streamline the way that they can get the best possible information so they can make their best decision even about things like what technologies to use or not goes a really long way.

十二、服务"弱势方"：把技术送到市政小机构

Maybe in a similar vein, I want to talk about delivering technology to the underdogs and how you're able to scale this very deep customer motion into a very different customer base than, you know, the other company that notoriously has scaled this motion, Palantir, which notoriously doesn't take anything less than eight figure contracts.

Did your mentors try to convince you not to do this? Did people tell you like the economics of this are not going to scale? And what made you think it was going to be possible to deliver technology to the underdogs and serve them in this way?

I think it takes confidence. I think it takes confidence to to believe that if you build something well, you can solve problems that have never been solved before that will scale later.

And the idea of going deep to build a a vertically integrated tech stack that everything from network access to the permissioning and the governance and the ETL and the pipeline and the ontology and the UX and the APIs. It's a to configure all of that and create a system that's open interoperable and can check these boxes. It it the audacity I think is is is real.

Um and and to build each of those components in a way that's first class, not just a check the box. I mean, it's we were truly thinking about how to deliver these types of technology solutions to an end market that has never been able to use these solutions before, let alone at the price point that we were able to to deliver them.

I think the the uniqueness about Peragrine is for each organization we'll take the time to deliver solutions all the way to the outcome and then we'll own the responsibility with our customers of getting to that outcome which might seem like extremely manual extremely laborious extremely unstable or or unscalable.

And what we found is being able to do that resulted in a technology platform that could show up and do something very different for these organizations and also scale.

十三、Deployment Strategist 的选拔与训练

I've had the chance to talk to a few deployment strategists at Peragrine and they are they're amazing. They're so smart, so humble. They so deeply embody the mission and so I think you guys have selected for and trained a really extraordinary group of people.

How do you do it? What do you look for? What do you what do you what do you interview for? How do you train these people up?

First of all, I mean, I it's it's the great it's the greatest compliment because I and we love our team. When you can build a culture where people are trying really hard and can achieve excellence, it's almost like how could you not create the environmental factors and the the feedback culture, which sometimes isn't easy, right? Sometimes it's it can be really intense.

Ben and I, I would say, you know, we've aligned we've taken tests and we've aligned on some character qualities. One of which is definitely the the pursuit of excellence.

"洞穴与绳索"的组织哲学

I think a lot about these environmental factors of um uh like trusting the individual contributor. It's a very um important thing that we're trying to hold on to.

And to do that with a forward deployed engineer actually to truly do it really requires trust because you we use this analogy of a a dark cave, right? Will will send a person into a cave and they have a tool belt and hopefully the tools are pretty good, right? And and there might be a rope, you know, with a friend at the the entrance of the cave that, you know, if they yell for help, you can you can kind of pull them out.

But truly, we are sending people into these zones and we're saying maintain your integrity like maintain your principles. Here are the tools. Go do good.

And to do that at scale, I really believe requires um institutional trust and and a belief system that innovation actually happens at the farthest fringes of our organization. That the way that our engineering product design organizations are fed absolutely is through that innovation process across the country and and now now across multiple countries with our with our forward deploy team.

Yeah, it's fascinating. So different from when I talk to companies who view forward deployed as a cost center. Uh you guys are it's fundamentally very different talking to you.

Definitely R&D. Definitely R&D and and growth. I mean that we there after we land inside of a customer base, we have these models where we'll we'll do these within customer pilots for all intents and purposes where we'll keep sprinting on additional use cases. And in many ways the you know how we land and then how we expand in in a customer base is fundamentally about um leading from the front through our forward deployed engineers.

十四、FDE 如何驱动产品创新

Have you discovered any new products through this motion?

[clears throat] 100 I mean 100%. It's it's just the whole thing like I think it's [laughter] hard to even separate that.

I mean, I remember walking or walking uh driving uh across the Bay Bridge, San Pablo, typing on the computer and Nick's like, "Okay, we got to get these reports done." And like this is and this is what this detective needs and literally typing as fast as I could to try and code what we needed at the time and when you're — and it wasn't theoretical. It was Aaron Blazale who had an extraordinarily urgent request.

Yeah. And and [laughter] like I feel it. And so it's so hard to separate. Very rarely are we in a room pontificating about you know what to build.

两类产品来源

I I really think about the FD motion and how it impacts products our product in in two ways.

类别一：产品基础原子（Primitives）

One is kind of what are the primitives basic primitives that the technology platform needs and there's a couple of examples of this that I think are are fascinating and reflect the ingu ingenuity of our forward deploy team.

For the longest time in Peragrine, we had no ability to edit specific fields and properties. And so one forward deployed engineer to get around that made an integration based on the comments people would write on these objects and that comment would be read by Peragrine and then update a property and that was the way they implemented editing.

And so we saw that we're like we need to implement [laughter] editing. And by the way, the reason that teammate did that is because our intent was — and and this is the way that the coaching and leading happens — it's like your job is to hit the objective like to hell with the technology.

Yeah.

I mean, our our our job is to build the technologies and the tools that empower you to do higher and higher levels of work, but your job is to achieve.

Yeah. [laughter] And that's what creates these crazy things that might look very unscalable, very hacky, but ultimately are the absolute best signaling network.

It's great signal for what actually works. And it's it's like the quintessential rapid prototyping.

So so that's like category one. You get these these product primitives that you know that you need to provide the team in order to to achieve the objective they're trying to achieve.

类别二：创新实验室

[gasps] I think like category 2 is almost uh what I call like innovation lab where the deployment strategist goes and builds something totally unique that we're probably not going to integrate back into the product just because it's it's such a unique capability specifically for that customer.

And this stuff gets me really excited and I I love watching and seeing what our deployment team builds. Was just looking at one the other day where someone had built a hurricane simulator in Peragrine and I was like, "How did you do that? [laughter] I didn't know you could do that."

And so that was that was really interesting. There was another deployment strategist who built this thing where you could you could it it it integrated a bunch of data from all these different sources, 911 call times, like budgets, and you could place a fire department in in the city and it would give you an estimate on uh how many people that would impact.

Unbelievable.

And she was at the company for a month.

十五、十年愿景：机构记忆层与责任

Maybe last last set of questions. Uh 10 years from now, suppose everything's gone right. Peragrine is the institutional memory layer for 10,000 cities.

Um, I think that's great power that outlasts any one administration and with great power comes great responsibility. How do you think about that?

I think there's the outcome and then I think there's the path to get there.

Um the end game of 10,000 cities um uh I think requires an operating model that is fundamentally um about uh infrastructure — actually it's like we as a technology organization are delivering technology infrastructure that empower these organizations to do with their data as they would like and as they are required to do.

And every city, every jurisdiction I deeply believe is unique and I think the idea of um preserving that uniqueness is actually beautiful.

And so I'm really excited about that. [laughter] Like how do you make how do you make each you know the potpourri of cities make each one more awesome in their unique way?

Um that's cool. Uh the path to get there requires serious integrity, moral compass, core values um not just in words but but in um our ways of working, our actions and that never goes away. It never goes away.

The way that we think about the next marginal customer that we support um requires a level of um handholding and delicacy that candidly I don't think was possible even 5 years ago because the marginal cost of doing what we do to drop it below a million bucks a year I mean it's radical right coming back to the origin stories.

In many ways, you know, supporting state county and city level public safety was — you know there were there are a a lineage of failed business units of major astounding organizations that tried to do it and failed because to deliver these solutions in a way that's tailored at a price point that these organizations can afford was never possible.

And so to drop the to create the efficiency to drop the price by an order orders of magnitude is um has has earned us the right to to try to deliver on what you just said. It's like who are who are we to to think that we hold any power over that? I mean, it's the institution that has the power.

Go make every city awesome.

I love that. [laughter]

结束语

I think you're in a very very serious seat and just in this course of this conversation, it's clear that you're approaching this with with great care and great stewardship. So, thank you for what you do. I think the world needs more examples of AI being used uh to improve lives, to improve communities, and um thank you for what you're doing, and thank you for joining the pod today. Thank you, Sonia.

[music] [music] [music] >> [music]

item.description:
## 一、反网络效应的悖论：Peragrine 是一家"故意反规模"的规模化公司
大多数数据公司的护城河建立在"数据越多越值钱"的飞轮上——Flock、Axon 都是如此。但 Peragrine 走的是一条几乎**在商业教科书上被判死刑**的路径：**他们明确不拥有数据、不聚合数据、不让数据跨客户流动**。Nick 甚至发明了一个我在硅谷从未听过的说法——"anti-network effects business"（反网络效应型企业）。
真正让人意外的是：**这种"反网络效应"本身反而构成了一种更高维度的网络效应**。因为城市之间会互相打电话咨询，警长会问同行"你们用什么"，正是"数据不出本地"这种自我克制的姿态，成了 Peragrine 在保守型公共机构之间口碑传播的加速器。**信任本身成了他们的分布式协议**。
这与比特币的哲学惊人相似：主权在边缘、共识在中心。Peragrine 本质上是在为美国的公共安全部门搭建一个**"去中心化的智能层"**，其内在结构比它自我描述的"平台公司"更接近一个联邦制协议。
## 二、"洞穴与绳索"的组织隐喻：他们把 FDE 当作生物神经的

item.title: [Lex Clips] Most programmers suck - DHH explains | Lex Fridman Podcast Clips
item.dc:creator: Lex Clips
item.content:encoded:
💡 创造性洞见

一、被颠倒的"守门人":从人类审核代码，到代码审核人类

DHH 说的最颠覆的一句话不是"大多数程序员很烂"，而是隐藏在后半段的那个反转——他已经不亲自审 PR 了，是 agent 在替他审 agent 写的 PR。这意味着开源治理的权力结构正在悄悄倒转：过去二十年，"maintainer 的注意力"是开源项目最稀缺的资源，所有贡献者都在竞争这份稀缺；而现在，maintainer 把这份稀缺外包给了机器，自己只保留"审美判断权"——也就是"这个东西该不该存在"。

换句话说，开源社区正在经历一次从劳动密集型协作到品味密集型策展的转型。maintainer 不再是工程师，而更像美术馆的策展人或杂志的主编。

二、意外观察：agent 让"拒绝"变得道德无痛，这才是真正的生产力革命

大多数人关注的是"agent 能写代码"，但 DHH 点出了一个几乎没人谈论的心理学层面——开源维护者最大的隐性成本从来不是写代码，而是拒绝代码时的愧疚感。一个人类花了周末写的 PR，你说"不"，你就在伤害一个真实的人；而一个 agent 写的 PR，"clanker won't mind"。

这跟心理学中的"社会性负债"（social debt） 完美对应：Robert Cialdini 研究过，人类在收到"付出型礼物"后会自动进入互惠模式，即使那个礼物是他们不想要的。开源 maintainer 长期背负的"neuroticism"，本质就是无数次未偿还的社会性负债累积成的情绪债务。agent 之所以是革命性的，不是因为它写代码更快，而是因为它切断了这条互惠回路，让 maintainer 第一次可以"心安理得地拒绝"。

这也解释了一个悖论：为什么这么多开源项目死于 burnout，而不是死于没人贡献？——过多的善意本身就是负担。

三、跨领域连接：这是"手工业 → 工业设计 → 策展"三段论的又一次重演

DHH 描述的这场变化，其实是每一个成熟行业都经历过的"金字塔重构"：

  • 服装业：手工裁缝 → 成衣工业 → 时装设计师（决定"该做什么"，而非"怎么做"）
  • 建筑业：石匠 → 承包商 → 建筑师
  • 电影业：布景师+摄影师 → 制片流水线 → 导演/剪辑师
  • 音乐业：乐手 → 录音棚 → 制作人/DJ

每一次，执行层被工具化后，价值重心都向"审美+方向感"上移。DHH 说的"骨髓（bone marrow）"—— "决定这个东西该做什么，往哪里去" ——就是软件行业的"导演位"正在形成。

而更意外的推论是：未来最有价值的程序员，可能不再是最会写代码的人，而是"读代码品味最好的人"。就像顶级美食评论家自己未必是最好的厨师，但他们决定了哪家餐厅能活下去。开源项目 maintainer 正在变成"代码的米其林评审员"。

四、藏在最后的哲学炸弹

DHH 最后那段"I have seen things you people wouldn't believe"是《银翼杀手》Roy Batty 的临终独白的直接化用。这个引用不是随意的——Roy 是一个被认为"只会模仿人类"的复制人，却在死前证明自己有真正的灵魂。DHH 用这个典故来说 agent 的原创性，是在暗示一个更深的判断：关于"什么是原创"的定义本身，可能才是被 agent 淘汰的东西。

如果一个 idea 好到让 DHH 这种自视甚高的人"humble"，那么"这个 idea 是谁想出来的"这个问题，可能从此变得像"这首诗是笔写的还是键盘敲的"一样无意义。

📝 转录文本

关于"程序员大多很烂"的论断

Lex： Don't you need the wizards to keep a high bar of excellence in the code base?

DHH： 100% you do, which is also something that's always been true about open source, which is the second argument that really grinds me.

I've been running open source projects for 25 years. I have literally looked at the output of thousands, if not tens of thousands of programmers. I feel like I have the statistical basis to assert that most programmers—they suck.

[laughter]

And I don't mean that in the way it sounds. That was why I paused for a hot second here. I mean they suck in the sense that they don't write the code I want to have written. They don't prepare their bug reports with all the relevant information. They don't detail their pull requests with the why. They don't bother to fill in needed code comments. They don't double-check their work. They don't write unit tests. They don't do all of these things it takes to create good software.

Agent 才是真正"合格的贡献者"

But you know who'll do all that stuff? Agents, if you tell them to. They're very diligent at following your instructions most of the time, sometimes to a fault. But it actually means that if you take the median programmer and their pull requests towards an average open source project, they're already getting outclassed by agents.

I would rather get an agent-written pull request to one of my projects than I'd get one written by a human. And it's not just because the quality is better. It's also because I feel a lot less bad if I just reject it. You didn't even write it. So I could simply look at what your agent wrote on your behalf and go: don't want it.

开源维护者的心理负担

That's always been true in open source. And in fact, I think this is one of the problems with open source maintainers. They have way too much ball of neuroticism and anxiety that requires them to look upon any contribution as an obligation on their part to do everything to get that to land in the code base.

That's not true at all. You can simply say no, or even better, you can say "no, thank you." And if you get into the mode of realizing that your project is allowed to exist and evolve according to your vision, according to your road map, it becomes so much easier in the agentic age to decline the contributions you don't want—because you don't even inconvenience or hurt the feelings of a human. It's just a clanker. And the clanker won't mind. In fact, the producers of clankers, the labs, love when you spend tokens in vain. They get paid just the same.

开源维护者的黄金时代

So, in my opinion, this is the absolute best time to ever have been an open source software maintainer. Not only do we get this wealth of glorious pull requests made by agents with all the boxes ticked, we also get to tap into a creativity of people who did not have access to contribute to your project before.

I've been running the Samachi project now for a little over a year. And in the last 3 months working on Quattro, I have merged over 1,000 pull requests. Quite a lot of those pull requests were written by people who were not classical programmers, or were programmers in other domains—not Linux operating system or distribution development. They were able to contribute their good ideas because of agents, and I got to cherry-pick the very best of that because it was there. Otherwise, those ideas would just have lived inside their heads.

Again, is this not the purpose of open source? That we tap into the collective intelligence and creativity of the whole goddamn planet and we channel that towards a commons where we all benefit from the combined efforts of everyone.

Lex： Mhm.

让 Agent 审 Agent：新的工作流

DHH： Now, there's currently I think about 400 unmerged pull requests on Amachi, about double what it was a week ago. So, the acceleration is real, but so are the tools.

I'm not reviewing every pull request anymore. I haven't been reviewing them for quite some time now. I have the agents review them for me—

Lex： Mhm.

DHH： —and then they will give me a summary about whether something is ready for the decision, the human decision. Should we merge or should we not merge?

[clears throat]

Lex： Mhm.

DHH： I don't need to look at all the pull requests that are either wrong, duplicated, bad. An agent can sort that chaff away from me. I just get to look at the pearls, the good ideas that are ready to go—the bug fixes that the agent has validated in a VM on my behalf.

All the drudgery of replicating and managing open source projects is evaporating at lightning speed, and we are left with the golden juicy parts, the bone marrow of software development: deciding what should this thing do and where should it go.

好点子还必须来自人类吗？

Lex： Do you think the good ideas—ultimately the kernel of the good ideas—originated in the human mind? So, the individual contributes... like, can it be done by agents, or is the PR ultimately requires a human idea? Like how to improve Amachi. All those incoming, or can it all just be a pool of agents?

DHH： That was the mode and the way I was thinking about agents in the first agentic age, from November 24th to February 28th.

Lex： Mhm.

DHH： I thought [clears throat] all the ideas would originate with the humans. They would tell their agents what to build and off they went.

Lex： Mhm.

"我见过你们人类无法想象的东西"

DHH： I don't think that's true anymore at all. I have seen things you people wouldn't believe. Ideas coming out of models so great that it makes me humble as a person who otherwise prides himself on having good ideas.

The agents are incredibly capable of creative thought. And folks who are still stuck in the analysis that agents are parrots—

Lex： Mhm.

DHH： —just regurgitating the ideas that are already there, are delusional about the progress that's been made in the last 6 to 9 months.

观看原视频 →
