item.title: [Lex Clips] DHH on AI psychosis | Lex Fridman Podcast Clips
item.dc:creator: Lex Clips
item.content:encoded:
💡 创造性洞见

一、把"精神病"这顶帽子反戴回去——一次修辞上的柔道

DHH 最锋利的一击不是辩护，而是诊断反转：真正处于妄想状态的，是那些看着世界剧变却坚持"不过是电子鹦鹉"的人。这不是简单的口舌之快，而是暗合了库恩（Thomas Kuhn）在《科学革命的结构》里描述的"范式的不可通约性"——两个范式内的人看着同一张纸，却看见不同的图案。有趣的是，DHH 自己 9 个月前就是那个"看不见"的人；Tobi Lütke 把备忘录递到他手上，他嗤之以鼻。这种"曾经是自己现在要说服的人"的经历，让他的辩护带有一种福柯式的自省：谁在定义疯狂，往往取决于谁尚未跨过那道感知阈值。

二、勒芒赛道上诞生的操作系统——一个几乎没人注意的元隐喻

一个容易被忽略的细节：Omarchy 起源于他在勒芒 24 小时耐力赛间隙看 YouTube 时的灵感。这不是巧合，而是一种几乎潜意识的宣言。勒芒的核心不是极速，而是在极限速度下不炸引擎的持续输出——法拉利的极速 P4 在勒芒输给了看起来更慢但更聪明的福特 GT40。DHH 对 AI 的哲学正在复刻这条曲线：他反复强调"由我引导"、"我有使命"、"不感到过载"。当 Lex 描述自己像《梦之安魂曲》里的角色被快感冲垮，DHH 描述的是赛车手在漫长夜晚保持节奏。他不是在拒绝加速，他是在拒绝无方向的加速。这可能是这段对话里最容易被漏掉的哲学。

三、稀缺资源的迁移：从"能力"到"意图"——AI 时代真正的心理学转折

这里有一个跨领域的连接值得挖：心理学、经济学、脑科学都在讲同一件事，但没人把它们拼起来。

  • 心理学（Viktor Frankl）：过载不是外部信息量的问题，而是意义系统的缺失。
  • 经济学：当一种生产要素变得几乎免费（AI 让代码变得像空气），瓶颈就会跳到剩下的稀缺要素——方向、品味、判断力。
  • 神经科学（Lex 顺口带过的 Neuralink 带宽论）：真正的限制不再是打字速度，而是"想清楚一件事"的速度。

把三者叠加，你会得到一个反直觉的结论：AI 让程序员变得像艺术总监，而大多数人抱怨的"AI 精神病"其实是"没有作品目标的人第一次被迫直面自己没有作品目标"。DHH 没被冲垮，不是因为他更聪明，而是因为他早就有 Omarchy 这个执念在等这批算力落地。Lex 描述的燃尽感，本质上是多个 project 争夺同一个稀缺资源——但那个稀缺资源不再是时间，而是"专注在某一个未来"的意愿。

四、一个隐藏的历史类比——为什么"看不见的人"这次会输得特别快

40 年里，Lisp、Smalltalk、四代语言、低代码，都承诺过"普通人也能编程"，都失败了。DHH 说这次不一样，但没有点破为什么这次不一样。我给你一个更狠的类比：这更像 1900 年前后电力从"工厂动力源"过渡到"配电网络"的时刻。之前的电力革命，工厂主必须重新设计整个车间才能受益，多数人观望了 20 年；等到通用电气把电力做成"墙上插座"，观望者用 5 年被彻底甩开。Claude Code / agent 就是那个"插座"。DHH 说的"laggards will be overwhelmed by evidence"不是威胁，而是电气化历史正在重演的具体形态：不是技术突然变神，而是摩擦力突然消失，之前需要重构工作流的能力，现在直接从命令行滴出来。这也解释了他自己的时间线——2 月 Claude Code 发布，他 9 月才装上，然后 3 个月内世界翻了个面。摩擦消失的临界点，往往就是这么短。

📝 转录文本

The Steel-Man Question

Lex: So, some people listening to you right now will say DHH is suffering from the old case of AI psychosis. Yeah, can you steel-man the case that you are in fact experiencing a state of delusion, like One Flew Over the Cuckoo's Nest, and can you argue against it?

Not Psychosis — Delirium

DHH: I'm in a state of delirium. That's the state I'm in. Because I have been working with computers for 40 years, and I've never seen the things that I've seen in just the last 2 months. A whole career, a whole life dedicating to the love of computers as my main focus for the working hours and then some — suddenly completely upended, suddenly completely rewritten. Of course I'm delirious. Who, looking at this reality, is not? If you are not delirious, or at the very least very excited… actually, I guess that's not even true. If you're not recognizing the gravity of the moment, that's the delusion. That's the psychosis. The psychosis is believing that the world is barely different, that we just have some electronic parrots reciting things to us.

Now, in my opinion, the reason this argument is actually brought up is because people are not able to see the fruits of the progress. That goes to your point earlier: where is the amazing software? Why isn't American GDP running at 12% year over year? First of all, give it a minute. It hasn't even been a year, god damn it. But second of all, I feel on my own account I have actually brought the pudding.

Omarchy Quattro — Bringing the Pudding

DHH: Omarchy Quattro launched on Friday. It's been downloaded by tens of thousands of people. And they like it. They like it a lot.

Lex: We should mention — going to Perplexity here — Omarchy is a highly opinionated Arch Linux–based desktop distribution centered on the Hyprland Wayland tiling compositor. It was created by David Heinemeier Hansson, DHH, as a polished developer workstation setup with a cohesive visual style and many everyday tools already configured.

DHH: Let me put it: Omarchy is a beautiful, modern, and opinionated Linux system. It's an alternative operating system to macOS and Windows, and it's freaking amazing.

Lex: And the Quattro thing is — you're pushing towards the age of agents.

Origin at Le Mans

DHH: That's right. That's the latest version that we just dropped out, which is also funny. The Omarchy project is only a year old and a little bit. I started it last summer in between sessions at the 24 Hours of Le Mans, where I had watched one too many YouTube videos on Linux ricing and got bitten by that bug. Started working on this second iteration of my attempt at creating a better Linux operating system.

The first iteration we talked about last time was called Omakub, was built on top of an existing system called Ubuntu, and it was fine. But the ambition I was able to pour into the new version, Omarchy, because I started seven layers deeper down the stack, was completely different — but it was still done in a pre-agentic world. I wrote all those bash scripts by hand in the beginning.

The Switchover to Agents

DHH: And then I got to see the midway point where things changed over. I did a couple of versions of Omarchy that had partial agent acceleration, and then 3 months ago it was full throttle: 100% everything is written by agents, but steered by me. And that just ended up being a very different experience and a very different operating system, because I was suddenly granted a limitless ceiling on my ambition.

I could look at any feature in Windows, on Mac, on other Linux systems, and say, "I want that." And the agents would deliver. So everything I wanted was suddenly within reach — which meant that I got a little delirious.

Who would not get delirious if suddenly a genie pops out of the bottle and says, "You can have whatever you want. Every feature you've ever dreamed of in an operating system, I can deliver them to you. Most of them in 5 minutes, a few in 20, and if we really go hog wild, it's going to take me 2 hours."

Overwhelm vs. Mission

Lex: Have you seen Requiem for a Dream, the movie? There's a drug-like effect here. I find, personally — we'll talk about many levels of this, but it is overwhelming how much power is placed in our hands so suddenly. And it's very hard to know, it's like with the Hobbit or something, what to do with it. I find myself truly overwhelmed with the multitasking, on the verge of almost burnt out, super excited about so many things, but ultimately looking back, you want to focus on one thing in a relationship.

DHH: I don't have that sense. I don't have the sense of overwhelm, I don't have the sense of dread, I don't have the sense of distortion — because I have a mission. I'm going somewhere. And therefore, I can channel all this new power towards a singular goal and outcome: creating the perfect computer. And therefore, all my investigations with AI are focused towards that end.

Now, I also have a day job, and we also use agents there, and that's also targeted towards specific outcomes. But with the Omarchy experience, I got to tap in straight in the back of my head and increase the bandwidth between ideas arriving in my brain and software emerging on the screen.

From Dial-Up to Fiber

DHH: It was like going from dial-up to fiber. I think on your podcast, Elon talked about the actual human bandwidth that Neuralink and other projects are trying to accelerate. Like, the bandwidth we're communicating over right now is quite low, because we're limited by our cognition, we're limited by the rate of speech. You're not limited by those things when you're working with a swarm of agents.

A Confession — The Nine-Months-Ago Self

DHH: Now, let me caveat this by saying: if I'd heard myself talk like this 9 months ago, I would probably use the label "AI psychosis." I think it would be fitting. Because 9 months ago, when people were talking like this, they weren't shipping. And I think that's the ultimate difference.

There were people who saw this early. I was not actually that early. As we've talked about, I was rather skeptical, and I was using AI in certain ways, but I was not the first person who downloaded Claude Code. I think Boris released that in end of February. I don't think I installed Claude Code until September. So there was about 6 months there where pioneers saw these glimmers of what the future was going to look like. It wasn't there yet — because the intelligence wasn't there, the harnesses weren't there — but they could see the glimmers.

Tobi Lütke and the Rocket

DHH: Tobi Lütke, the CEO of Shopify — and now my partner in crime on this Omarchy project in part — he's gotten pilled with Omarchy as well. He saw these things very early and he tried to tell me. And I wasn't seeing it. I was not seeing what he was seeing.

Lex: You were a hater.

DHH: Yes. I was still on Earth.

Lex: Okay.

DHH: And he had already boarded the rocket and was heading towards space. I remember actually reading his memo to the company, the AI memo, and thinking, "Ah, seems a little much. Like, you're making a big deal out of something that I cannot yet feel is a tangible thing." Because — where's the output of this? I try using it, it writes code I don't like, it wants to interrupt me all the time. Where are you getting this from?

So I get it. I totally get it. If you're not seeing what the current quality of intelligence can produce, of course you're going to look at someone and go, "They sound a little nutty." Because all your experience up until this point would tell you that they are nutty.

The 40-Year False Promise

DHH: If you look at the history of computer programming for the last 40, 50 years, people have been promising that regular people could write code just by talking. We're going to have fourth-generation languages. Lisp was once upon a time presented, Smalltalk was presented, as these environments that would let regular people write their own applications. And none of it came true — in the sense beyond, like, Microsoft Access databases or Excel spreadsheets. Those are end-user programming environments, but it's nothing like what we're able to do now.

And then — I mean, I'm not even talking about end users. I'm talking as me, someone who's been programming for 25 years, seeing the output and the acceleration and the quality, and then shipping it.

The Flood of Evidence

DHH: And I think that's what's going to change the entire conversation quite quickly. The few laggards who are still on the fence about whether this is actually useful, who are still trapped in a meme from early '25 about mechanical parrots — they're simply going to be overwhelmed by the evidence that's about to flood over them.

Lex: So, I hope to see projects like Omarchy — several of them — that really show agent first.

DHH: It's coming. All of it is coming.

Lex: In the silly spaces already mentioned — like video editing, all these kinds of apps that were like Type-Ora…

DHH: Yes.

Lex: …this kind of stuff.

item.description:
## 一、把"精神病"这顶帽子反戴回去——一次修辞上的柔道
DHH 最锋利的一击不是辩护，而是**诊断反转**：真正处于妄想状态的，是那些看着世界剧变却坚持"不过是电子鹦鹉"的人。这不是简单的口舌之快，而是暗合了库恩（Thomas Kuhn）在《科学革命的结构》里描述的"范式的不可通约性"——两个范式内的人看着同一张纸，却看见不同的图案。有趣的是，DHH 自己 9 个月前就是那个"看不见"的人；Tobi Lütke 把备忘录递到他手上，他嗤之以鼻。这种"曾经是自己现在要说服的人"的经历，让他的辩护带有一种**福柯式的自省**：谁在定义疯狂，往往取决于谁尚未跨过那道感知阈值。
## 二、勒芒赛道上诞生的操作系统——一个几乎没人注意的元隐喻
一个容易被忽略的细节：Omarchy 起源于他在**勒芒 24 小时耐力赛**间隙看 YouTube 时的灵感。这不是巧合，而是一种几乎潜意识的宣言。勒芒的核心不是极速，而是**在极限速度下不炸引擎的持续输出**——法拉利的极速 P4 在勒芒输给了看起来更慢但更聪明的福特 GT40。DHH 对 AI 的哲学正在复刻这条曲线：他反复强调"由我引导"

item.title: [a16z] Why Top Founders Are Racing Into AI Infrastructure
item.dc:creator: a16z
item.content:encoded:
💡 创造性洞见

一、被忽视的"心理反转"：我们正在见证软件行业最深的信仰崩塌

过去 40 年，硅谷奉行一条铁律——"神话的人月"（Mythical Man-Month）：你不可能靠砸钱和堆人追上一个领先两年的对手。这条定律塑造了从 Fred Brooks 到 Paul Graham 的整个软件哲学，也定义了 VC 的判断范式：技术领先＝时间壁垒。

但 Ben 在对话中悄悄扔下了一颗炸弹："Now that works."（现在这招管用了。）

这不是一个技术观察，而是一次范式颠覆。当 xAI 用 30 亿美元点亮一个集群就能几个月追平多年积累的 OpenAI，当 Kimi、Grok 可以"凭空冒出来就是真的"——软件行业赖以生存的"复利护城河"神话首次被资本一次性击穿。这意味着过去所有关于"先发优势"的投资逻辑正在失效，而这才是 a16z 悄悄改换赛道的真正原因，不是"AI 需要基础设施"这么表层。

一个让人不适的推论：如果金钱可以直接兑换智能，那么 VC 行业本身的价值主张——识别"稀缺的判断力"——正在被稀释。他们成立 Machine Age 基金，某种意义上是在逃向一个金钱仍然买不到答案的领域：物理约束、供应链、许可证、变压器交货周期。

二、跨领域连接：这不是"AI 泡沫"，这是"爱迪生 vs. 特斯拉"的 2.0 重演

对话里有一个几乎被一带而过的技术细节，却是整段访谈里最富历史反讽的时刻——当机架功率突破 100kW 时，交流电（AC）不再够用，数据中心开始改用直流电（DC）。而 Ben 顺口提到：这正是当年爱迪生所拥护、特斯拉击败的那种"危险的直流电"。爱迪生曾用电死大象和马来"证明"交流电危险，最终却输掉了整个电气化时代。

一个跨越 135 年的镜像出现了：电力工业的第一次基础设施浪潮由 AC 定义，第二次浪潮却在悄悄回归 DC。这不是复古，而是一个更深的规律——当负载密度极端集中时，物理定律偏爱直流。数据中心里 800V DC 的回归，意味着我们正在把电网重新分裂成"高密度节点集群"，就像互联网早期从主机集中式回到分布式，而现在又回到"AI 大教堂"式的集中。

更深层的连接：这场基础设施重构的隐藏对手不是英伟达的竞争者，而是19 世纪的水泥标准、20 世纪的电工执照制度、以及 21 世纪的地方噪音法规。整个 21 世纪的最前沿产业，正在被 19 世纪的钢筋混凝土供应瓶颈所限速——只有 2% 的美国电工持有 DC 认证。这是一场时代错位的战争。

三、最出人意料的观察：AI 正在重新发明"公司"这个概念，而它的操作系统还没写出来

Martin 提到 Grokbot 时说了一句轻描淡写却极具穿透力的话："AI 不再是你的延伸，它是一个员工——有自己的电脑，自己的浏览器。"

大多数人把这当成 UI 层的进化，但真正的震撼在别处：这是自 1602 年荷兰东印度公司发明"股份有限公司"以来，公司这个组织形式第一次遇到"非人类成员"。而 Ben 补充的那句更值得咀嚼——"我们花了很多年才学会怎么和人类员工共事，现在要重学。"

这里藏着一个几乎没人讨论的悖论：过去 400 年，管理学的所有工具（KPI、OKR、绩效考核、企业文化、组织行为学）都建立在"员工有生存需求、有社交需求、会疲劳、会走人"的前提之上。当这些前提全部消失，我们发现自己没有任何理论工具来管理一个"会烧掉大量 token、会编造事实、会突然聪明也会突然愚蠢、没有职业规划但可以 24 小时工作"的实体。

跨领域连接：这更像18 世纪工厂主第一次面对"机器"时的情境——他们不知道该按小时给机器发工资，还是按产量分红，最终发明了"折旧"这个会计概念。我们即将进入一个"AI 折旧学"和"AI 组织行为学"被发明的时代，而现在整个行业连基本词汇都还没形成。当 Ben 说"我们不是要慢慢淘汰人类"，那句话背后是没人知道新的组织均衡点在哪里——这才是 Machine Age 真正的"未开垦地带"，比任何芯片投资都更大。

而一个终极的反直觉推论：这一波 AI 最先淘汰的不是知识工作者，而是"管理学"这门学科本身。

📝 转录文本

开场：一个全新的时代需要全新的基础设施

We have a whole new technology. That's the most important technology ever. And you need a whole new infrastructure.

Normally when we talk about the infrastructure world, we're talking about the servers on the storage and the network. Here it goes all the way down to the mines of copper min. That's how widespread this thing is going to be.

It used to be when you built something, it was an engineering problem. And here it feels like it really is a resource limitation. So whether it's tokens or not, we're pouring a ton of money into systems and then those systems are producing a result. And right now we're bottlenecked on the systems ability to actually match the resources we're pouring into them.

The leading memory vendor said the demand they have today will take them 3 years of capacity to supply.

If this fund does what we think it will do, how do we see the world in 5 to 10 years?

America wins in the infrastructure and that would be awesome.

Ben, Martin, Ragu, welcome.

Thank you.

All right. Thank you.

一、引入 Machine Age Fund：史上最大的技术革命

I want to start with a Mark quote to introduce this new fund. This is the biggest technological revolution of my lifetime. This is clearly bigger than the internet. The comps on this are the microprocessor, the steam engine, and electricity, or maybe the wheel. Guys, the machine age fund. Please introduce it. Ben, start us off.

Well, um, basically what's uh happened is we have a whole new technology that's the most important technology ever. And what happens every time um there's a dramatic new way of using all of the things that we love infrastructure um you need a whole new infrastructure and never has it been more high impact as it is on this one. So not only do we need new chips, new system software, we need new ways of doing power, we need to replace copper. I mean like it's absolutely everything. So it's a very exciting time. So you know particularly for the kind of hardware aspects of of this new era um we needed a new approach.

Yeah I would agree. I mean normally when we at least in the computing when we talk about the infrastructure world we talking about the servers and the storage in the network here it goes all the way down to the mines copper mines. That's how widespread this thing is going to be. Um that's number one and number two I think what we have seen over the last 3 years is the steady increase of the capabilities of the models where the model is no longer the bottleneck and in fact using AI these models are getting better faster and faster and faster. Now the bottleneck is all what I call south of the model and so that's why we need to work on that.

You know, the only thing I'd add very quickly is like we tend to follow founders and we've been watching over the last couple of years is the number of very strong teams going after complex hardware problems has increased. I don't know the actual numbers but I was trying to estimate it over the weekend. So I think we'd get you maybe 5% of the deals from top founders would come in would be hardwood before. Now I would say north of 20% or 30% right now. So like the founder community which tends to be much smarter than the VC community has identified this as a very active area for innovation and they're responding.

I think 5% is probably generous.

Yeah, it's very low. Is very low. Yeah. 3%. Yeah.

二、宏观条件：为什么现在是硬件创业的时刻

And explain some of the macro conditions that have led to this this trans this change in terms of the surplus of founders pursuing these idea. Like what are they seeing that's that's enabled?

Well, I mean the obvious is like you know the the demand for AI is basically infinite and as a result of that every part of the supply chain is under under duress. I mean everything including like materials used to make things like like memory.

Um it's also very interesting whether there's something unique about AI. Um which because the demand is infinite and growth is infinite. Um uh what you tend to worry about is the margin of companies which is how efficient it is. Like normally you worry about growth like can I just you know can I just get people to buy this stuff. You don't have to worry about that here. The question is is can you do this in a way that's profitable? And a lot of the um efficiencies are actually strictly a physical limitation of hardware.

And so even the business model of the AI wave is really putting a lot of stress on the existing systems because they weren't built for AI. They weren't built for those workloads. And I think there's just this you know this global observation that we actually need to change the core components to get that efficiency to help drive the growth and to drive the value of the businesses.

需求真的超过供给了吗？

Yeah. And how did we know that demand is actually outpacing supply here rather than this being you know another hype cycle?

Well, I mean, yeah, there are any number of cities today. Um, firstly, it is that some of the smartest judges of demand are cutting huge purchase orders. I mean, if you look at the hyperscalers, right? Their capex spend has been exploding. Next year supposedly, it's going to reach a trillion dollars collectively across the big hyperscalers. This year, it's about 700 billion dollars, right?

And if you think about the hyperscalers position in the industry, they see demand from everywhere, right? They see obviously the frontier labs um wanting their compute, they see the AI native companies, they see the enterprise, they see the US geography, the international geography. So if anybody has visibility, it is down and they've been jacking up their capex like it's never been seen before, right? So that's a clear clear sign.

And secondly, if you look at the companies that we see on a day-to-day basis, they are all ripping. All the application companies, the growth is insane. The frontier labs, the growth is insane. It's been documented. So I would say on the demand side, the signals have never been clearer that this is not a hype. It's to top it all, all of it is just and prices are going up.

Like we've never seen prices go like up on chips.

You keep your prices went down. They always go down. Yeah. It always goes down. If you look at the price curve, it it went like this and then went back this.

Yeah.

And we know only like 5, 10% of the address for the market to stop today.

I mean, the the the supply, if you look, if you look at the supply across the board, it's basically all booked out to 2028. I mean, it's so bad we've actually seen multi-day auctions for a few thousand GPUs.

Um, you know, the other side of that, of course, is demand. And as Ragu said, we've seen the fastest growing companies we've seen in the history of the industry.

But also the unit of work that AI can do, the value of that unit of work keeps increasing. But underneath the covers, the number of tokens that are consumed is going by orders of magnitude, right? If it's one token for I mean 100 tokens for chat or an agent, it's thousands of tokens, right? So you got expansion of both sides of demand. One is the unit of work is becoming more and more consumptive of tokens and then secondly the number of people therefore that are going to be benefit it's not just the developers it's going to be all knowledge workers and then all of beyond that so that's that's what we see.

三、一个史无前例的现象：整个行业被预订到 2028 年

You said the key components in supply are sold out to 2027 maybe in 2028. What does it mean for an entire industry to be sold out that that far? Like I don't know this has ever happened before. Do you guys recall?

I mean remember in the Um, in in in the internet days when we were doing massive buildout, the majority that was actually being put in the ground was speculative and was dark. Remember the dark fiber? And here basically every GPU that's being created is already pre-sold. So

yeah, we weren't quite there. I mean there was there was a lack of bandwidth like in the 98, 99 time frame, but there wasn't there there wasn't that much real demand for it because there just weren't that many people on the internet. So like it was a two-sided thing and the companies were all rushing there and needed more bandwidth theoretically, but there weren't the users on the other side to consume it necessarily. And then to really consume a lot of bandwidth, you have to do high bandwidth things like video, which weren't really viable for, you know, a number of reasons that that had nothing to do with how much bandwidth was in the data center.

So it smelled similar, but it wasn't this. This is like we're flat out and people are reselling GPUs for four times what they bought them for and this kind of thing. Like it's just not. And then, you know, we're we're also out of power and cooling. Uh and then on top of that, it's really hard to build because there's these incredible political headwinds going into it. So, it's it's really unprecedented in my career.

Uh that we've had anything anything like this. No, I want to give you a quick anecdote. So, this I was talking to a CFO of a large company, large public company who had historically been very resistant about going into the cloud. So, they had a lot of servers and they were doing an inventory uh check and they realized that the memory in their servers had increased so much it could uh fund the entire migration to the cloud. So, I just feel like we're in a very unusual situation.

Yeah, that's right. We're out of many things. Power, cooling, memory, GPUs, like you name it, we're out of it.

Yeah. So, the flagship uh conference for the industry is the one called Hot Chips is going on in Stanford and the leading memory vendor said the demand they have today it will take them 3 years of capacity to supply it. It's just today it's not even future demand.

为什么没人预见到这样的爆发？

So in terms of being about everything simultaneously, is it because people just underestimated how good the models would be, how how useful they would be, they just couldn't have foreseen the demand?

Well, I don't even think it's that. I mean, this stuff came out of nowhere, right? We we're only four years into this. Like it wasn't really a technology problem. Like once you got the business working, you tended to have pretty good margins because that's just kind of how software works.

Certainly when you shipped it but even as a service uh and that's not necessarily the case with AIS we may actually be entering an era where the optimization in the hardware is absolutely meaningful to the upside of the business in a way that we haven't seen in the past so there's a lot of opportunity here.

十一、投资细分与创业者特质

Let's get deeper in talking about the types of companies we'll be investing in um maybe we could start by either illustrating the the the subsectors or if we can talk about a few um or a couple investments that we've I know there's some that haven't been announced yet, but Robert, do you want to take us down?

Yeah, I mean the sub sectors as we've been talking all is every one of these categories, right? The obvious ones are um uh computer chips, but these days it's not enough to build a chip. You need to build a full system, right? And then therefore, what goes into the system? There's potentially memory innovation. There is potentially networking innovation. There's potentially power chips and so on and so forth. So each one of these categories are categories where you can see public company style companies emerging and those are all things that we are looking into.

Um and then once you put it all together there's a layer of software around it to automate all of these things to manage these fleets and so on and so forth. So that is another important area. So these things keep building on each other but every one of these categories is important.

这些公司有什么不一样

Talk about what's different about these kinds of companies from from the usual company. I mean one thing you can tell from the companies we announced is their first rounds have been massive. You know hundreds of millions. Is it a different kind of founder or what else is different as we think about just the practice of you know building and investing these kinds of businesses relative to our traditional software?

Well I I think the big thing is you hit on one of the big things which is a lot of money goes in um before they get to a product. Um and that's just kind of the nature of it. Now that's true on big models too, but I I would say that's a little more of a known path. Uh whereas this has got a little more risk and a little more money than uh than some of the other things that we've done.

But um and you know, look, a lot of a lot of the chip founders um are here from the past. You know, like the guys who know how to make memory, they're not young. Yeah, you know, so it's uh you know that part is different too, but it's kind of exciting, you know.

Yeah. The other thing about these founders, they have all got to be systems founders. So what I mean by that is you can't just be a researcher or a great computer scientist, right? You got to be able to architect and design the chip or the system, whatever it is. Then you got to think about how is this thing going to actually get manufactured, right? Who's going to be supplying this and a whole bunch of these downstream things which normally if you're building software you don't have to think about all of these things. So the to really the best founders um and of course Jensen is the Michael Jordan of this right they think the entire ecosystem right from the get-go before they start designing the chain right because of the nature of the bottlenecks and all these things that have to come together. So that's that's a big characteristic that is different.

There there's two environmental factors that are important too. The first one is the labs are so desperate that they will engage with startups. And so like we actually have quite a bit of signal early on because they're you labs are inking deals with companies before they actually have hardware available. And that's a big big shift than you know 5 years ago, right? Like you just didn't go and you know sell your kind of janky hardware thing to Google or whatever. So that that's a shift.

The second one is the the capital availability has loosened up a lot. I think there's general consensus that that you know it is the time that to reshape this stuff and so follow on rounds there's a lot of capital available which you know of course you want to be investing into areas where there's capital available and so the atmospherics are also just different.

为什么现在的硬件创业者往往更年长

Patrick Carlson, you know, remarked a few years ago said, "Hey, it feels like there's less younger founders today, you know, in the way that you know, Zuck, you know, in college building next Facebook or or Gates, um, you know, in the same way with Microsoft and of course, you know, the Michael Trolls of the world, there there's still, you know, some young founders building iconic companies, but it does seem, you know, to your point that there's more older founders building these these these companies or or less 20-year-olds." I'm I'm curious if you resonates and why.

Well, I think it's Ragu's point that if if you're building something that has like a very complicated supply chain, has to manufacture things um and is technically complicated that you know some experience helps uh and you know if you look at Elon or Travis Kalanick their companies when they were young were software companies. It wasn't until they got like a lot even those guys the best guys um needed some experience in building a companies building technology and so forth to kind of graduate to the much more kind of complicated or I would say elaborate domains you know there's just much more there many more moving parts in these things.

And so look when you're learning how to build a company it's hard enough if you completely understand the product. If you don't completely understand the product and have to learn it while you build the company, um that's just such a steep learning curve for a brand new entrepreneur. So, I think that what we're seeing is you see Michael on the one hand, um who is a very young guy, brilliant, but what he built was kind of a pure software AI thing.

Yeah. And then on the other end, you have like an Elon or a Travis who can who's got enough experience. I think Michael could probably do that, you know, 10 years from now, but today that would have been hard.

And it's important to remember like it's been defocused by the entire industry and academia for the last 20 years, right? It just there just hasn't been the same opportunity. Like it's been there, but like it's never been a growth area. The growth areas have been, you know software um networking things like that. And so I also think we just have a posity of people coming out of the universities or having experience at large companies that have have done this. I there just not that many.

Like you don't go intern and like build a chip. So but a lot of that's changing now. Like listen we're going to create a whole generation of of you know founders that come from these new companies that will know how to do this and you know they'll be hired in much more junior and like I would say actually one of the greatest legacies of Elon towards this is is of course he's created these great companies but the amount of entrepreneurs that have come out of SpaceX that that have are changing the entire industrial complex maybe even greater um legacy than than the companies themselves and I think we're going to see the same thing uh for for computer science and hardware.

Y as a matter of All of our investments was started by uh two founders in their 20ies. But if you go watch one of their offices, you see the experienced people as well. So it's ideal combination here.

Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. It doesn't necessarily have to be the founder with experience, but that founder better be able to tap into that experience with it.

Yeah. Yeah.

十二、为什么由这几位 GP 领衔

Well, and then be able to work with them and and and they have to be good and and all these kinds of things. It's complicated. Speaking of experience, this is a a big new fund we're we're launching and there's no new GPS. Um yeah, we're sort of collecting. It's because you guys have a lot of experience and the rest of the group, you know, in in this field that it's been kind of latent and uh dormant.

Yeah. Well, it's kind of funny. I think we almost had to be warned against it almost just because like our backgrounds are from is hard. And I think the reason that we needed a reminder is because all of us have spent so much in our careers existence and hardware. We're kind of drawn to that.

And so listen, we've been clearly invested um in harbor over other years, right? We're in SpaceX, we're in Andrew and all. These are very early checks. We're in astronomics, we're in Whimo, you know, so we even even early on we did a number of those investments. Um but like you know this is because it's so much in our DNA and so I don't think this is necessarily need to increase the team competencies just bonus.

十三、五到十年后的愿景

If this fund does what we think it will do, how do we see the world changing or looking like in 5 to 10 years?

Well, you know, hopefully uh America wins in the infrastructure game. Um and we have lots of like super eco-friendly efficient data centers out there and lots and lots an abundance of chips and abundance of memory and abundance of power. Uh and you know that would be awesome.

Uh, and I think we look we we, you know, it goes back to like we really think uh America is a special place and um we're important not only to everybody here but anybody in the world who wants to kind of make a contribution and do something bigger than themselves that it's kind of the best place to come with nothing and do something profound. So we'd like to keep that going and I I think that doesn't continue to go if we lose our lead in technology. Think I think we'll be in another era and it'll be another country and maybe they have a different set of values around that.

Thanks. That's a wrap.

Great for seeing me fun. Martine Beni. Thank you. Thank you.

Thank you. Thanks. Yeah.

但 Ben 在对话中悄悄扔下了一颗炸弹："**Now that works.**"（现在这招管用了。）

item.title: [Lex Clips] Cases where AI can write 100% of the code | DHH and Lex Fridman
item.dc:creator: Lex Clips
item.content:encoded:
💡 创造性洞见

一、被忽视的"代码烂摊子悖论"：AI并没有制造垃圾，它只是把人类一直在做的事情可视化了

DHH最锋利的一击藏在最后——当人们指责vibe coder是"垃圾生成器"，他反问："你看过普通程序员的产出吗？"这句话背后其实是一个残酷的系统性真相：软件行业几十年来一直用"人多"这个变量掩盖了"代码熵增"这个常量。AI没有让代码变差，它只是把3000个工程师用20年制造的混乱压缩到了3个月内完成，让熵增速率从慢性病变成了急性发作。

这是一种"时间显影剂"效应——就像高速摄影机让我们第一次看清水滴溅起的皇冠。行业震惊的不是AI的糟糕，而是终于看清了自己的糟糕。

二、跨领域连接：AI安全审查 vs. 冷战情报机构——"combo move智能"的稀缺性突然被商品化

DHH提到Fable模型能"串联组合技找到RCE"这一点，几乎被所有人当作技术细节滑过去了，但这里隐藏着一个地缘政治级别的系统扰动：

过去，能把"5个小漏洞串成致命链条"的人几乎只存在于三个地方——NSA、Unit 8200、以及朝鲜的Lazarus Group。这种能力被称为"vulnerability chaining intelligence"，是国家级战略资产。而现在，这种曾经等同于核武器级别稀缺性的认知能力，正在以API调用的价格被批发。

类比一下：这就像1945年之后，铀浓缩技术突然出现在了民用五金店。DHH说Fable"不安全发布"其实是软件史的一个不扩散条约时刻——但没人在讨论这个。所有讨论都还停留在"AI能写多少代码"这种表层问题。

三、令人意外的观察：Vibe coding的失败模式和"民主化设计"的历史重演

最反直觉的一点是：Basecamp 5让设计师去vibe code，结果每一个单独的PR都"在某个瞬间是合理的"，但加起来毁掉了系统架构。这不是AI的锅，也不是设计师的锅——这是一个古老的现象：

局部理性的总和 ≠ 全局理性。

这和城市规划里的"雅各布斯诅咒"完全同构——每一栋新建筑都符合规范、都美观、都提高了容积率，但整个街区变得无法居住。也和金融市场里的"合成谬误"（fallacy of composition）如出一辙——每个理性交易者的最优选择叠加成系统性崩溃。

真正的洞见在于：AI暴露了一个软件工程从未真正解决的元问题——架构一致性是一个"负熵"任务，它需要一个持续存在的"叙事者"（narrator）来维持系统的语义连贯性。以前这个角色由资深工程师隐性承担，现在它突然被抽掉了，暴露出软件的"意义"其实一直悬挂在少数人的直觉上，而不在代码本身里。

所以未来最值钱的技能可能不是写代码，而是"架构叙事的守护者"——一个能在AI的局部理性洪流中，持续为系统注入全局意图的人。这是一个全新的职业类别，还没有名字。

📝 转录文本

编程的不同领域：哪里可以让 AI 写 100% 代码？

We should mention that there's all kinds of domains that programmers operate in. There is — I actually don't know, but I think the most common domain in development is like web dev CRUD. You have a database.

Yes.

User facing interface and it does something back and forth. And it could be internal to just one person, to multiple people, to a small number of people, or to the world.

I think for that, it's — I mean, you could really get to the 100% of code written by AI. And really, almost, if you're a good programmer and you have a good intuition about what's happening behind the scenes, you can legitimately not look at the code. At least that's been my experience.

I don't know how much a prior experience with programming you need to have to kind of know that things are working correctly behind the scenes — like intuitively, by observing the ripple effects, of symptoms of the system. But I think for that domain, it's close to 100%.

And then there's domains like you're also operating in, which is writing Linux distribution. There, maybe there's more, because you're obsessed with speed and all that kind of stuff. There maybe you need to look at the code a little bit more.

Then there's maybe safety critical systems, all the way down to operating a nuclear power plant, or a self-driving car. Maybe you need to look at the code more carefully.

AI 与安全漏洞：串联"组合技"的稀缺智能

Yes, but that said, AI is insanely capable at both finding —

Yeah.

— and fixing security vulnerabilities. This was the whole blow up about Fable. This model was so capable of finding holes that an attacker could exploit that was simply not safe to release.

So the irony here is that when you look at that field, it seems like we've reached levels of intelligence that virtually no human can match. Because many of these security holes are about stringing combo moves together. You find one little vulnerability here that by itself might not be the worst thing in the world, but then you combine it with four others, and suddenly you have RCE — remote command execution.

Humans who are able to do that are very rare. Usually work inside state-sponsored organizations or other clandestine operations. They're not just out and about finding things. So they've gotten so good at that.

HEY Quattro：一个 100% 由 AI 构建的产品

The Linux distribution is why I've gotten 100% AI built. Because I've been working on HEY for the last 3 months — this version that just dropped a few days ago called Quattro. And almost right from the beginning I'm working on that version, the agent acceleration neared 100%. And in the last 2 months it has been 100%.

I have not written — Really? — any of the code that shipped in Quattro by hand. I've reviewed the shape of all of it. I've reviewed the individual lines of anything that's critical in the model layer of the system. And I've not looked at a bunch of the UI code. I have not looked at a bunch of the auxiliary code. And I've not written any of the new functionality entirely by hand.

成熟代码库的困境：Basecamp 与 HEY 为何更难加速？

But then the web part — actually evolving Basecamp and HEY, are professional products that have lots of users and are relatively large code bases — have proven surprisingly tricky to fully accelerate with agents.

We just released Basecamp 5 not too long ago. That was the first product at 37signals that was really agent accelerated, because we were in this final sprint phase from around February. By then, agents were already good.

And we had this early surge of "it's solved." We could just have the designers do the programming. They know what features they want. They know what shape they want it to take. Let's just let them vibe.

And we let them vibe.

Yeah.

And we ended up with a lot of PRs that individually perhaps could have been justified for a hot moment — taken all together, destroyed the architecture of the system. And we actually had to clean up — manually mop it up by hand, by human hand — to get back to an architecture that felt cohesive and coherent.

So we still have a bit of that. That was February, by the way. Things are quite different now.

Vibe Coding 的前提：你必须是个程序员吗？

Oh, hold on a second. What's the lesson from that? Is one of the lessons from that that you have to be a programmer at this stage to be able to vibe code?

To be able to vibe code on existing substantial code bases — even if they're CRUD — if you want to retain the elements of architecture that got that system to where it was.

对"垃圾代码"指控的反击

Now, that's also a point where I've stressed many times that when people accuse vibe coders of being slob generators, I go right back at them and say: "Have you looked at the average programmer's output?"

That is some other slob, too. If you've looked at behind the scenes of many great companies and what their code bases look like after there's been 3,000 humans through them — they're awful. Absolutely awful.

Mhm.

观看原视频 →

item.title: [Business of Sport] Celtic Rock Bottom, Football Clubs Have an Investment Problem, FedEX Cup Shows PGA TOUR’s Strength
item.dc:creator: Business of Sport
item.content:encoded:
💡 创造性洞见

失败作为一种商业模式：凯尔特人的"负向护城河"

大多数俱乐部把失败视为成本，凯尔特人却把它变成了资产负债表的润滑剂。他们的运营逻辑令人惊讶地类似于保险公司的精算模型——预设每年欧冠出局的"损失概率"，然后通过压低支出、囤积现金来抵消这种失败带来的收入缺口。但这里有一个致命的悖论：保险公司卖的是"你不出事我赚钱"，而凯尔特人卖的是"我们出事你还得买"。90 million镑现金堆在银行，主看台亟待重建，而 Dermot Desmond 却像一个把股东红利锁在保险箱里的信托管理人——问题在于，他管理的不是资本，而是60,000人的文化身份。

这里有一个跨领域的连接值得思考：凯尔特人的困境与日本"僵尸企业"的现象惊人相似——不是因为亏损而僵化，而是因为过度稳健而丧失了冒险的肌肉。当一个组织的KPI从"赢得欧冠"退化为"不破产"，它就已经在心理上离场了。

英国板球的"男孩终究是男孩"叙事：一种被制度化的幼稚

真正令人意外的观察不是球员喝酒，而是整个板球生态系统对"稚气未脱"的集体默许。Charlie点出了一个关键结构性问题：16-17岁就获得保障合约的团队运动员，其个人绩效与收入的反馈回路被人为切断了。这与高尔夫形成了极其鲜明的跨领域对比——高尔夫选手是"个体经营者"，一次宿醉直接体现在奖金支票上；而板球选手是"契约雇员"，宿醉的成本由团队和粉丝共同承担。

这里有一个更深层的洞察：英国板球把"表现问题"重新包装成了"公关问题"，这是所有失败机构的经典自欺——把因果关系倒转，从而免除结构性改革的责任。这与凯尔特人董事会把"失败"包装成"审慎"是同一种病理学。

FedEx Cup vs LIV：一场关于"稀缺性经济学"的公开课

最反直觉的观察是：LIV通过取消淘汰机制、保证出场费来"降低摩擦"，反而摧毁了自己产品的价值。这违背了体育产业最古老的定律——观众买的不是舒适，而是不确定性。FedEx Cup的天才之处在于把"精英meritocracy"和"叙事张力"焊接在一起：70→50→30的漏斗设计，本质上是把整个赛季压缩成一个三幕剧结构。

而这里的跨领域连接才是真正的"啊哈时刻"：FedEx Cup的奖金进入球员养老金这个细节，暴露了一个远比表面更深的博弈——PGA Tour正在用德国式的"共同决策制"（Mitbestimmung）来对抗LIV的沙特式"金主赞助制"。前者赢在制度韧性，后者输在缺乏共谋。这解释了为什么英超足球在与球员工会的关系上如此脆弱：因为PFA还停留在"要更多钱"的原始工会阶段，而PGA Tour的球员已经进化成了准股东。

隐藏的系统性真相：足球俱乐部市场正在经历一场"流动性坍塌"

Rob提出的"42/72俱乐部待售"数据背后，是一个远比表面严峻的结构性问题：当年度亏损接近资产估值时，破产比出售更经济。这不是足球问题，这是任何长期依赖"更大的傻瓜理论"的资产类别都会遭遇的市场失灵——想想2008年的次贷、2022年的加密货币，或艺术品市场周期性的崩盘。10-100 million镑这个中间地带的买家真空，本质上是"新贵已经买不起，超富看不上"的经典中产陷阱。IFR即将面对的挑战，不是监管问题，而是流动性做市商问题——他们需要的可能不是更严格的所有者测试，而是像美联储那样的"最后购买人"机制。

📝 转录文本

Celtic 触底、足球俱乐部的投资困境与 FedEx Cup 展现 PGA Tour 实力

开场：凯尔特人的历史性崩盘

第一部分：凯尔特人的欧战溃败

一场无以复加的崩盘

Things which will have annoyed some people. Um — Celtic exiting the Champions League qualifying stages last night. I'm not sure I know of a greater footballing collapse than this, Charlie. I mean, I've seen matches — I've even been at matches — between two highly competitive teams where one team goes 3–0 up, and famous Champions League final of course, and then the other one roars back in some way.

But last night, Celtic actually collapsed. And it's a slightly different thing when you're watching it.

So, let's just, for those who don't follow it closely or haven't seen the result from last night — it was a two-legged game against LASK of Austria, the Austrian League being ranked somewhere below the Championship in European football terms. Okay, so it's sort of bottom-end Championship, top-end League One in quality. It's that sort of thing.

Celtic won the home leg at Celtic Park at Parkhead 3–0. Happy days. Job done. We're finally going to qualify for the knockout stages — or the group stages rather — of a Champions League. Great. Fantastic. We're back on top.

Go to the away leg. Go 1–nil up away from home. 4–nil up on aggregate. Even that was not enough as they then proceeded to concede five goals in the following 70 odd minutes to lose 5–4 on aggregate.

It's a football disaster.

一门以失败为基础的生意

It's a business disaster as well. Right. And that's why you look at — I mean, look, are we just commenting on a collapse in a random game? No, that's not our style. Are we commenting on the collapse of a performance in a really really important part of a season when they have built a business model, as we've discussed before, that they have claimed protects them from missing out on European football?

Oh, it does. You know that — "That's why we don't spend the money, guys. We can't overexpose ourselves."

What they've really done now is they've gone back-to-back years going out in Champions League qualifying to Kairat — Kairat Kazakhstan.

Goes back a lot longer than that. So this goes back quite a long time. This goes back to pre-Covid. During the last seven years they've lost in these qualifying stages to AEK Athens, to Cluj, to Ferencváros, to Midtjylland, and to Almaty. Okay. And now LASK. So that's six defeats over a seven- or eight-year period to clubs who — with the greatest of respect, and absolutely respecting all different clubs of all different kinds; my own clubs and the clubs I've worked at have not been huge huge huge clubs, and I'm very respectful of all different types of clubs — but this is Celtic. This is Celtic. This is one of the biggest franchises in the world of football losing every single year to European minnows.

内置失败的商业模式

Now, you mentioned that this was a financial disaster for them. It just unfortunately isn't — because they've built an entire business model out of failure, right?

So, in other words, they set out basically saying: we're going to fail. And how can we be profitable despite failing?

So they basically bake in their own failure as part of their business model to make sure that they make a profit, to put money aside for rainy day in case they don't make it to Europe.

No, no, no — because that's already baked in. They're profitable even without going to Europe, right? So this money has just been piling during these years, these seven or eight years that they've been failing in Europe. They've been piling up cash in the bank. They're now sat on about 90 million pounds of cash in the bank with a main stand at Parkhead that desperately needs knocking down and turning into a massive cash machine, which would then give them the revenues to then go and be seriously competitive in Europe.

But the board refuses to spend that money, right? It just leaves it in the bank account and every year the same thing happens.

转会窗口的时间错配

What happens every single year is they go and sell three or four players in the relatively early stages of the transfer window. They then sit on that money to wait for bargains towards the back end of the transfer window.

What's the problem with that within a European calendar, Charlie?

The European qualifying games happen before the end of the transfer window, right? So every single year they start European qualifying with a squad that is short — on the basis of "well, we don't want to overpay to bring players in before we play our European games." Right? So they're already accepting that they are going to be weak in Europe. They've got a business model that's predicated off then failing in Europe.

董事会与球迷的错位

And meanwhile, the fans are providing all of the money — because the board is a quoted company. It's a stock-market-quoted company. So the board — it's so dysfunctional as to be almost unfathomable, right?

The board is led effectively by a non-executive director. So last year when they had big ructions over changes of managers and all this type of stuff, there was a statement put out on behalf of the club by the club's non-executive director who owns about 30-odd% of the shareholding, Dermot Desmond.

What's a non-executive director doing making statements in the public domain? He bought his shares and built up a shareholding in the club as a listed-company investor, and yet effectively he's now running the club and putting out statements on behalf of the club and overseeing a strategy — if you can dignify it with that word — which basically says: "We're going to take in all of our fans' money because we've got such an enormous fan base. We know they're going to carry on spending money with us no matter what. We're going to chuck it in the bank account here and we're just going to sit back and watch our club — one of the biggest clubs in the world — beat St Mirren and claim that that's successful."

流浪者衰落带来的意外庇护

Now, the one thing that has saved them during this terrible period under Dermot Desmond has been, of course, that Rangers went into a meltdown. If you remember, they went through a period. They overspent. They got themselves way in over their head. They went bankrupt. Had to go all the way down to the bottom of the Scottish pyramid and fight their way back up again. And it's probably only just about now when Rangers is in a roughly stable financial position.

So effectively, because Celtic have been winning the title more or less every year — although last year they shouldn't have done; they should have been beaten by Hearts last year, which would have been an epic upset, but they still just scraped across the line with a hell of a dodgy refereeing decision in the second-last game, a penalty which I would have been very upset if it been given against my club if I was Hearts — a handball on the edge of the box. But leaving that to one side:

Because they're winning the title, the board claims that that's success. And the fan base says, "No, no, no, no. You misunderstand the nature of why 60,000 of us turn up. We don't turn up to support a club because we beat St Mirren. We turn up to support a club that represents our entire culture, our entire identity, which has a proud history of operating at the top table, indeed being former Champions League winners themselves."

罕见地站在球迷一边

So there's a total mismatch between the fan base and the directors. And for once, I'm on the side of the fan base. And I'm on the side of the fan base because they're the ones putting all the money in.

Normally it's the owners putting the money in and the fans shouting at them — telling the owners "you should be putting more in," right? And I go, "Well, hang on a second. If you want more money to be spent on your club, how about if you start paying more in ticket prices?" At Celtic, it's the other way around. It's the fans who put money into the club and the directors who then sit back and say, "Well, you know what? On balance, actually, we're not going to spend your money on what you want us to spend it on. We're just going to stick it in the bank."

场上溃败的责任归属

Where does that feature from the behind-the-scenes perspective — looking at, as you've just said, probably one of the biggest chokes? Where you could have had a manager who had done X number of things throughout a game; you could have had an ownership who'd operated incredibly well — as you said, when you're 4–nil up in a game to qualify for a Champions League and, you know, cruising — there's an element of that which is just players on the pitch taking your responsibility. Is it all a product?

Of course. But who do those players, where do those players come from? How much have those players played? What is the recruitment team in place that selects those players? Does Celtic have a technical director? No. Who is the Celtic head coach? Martin O'Neill — bless him. A good manager 20 years ago, but in his mid-70s now and having had health problems, etc.

It's almost like the Celtic board don't actually know any managers other than Martin O'Neill. Every time that they're in trouble, they go, "Oh, what should we do? Should we give Martin a call?"

结构性僵化与出路

The whole situation is so sclerotic and mad. Now, I know the Celtic fans have gone into sort of this little campaign saying "not a penny more" in terms of extra-mural spending. They don't want to give up going to games, but they don't want to be spending on lots of other things to prop up this bonkers, failed non-strategy.

But you can't help but think at some point something has to give here. This club needs to be bought out. It needs to be bought out — or it needs to use the fact that it is a big financial beast to become a proper quoted company with a proper independent board to actually apply the fans' money in a strategic and progressive way.

I just don't know how the lack of self-awareness and the lack of ability to sort of just look in the mirror and ask questions of myself — that must beset Dermot Desmond and the crew around him — is that surely you are, surely you should be able to see as an intelligent man that what you are doing is not being seen as successful by your entire customer base. You cannot enjoy the fact that whenever you come to Celtic Park, you're being made not to feel welcome.

Is this a 15-, 20-year thing really, you know, at a time when clubs of Celtic size are generally speaking being perceived as being quite valuable in terms of asset class? He could walk out of here with a very healthy profit in terms of what he originally paid for those shares in the first place. So what's the purpose of hanging on?

That's what no one knows. It's not about money. Desmond's a billionaire and he would make a profit out of getting out at this point anyway. It's not because he's got some alternative plan — because the only plan that he and his board have got is to suck in all the money, stick it in the bank account and reappoint Martin O'Neill.

Right? So, I just don't understand what's going on in their mind. I can see what's going on in the fan base's mind. I think it's totally reasonable. Anyhow, there we are. It is what it is.

PR 问题掩盖了真正的问题

Just like Celtic losing to LASK is a PR problem. But the PR problem bit of it is less fundamental and less important than the actual core bit of it, which is: professional elite sportsmen who need to be operating at the peak of their performance — potentially, in Carse's case, he's one tweak of a hamstring away from one of the other bowlers from actually having to run out and open the bowling at Lord's four days later, something like that.

It's like the performance element of this is what continually irks me.

"两杯啤酒"的稻草人谬误

I'll tell you the other thing that irks me: English cricket — and I will put it really broadly, including the cricketers themselves, the coaches, the people at the MCC or the ECB, the cricket media, ex-players who are in the cricket media — they create this fake straw man, Charlie, which is: "Well, of course, no one minds, you know, no one, you know, anyone who's against a couple of pints, a couple of pints" (hence your quip early on about us on Sunday night, you know) — "No one's suggesting that people shouldn't have a couple of pints. If it were a beer or two, we would never hear about it. We would never hear about these things if it was a beer or two.

Do you think that Harry Brook gets chinned by a bouncer in New Zealand after two beers? Do we think that Ben Duckett wanders around New Zealand asking where his hotel is after two beers? Do we think that Brydon Carse gets handcuffed outside a nightclub in Derby after two beers?

This is not two beers. This is a drinking binge. Not to say that one doesn't do it from time to time, but this is clearly something that's happening on a very very regular basis and is being smiled upon by the whole cricketing establishment as a "boys will be boys" type thing. And then subsequently there's a "Oh, well, I mean, you shouldn't be so stupid as to get caught." Okay, but how about not doing it in the first place?

Well, how about not getting arrested? I mean, even if you're going to go — I mean, you know, genuinely I joke, but you know, how many times do you go out and get in trouble with the police? It seems ridiculous.

宵禁与合约体育的成人化难题

And Charlie, I wanted to ask a question on the curfew piece because that was something that we brought up. True of professional sports people in general. But I just want to — that is true of a lot of professional sports people. I'm going to except golfers from this, who tend to mature over time and have to look after themselves and their own performance is — they have to work out, "if I go and get absolutely smashed and don't play very well, I don't earn as much money."

The problem about team sports and contracted team sports is that from the age of about 16, 17 these guys are being given quite a lot of money on a guaranteed basis to be part of a team, where your own individual performance, yeah, might dip a little bit, but does that change your contract? No. So as long as you turn up enough over the course of a season —

Now, the very very top players hold themselves to a very high account and there will always be those people. You know, I remember hearing from a friend of mine who was a journalist who was on the Ashes tour last winter, who said, "Do you know who the two batsmen netting on the MCG on Christmas Day were? Steve Smith and Joe Root."

Shock. QED. The two best batsmen in the world are the ones out practicing.

So, there are certain elite sports people even in team environments — where you're on guaranteed contracts — who are able to hold themselves to a very high account. But in general, I wouldn't trust I wouldn't trust them an inch.

足球俱乐部的宵禁实践

I can't remember — did you have curfews when you were running football clubs?

Oh, yeah. Yeah. Oh, yeah. I mean, not imposed by me. Yeah. I have to say. I mean, the m— the so — football clubs every single week —

Let's say you got an away game on a Saturday. They will travel on at the very Friday morning, sometimes even Thursday, but Friday morning, right? And on the Friday evening. But sometimes also the Tuesday night they'll be staying in a hotel away, and sometimes they'll be staying even in the night after being away.

So quite often, given the amount of away matches there are because of the cups and all this type of stuff, you know, two to three nights a week professional footballers are staying in hotels in a team environment away from home.

If the question you're asking me is: do football managers place considerable restrictions on what footballers do under these circumstances? Bloody right they do. Absolutely they do. 100%. Yeah.

I mean, the idea that "oh yeah, don't worry lads, go out and have a few beers" — not in a million years.

And that is the thing which most worries me about this. I read an article the other day when someone said — it was an English cricket person, I can't remember who it was, it wasn't a player, it was a commentator or a former player — said, "Of course, you know, I was quite surprised actually when I was over in India to find that actually when they win matches they don't go out and get smashed afterwards."

Why are you surprised? I don't — this is totally bizarre. You know, "Yeah, so it was interesting watching Sachin. He seemed to be quite happy with a cup of tea and a bottle of sparkling water afterwards."

Oh, no Sherlock. Right? They have got themselves into this bubble where they honestly think that getting absolutely smashed all the time is absolutely fine and has no impact on your performance and has no impact on injuries. "Oh, just make sure not to get caught, lads."

It's just wrong. It's just wrong. I'm sorry. It's wrong.

骨灰杯赛程与北方赛场的缺失

The performance side reminded me — with the fact that after a really good result at Headingley, one of the great grounds in the north of England — there are going to be no Ashes tests in the north. Old Trafford and Headingley most notably left out of the five venues that will be played at in 2027.

I've seen a lot of people come out and start talking about this, questioning that decision again because it doesn't seem to make a huge amount of sense — and whether it is from an England performance perspective, a business perspective, or whether it's just from ensuring that the parts of the country which have cricket at their heart, i.e. like a Yorkshire, being omitted from the opportunity to host a test match for a great series.

You would have thought one of Old Trafford or Headingley —

100%, Charlie. Absolutely. Funny enough, I actually think it's a bit odd — the focus on holding international matches at Southampton. Yeah. It was something that came off the back of that. But hey, look, should we celebrate something? England won a test match.

第三部分：Alexander Čeferin 的重磅访谈

一次难得的公开对话

Charlie, there was quite an impressive interview that came out this week moving into football between The Rest is Politics — Alistair Campbell — and Alexander Čeferin, which is a great scoop for them because Čeferin doesn't generally give many interviews. And I thought a really interesting kind of choice of platform in the context of where we consume most of our sports media. Campbell was probably a pretty good person to sit down and have that chat with, considering a huge amount of the stuff we've been talking about with FIFA and UEFA has a serious political edge. You know, what did you think of it? Because I really enjoyed it.

And it was great. I think it showcased so much — so many of the reasons why he's such a good leader of UEFA.

I thought it was a great interview first of all. It's easy to forget sometimes Alastair Campbell was originally a top-line journalist on the Daily Mirror. And when I saw Alastair Campbell — you know, I hope we're evenhanded enough to be able to praise other podcasts, right? — this was Alastair Campbell as journalist.

If you watch him on The Rest is Politics generally, it's just him going on and on about some sort of, you know, mad chip on his shoulder he's got about left-wing, right? It's seriously dull.

This was Alastair Campbell as a journalist. And what he did brilliantly, he let Čeferin speak. He didn't come with a whole bunch of his own views and his own opinions. He asked some reasonable questions and Čeferin just answered them. He answered every single one without any kind of top spin or side spin or any attempt to try and dodge it. It was calm, but it was absolutely clear.

I came away from that interview knowing exactly what Alexander Čeferin thinks. Even on stuff that was difficult. So he was asked, you know, "How do you feel now about the whole Super League fiasco?" "Well, I feel betrayed by Andrea Agnelli." He didn't have to say that.

That's a sign of a good interview. An interview where the person who's being interviewed feels like he can start to really say what he thinks and feels because the guy who's sat opposite him is creating that environment. I thought it was an outstanding interview.

「这是我们的钱」

But there was some stuff in there which I really want to pick out, Charlie, and talk about.

Čeferin said at one point in relation to UEFA compared to FIFA and the future and what's been happening recently and all the controversies — not just the one about FIFA Ford Enterprises, but all the rest — he said: "One leader of a national association or federation said to me the other day, 'Alexander, this is our money.'" Right?

And Čeferin then went on to say, "And that guy was correct — because 75% of the revenues generated by FIFA are generated by European countries."

Now, this is a point that I made a few weeks ago when this whole thing first blew up, which is: there's been a willing sort of murder from European football over the last 10, 15, 20 years to sort of hide the fact that basically the whole thing's paid for by Europe, right? "Let's not seem like we're colonialists" or whatever the — comes up with from various people is rubbish. But whatever, let's just play nice and let's try and spread our wealth around, and FIFA is the way in which that money gets spread around. And you know, that's all good. We want to see the game develop more broadly.
