一个「感觉良好」的赛季

Should we have a quick look at the PGA Tour?

Talking about organizations that not just are investable but have been heavily invested recently. The US PGA Tour is reaching the climax of what must — must feel good to be a PGA Tour executive right now.

Charlie, champion year, isn't it?

Oh, champion year. God, especially when you're — key, your golfers are coming out in their media, in their media chats. And as you said, you know, for the Čeferin piece, isn't it lovely when someone actually sits down and answers a question? And whether it's the executives doing it or the athletes like Rory McIlroy, or if it's Patrick or others just sticking the knife just further into those that —

Joyous exchange between McIlroy and Westwood in the last couple weeks. Did you see that?

I did. I loved it.

McIlroy basically came out and said, "I thought LIV — I always thought LIV was a shower of — and I've been proved to be right." And Westwood — in that sort of, you can imagine that 20 years ago, 25 years ago, he was the senior guy in the Ryder Cup team room and Rory was the junior guy. Yeah. Right. And he came out this — yeah, "Well, Rory just often gets these things wrong." But sorry, Lee. No, he got it right and you got it wrong. You know, the fact that he's rubbing salt on the wound now doesn't mean he wasn't right all along and he didn't call it right.

PGA Tour 的漂亮反击

Anyhow, the US PGA Tour — we've been through it before. They basically from a very poor position that they started the whole LIV war in, they then played an absolute blinder. They propped up the European tour here. They took in external financing here. They created an equity percentage of the commercial arm of what they do here for the big players to incentivize them to stick around. They increased prize money and they tightened up their FedEx Cup playoff system at the end of the season, which is now — I think — epic.

I think the FedEx Cup is brilliant. I don't follow the US PGA religiously week by week, but I do follow the FedEx Cup — because when you think about the format of the FedEx Cup, which Charlie will lay out in a moment, it's the exact opposite of what LIV was doing.

Right? So what LIV was doing is they were doing everything possible to make it as uncompetitive as possible, right? So if you're on the LIV tour, you are automatically on the LIV Tour unless you perform really, really badly, but basically you're on for the time of your contract. We're not going to bother having a cut. So in other words, in the US PGA tour and indeed the European tour and all other professional tournaments, halfway through the tournament, the bottom number of players — it's not quite half, but almost half — bottom number of players have to just leave and don't get any prize money at all. Have to bugger off back home having made a loss on the weekend.

LIV said, "Well, we're going to get rid of the cut, thus removing a whole layer of jeopardy. Um, we're going to basically pay massive appearance money contracts to be here, etc."

The FedEx Cup is the opposite of all that. It's the most brutally meritocratic sporting thing that you can ever ever see.

FedEx Cup 的漏斗结构

Do you want to lay it out, Charlie?

Yeah. So the reason we're talking about it actually is because the final tournament, the Tour Championship, actually is on right now. So this coming out on a Friday, it started on Thursday.

And really throughout the whole season — so the PGA tour season — you have all of the individual tournaments, but behind it you have a point system. And the point system, you're accumulating points based on how you're performing in various events throughout that season. And come the end of the season — pretty much where we are right now — you have three events.

And the three events are: first one, top 70 players. So first, if you haven't — you know, 140 odd players on the PGA tour — the bottom half don't make it to the FedEx Cup. These three events — so the top 70 players play in that first event. The second event, which we just had, the BMW Championship, which Wyndham Clark won. That then cuts the field down. That that's then 50 players that event. After the BMW Championship, we then go into the Tour Championship, which is what we've got on now, which is 30. The final 30 players.

从「让分」到「公平对决」

Now, previously what had happened on the tour is when it got down to this final event, whoever was one to 30 in those rankings — if you were number one, you would start on minus 10. If you were number two, you were eight under.

Minus 10 in the golf scoring system, which means that that is like starting off like you're 2–nil up in football.

Yeah. Now, if to make it fair, you really need to be starting Scottie Scheffler on plus 10, right? And putting everything else together. The challenge with it is that — well, the thought behind it is clear. You play very well throughout a whole season. When it gets to this flagship event, which has huge prize money attached to it — about 10 million for this specific event, and then there's a tour of merit type thing which is about $22 million, I think, on top of that for the winner — they get rewarded for their performance throughout the season by starting in an incredibly favorable position.

However, while that makes a lot of sense, it was a challenge from a viewership perspective. Because yes, the most likely candidate to be number one is probably the best player. If you give them the head start, it doesn't create a great product for the fans. That final little bit of the players who were already towards the top of the FedEx rankings —

You have the top 30 players coming in to an event. And this is — you said it — is the most meritocratic piece. It is the top 30 players throughout a whole season. No one can have a complaint that if you're not there, you should be there. Everyone knows what you got to do. Why not start it and have it as a flat-out shootout from word go?

粉丝调查驱动的变革

Now the PGA tour, from all of its learnings of the last few years, one of them has been a real focus on what the fans want. And what they've done to change this has been driven by the fans.

All of you who may skip through surveys and everything, right — won't skip through a survey if your sports organization that you follow and love gives you the opportunity to have a say to change how a tournament operates. So the fans — 50,000 people, 50,000 fans of the PGA Tour — got on one of these surveys and basically highlighted the scoring system in the Tour Championship as an issue for them.

And so the PGA tour listened to that. There would have been consultation with the players. If you listen to someone like Scottie Scheffler, he's actually kind of said, "Look, you know, I could win every tournament from now to the end of the season and get two shots at the final. Like it doesn't make it's not the end of the world." So the players weren't basically saying, "We have to have that advantage." And therefore, it was quite an easy change for them to make.

I think the difference that it has made to the product though I think will be huge, because you really then do come back to this incredibly exciting shootout of the best players against each other. They have also, interestingly, building into the whole live fan fair piece that everyone was very excited about — you know, they are going really hard at the concessions, the food stuff on site, the entertainment that's going to be around it. They're making this kind of Tour Championship final a proper thing.

The money obviously is a huge part of it and the PGA Tour has really upped its prize money. I mean, got to 200 odd million into the prize part. But at the heart of it still is a really great product. And this is a fantastic exciting way to round off a season.

顶尖 10 人的名单

Here are the players in the top 10, right? This is these are the people who will be playing off for FedEx Cup: Scottie Scheffler, Rory McIlroy, Collin Morikawa, Tommy Fleetwood, Matt Fitzpatrick, Wyndham Clark, Cameron Young, Ludvig Åberg, Sungjae Im, Si Woo Kim — these are just the best players in the world, right?

So this is a full-on major, but only for the top 30. Yeah. That's how — it's nice to have that sometimes a total outsider can win it, like happened in the Open, and sometimes in this case it's going to be one of the big stars who's going to win it because the only people who qualify it are the very biggest stars who have been winning a lot on the tour in the first place.

If you look at who's won it previously — I think Rory's won it three times, Tommy Fleetwood was the defending champion, Tiger won it twice — and that's just in the last 18 years it's actually been going, right. So it absolutely has been the apex of the game from a pure meritocracy and pure performance basis.

在传统中创新，把奖金放进养老金

So I just think it's an interesting example of a really thoughtful structuring of something where — innovation, you can innovate within tradition, right? So you can keep the absolute tenets — we're a four-round competition. It's 72 holes. It's all about who stroke play event and all this. But there's stuff that we can do that makes it more interesting and that gives it more of a narrative arc.

Another interesting thing I found about this is from the FedEx bonuses. A big chunk of them get paid into players' pensions.

Yeah, I didn't know that. You told me that.

Yeah. Again, it's something which has been done in discussion with the players.

Why do you find that interesting?

Do you remember I said to you about how I felt that really effective trade unions work with their employers to work out what is the best balance, the most sustainable best balance for all parties — balancing lots of different things.

So this clearly has been a result of negotiations with the players over a number of years where they say, "you know what, actually one thing we could do here, because there are some golfers and always have been who do blow their career earnings whilst they are at the peak of their powers and end up, you know, having to — dare I say it — sell stuff from Hooters outside the US Masters every year, which I know is great fun, but it's still a bit odd that a two-time major champion basically is hawking concessions outside the Masters."

Apparently, it is so fun. Apparently, it's great, but I'm just saying it's a bit sad he has to do it.

Charlie, we'd be there. Of course, we'd be there. Of course, we'd be contributing to John Daly's old age.

与球员的成熟合作

But I do think it's just a really interesting example of how mature current relations are between the US PGA tour and the leading players on the US PGA tour. You just mentioned there about Scottie Scheffler's very mature reaction to being told that he wasn't going to get a several-shot head start, etc.

And then you look back on how they actually beat LIV was through cooperation with the leading players. That cooperation happens because you're already on good relations with them. And the players get huge benefits from that.

Yeah. Right. Because once you start to get that influence — do you remember what I said about the PFA, which is I think the PFA should be very focused on the calendar. I think there are real risks to footballers' physical well-being and their career longevity from the current way in which the calendar's progressing.

If you're at the top table and if you have been shown to be cooperative on stuff which really matters to the organizations and the employers, you absolutely have the authority then to say, "guys, there's some stuff we do need to talk about here." But if you're the type of player organization, the type of trade union who's just got "give us more money, we want more money, more money," then effectively you're basically just pushing yourself down the food chain and you go, "okay, you're just one of those guys. Okay, well here have a bit more cash and off."

Right? So I think that that is a really good example — the US PGA tour of how the organizations and players can rise together. And I love it. I'm so, you know, happy with the way in which the PGA Tour has safeguarded golf. You know, if we talk about the way in which UEFA has been safeguarding football, the PGA Tour has been safeguarding golf from what was frankly in my view a really risky way of doing it.

一个警示：如果 LIV 消失了呢？

No, I will caveat it. With — now if LIV doesn't continue at all in any capacity, what continues on the PGA side, what gets dropped if it gets its monopoly back? Do we keep that balance?

I think prize money has to come down. And I've seen, you know, I think I quoted before a couple of players — senior players — saying, "look, it's not sustainable to keep prize money at current levels."

Paul McGinley said that, right? So they know that the reason why prize money is so high at the moment is because of the LIV threat. They know this and they're intelligent enough to understand it and they're intelligent enough to know that the US PGA tour can't keep on taking external finance because that external finance is going to eat away at the equity which they themselves have earned in their own commercial arms.

They're very aligned in that way. So I think it's a really good ecosystem and I would encourage anybody who's got an interest in golf to pay some attention to Tour Championship this week. It's going to be a cracker.

收尾

Yeah. Do you know what else is a cracker? Being back in the studio with you Charles.

Oh Charles, thank you very much.

It's been fun. I think as you said earlier on, we should go for a couple of beers now.

I've got meetings. I'm working.

For those of us who are interested, you'll be seeing Charlie outside a police station on the King's Road in about 10 hours from now after a couple of beers.

Be arrested. I'll just be handcuffed. Big difference.

Thank you guys. We'll see you next week.

Thanks a lot.

观看原视频 →
item.description:
## 失败作为一种商业模式：凯尔特人的"负向护城河"
大多数俱乐部把失败视为成本，凯尔特人却把它变成了**资产负债表的润滑剂**。他们的运营逻辑令人惊讶地类似于**保险公司的精算模型**——预设每年欧冠出局的"损失概率"，然后通过压低支出、囤积现金来抵消这种失败带来的收入缺口。但这里有一个致命的悖论：**保险公司卖的是"你不出事我赚钱"，而凯尔特人卖的是"我们出事你还得买"**。90 million镑现金堆在银行，主看台亟待重建，而 Dermot Desmond 却像一个把股东红利锁在保险箱里的信托管理人——问题在于，他管理的不是资本，而是**60,000人的文化身份**。
这里有一个跨领域的连接值得思考：凯尔特人的困境与日本"僵尸企业"的现象惊人相似——不是因为亏损而僵化，而是因为**过度稳健而丧失了冒险的肌肉**。当一个组织的KPI从"赢得欧冠"退化为"不破产"，它就已经在心理上离场了。
## 英国板球的"男孩终究是男孩"叙事：一种被制度化的幼稚
真正令人意外的观察不是球员喝酒，而是**整个板球生态系统对"稚气未脱"的集体默许**。Charlie点出了一个关键结构性问题：*

item.title: [Lex Clips] Secret to 10x productivity with AI agents: Why most companies fail | DHH and Lex Fridman
item.dc:creator: Lex Clips
item.content:encoded:
💡 创造性洞见

一、真正被 AI 取代的不是程序员，而是"中间协调层"

DHH 这段话最反常识的洞察是：AI 革命的真正牺牲品，不是媒体天天渲染的"码农"，而是产品经理、VP、CTO、审批链这一整套中层结构。程序员反而变得更重要——因为唯有他能直接和 agent 对话，把 10x/100x/1000x 的杠杆拉满。

一旦你在人和 agent 之间插入一个"human bandwidth"，杠杆就瞬间坍缩回 1x。这意味着过去二十年里，硅谷精心搭建的整套 Scrum/JIRA/sprint/design review 机制，本质上是对"程序员注意力稀缺"的补偿性组织架构——就像人身体里的阑尾，是对早已不存在的饮食结构的历史遗迹。当稀缺性消失，整套补偿机制就变成了纯负债。所以大公司做不到 10x，不是因为它们不够聪明，而是因为它们的免疫系统会主动排斥直接人机交互——那会让一大批高薪岗位的存在理由蒸发。

二、"每个人自己的 5%"：软件产品这个类目正在死去

DHH 顺手抛出了一个几乎没人展开的经济学炸弹：Office 每个人只用 5%，但每个人用的是不同的 5%。过去四十年整个 SaaS 商业模式的底层逻辑，就是把 10 亿人的 5% 打包成一个产品，让所有人为其他 95% 付费——这是软件的规模经济。

Agent 时代把这个模型彻底反过来了：从"打包分销"回到"自织自穿"。这不是渐进式创新，这是软件从"产品"退化成"手工艺品"。有意思的跨领域联想是：这正是古登堡印刷术之前和之后的镜像倒转——中世纪每本书都是手抄孤本（个人化），古登堡之后变成大规模分发（标准化），而 AI agent 让软件从"印刷时代"退回到"手抄时代"，但没有失去印刷的速度。DHH 20 分钟写出 Typora 替代品，就是软件领域的私人手抄本复兴。

三、"不耐烦"作为一种新的经济信号

这段对话里一句被轻描淡写的话其实是全场最狠的："impatience is the first step of doing it yourself." 在前 agent 时代，用户的挫败感是终端信号——你只能忍受、抱怨、迁移到另一个也很烂的产品。挫败感是一个死胡同。

在 agent 时代，挫败感变成了创业信号。DHH 讨厌 Typora 的臃肿——过去这只能变成一条 Reddit 抱怨帖，现在直接变成一个 C++ QT 应用。这里藏着一个更黑暗的洞察：未来最好的软件不会由"用户需求调研"驱动，而会由"个人怨恨"驱动。Grievance-driven development（怨恨驱动开发）会取代 user-centered design。

跨领域连接：这和博客对报纸编辑部的瓦解是同构的。1995 年一个人对某篇报道不满，只能写信到编辑部；2005 年他直接开博客反驳。中间那层"编辑审稿链"消失了，因为出版的边际成本归零。今天软件正在经历同样的时刻——"发布"和"发怒"之间的距离正在归零。而当这个距离归零，DHH 说的"polyglot programmer"就不再是精英标签，而是普通人的默认状态：语言精通被商品化，品味和视野变成稀缺资源。这是编程史上第一次，"想清楚要什么"比"能实现什么"更贵。

📝 转录文本

Lex 的提问：为什么成熟软件的开发没有加速？

Lex: Can you tell me the intuition you have? I seem to just stepping back and observing the different apps that we all rely on — I don't know, Adobe Photoshop, all this kind of stuff. There seems to be — the progress on development there has not accelerated. So why is it? What lessons can you draw from Basecamp, like well-established huge user base? Why aren't we seeing like super rapid increase in new updates, features, all this kind of stuff in these well-established apps?

DHH 的回答 (一)：瓶颈从来不是实现，而是人的带宽

DHH: Multiple reasons. I'll start with the first one that's the most critical.

As soon as you're having human teams work together on something, the bottleneck is rarely implementation. It's human bandwidth and communication. When you have a product manager and a couple of designers and a VP above them and a CTO above them, and everyone wants to be part of the shaping process because we're all justifying why we're here — that's where all the productivity goes to die.

The revelation I've had working on Amachi the last 3 months is that to get that magical 10x, 100x, in a few rare cases a 1,000x productivity boost, you have to interact with the agents directly. And you cannot intermediate that bandwidth with another human because it's simply too slow.

And on the one hand that's a bit of a bummer. I mean, I like humans and it's great to work together. But it also means we need to temper our expectations with what these agents can do if it's humans driving it and you have three layers of approval and all the other machinery of a large corporation — the implementation part is only a small segment of it.

(二) 组织真正缺的不是实现能力，而是想法、视野和品味

The other thing I'd say is that most organizations don't know what they want. They don't know how to make it better. They're not bottlenecked on implementation — they're bottlenecked on ideas. They're bottlenecked on vision. They're bottlenecked on taste. And if you don't have those elements in excess of your implementational capacity, it doesn't help.

So you can make a lot of shitty ideas come true — then what? Are you going to ship that? That sounds like, I don't know, something coming out of Microsoft. That's not what we're trying to replicate here. That process is not actually — because we already had this.

If you step back for a moment and think of the towering organizations we have who have had tens of thousands of programmers at their disposal — I mean, I'm picking on Microsoft here. I love Microsoft some of the time. But I'll pick on them in this case because they have had endless resources, endless programming capacity for decades, right? This is what's showing us that just being able to write a lot of code does not produce great compelling software.

(三) 对"AI 还不够快"的反击

Now, the other thing is — we've had this capacity for about 6 months. That's not very long in human life cycle capacity of internalizing what's going on.

And I think it's actually funny that the critique of AI is, "Why isn't it going faster?" What are you talking about? We've not had any other form of progress that has moved as fast as AI. And you're impatient because in the last 3 months we haven't rewritten the whole world and made it a utopia of software goodness.

Lex：那 Linux 桌面呢？谁来重写 Premiere 和 Photoshop？

Lex: You're basically saying everybody should be switching to Linux now. One of the arguments is like — we can rewrite all the software that's not available in Linux, in Linux. Linux has been the love of my life for many years, but one of the reasons I'm still attached to Windows and now Mac is because of video editing, Premiere.

DHH: We're going to fix that, but —

Lex: So the question is, who's going to build Premiere and Photoshop for Linux? And it feels like one person can now —

DHH: 100% one person can.

Lex: And so — and I'm allowed to be impatient. In fact, me or anyone else — impatience is the first step of doing it yourself, right?

DHH: Correct.

Lex: And there's a community of tens of thousands of people that use Adobe Premiere or DaVinci, all these non-linear video editors, that know the frustrations. Everybody shares them. You can look at Reddit, you can look at the forums. Everybody knows it.

I don't know what it is — maybe the management, maybe the meetings, all the things you've always discussed is the bureaucracy that's in development of features — but it feels like if you just let some of the developers loose with a bunch of agents, you can fix all that. But again, based on everything you're saying, maybe the way to do that is to start over from scratch, maybe through open source, or somebody launches a new company. Within large companies now, it's hard to really accelerate into the agentic era by letting developers just build.

DHH：这是经典的"创新者窘境"

DHH: This is the classic innovator's dilemma. These companies have gotten so good, so established at the old way, and therefore their entire structure — management layers, processes — are tuned for a time that no longer exists. But you can't pivot that. These are supertankers. It just doesn't happen.

This is why we're finally getting this upset in the technology industry. For a while, I was very upset about the duopoly between Apple and Google on mobile, because it felt like mobile was the most important computing platform that we had, and I could not see a path to unseat either Google or Apple sitting on top of that, controlling everything, taking their toll booth money.

But the game changed. This is no longer the most important platform. Mobile phones are important, but there's also a lot of other form factors coming — whether it's glasses or earpieces or whatever else have you. It's all in play now.

计算平台四十年来第一次真正松动

But the computing platforms themselves are in play for the first time in probably 40 years, if you look at the desktop.

Linux has been around since '91. It's not taken off or taken over on the desktop. It's taken over everything else. All the devices you have on your desk, your fridge, your toaster — everything runs Linux except for your computer. Now, funnily enough, your Android is actually Linux, but wrapped so sufficiently that you can't really recognize it.

But now there's an opening — and the opening is exactly as you say it. If there's a piece of software you depended on that bound you to Windows, it is completely within reach for you personally to start rewriting it. And maybe you won't get to 100% coverage, but — this is the old joke about Microsoft Office: I only use 5%. Yeah, well, we all use a different 5%.

Well, what if we all just built our own 5%? What if I just took the functionality that I need and just did that? That is a completely different challenge, and one agents are incredibly capable of doing right now today. And I've done it a lot of times over.

亲身案例：一个 Ruby 程序员如何变成 polyglot

So, one of the amazing things I found with the latest Agent to Gauge is I have become a polyglot programmer. Something I was absolutely not before. I was a Ruby programmer first and foremost, and then I dabbled a little bit in Bash when I had to.

And in the last 2 months I've written C++. I've written three applications that have shipped in a Mach Quattro.

20 分钟重写 Typora 的故事

I wrote a writing app. I was using this app called Typora, which is a very nice app, which in itself is based on another app called iA Writer, which was my real love on the Mac for a clean, simple markdown writing environment. That's where I write all my essays.

And then I moved to Linux and I couldn't get iA Writer, so I moved over to this other tool called Typora. It was a piece of — where — and it had a lot of features I just didn't need.

And about 6 weeks, 7 weeks ago I thought, "Do you know what? I only need 5% of Typora, which is already a basic app." I literally told the agent to get going — that I wanted it written in C++ and QT, because that would fit well with the aesthetic of what I was building with Quattro. And in, I think, about 20 minutes it had the first version.

I started using it, and it wasn't quite right. Within 2 days I'd given up Typora, and I wrote — and have written — all of my essays since that moment in iA Writer.

观看原视频 →

## 一、真正被 AI 取代的不是程序员，而是"中间协调层"
DHH 这段话最反常识的洞察是：AI 革命的真正牺牲品，不是媒体天天渲染的"码农"，而是**产品经理、VP、CTO、审批链**这一整套中层结构。程序员反而变得**更**重要——因为唯有他能直接和 agent 对话，把 10x/100x/1000x 的杠杆拉满。
一旦你在人和 agent 之间插入一个"human bandwidth"，杠杆就瞬间坍缩回 1x。这意味着过去二十年里，硅谷精心搭建的整套 Scrum/JIRA/sprint/design review 机制，本质上是**对"程序员注意力稀缺"的补偿性组织架构**——就像人身体里的阑尾，是对早已不存在的饮食结构的历史遗迹。当稀缺性消失，整套补偿机制就变成了纯负债。所以大公司做不到 10x，不是因为它们不够聪明，而是因为它们的**免疫系统**会主动排斥直接人机交互——那会让一大批高薪岗位的存在理由蒸发。
## 二、"每个人自己的 5%"：软件产品这个类目正在死去
DHH 顺手抛出了一个几乎没人展开的经济学炸弹：Office 每个人只用 5%，但每个人用的是**不

item.title: [Lex Clips] The biggest threat to Apple | DHH and Lex Fridman
item.dc:creator: Lex Clips
item.content:encoded:
💡 创造性洞见

一、"5% 悖论"背后的软件工业革命反转

DHH 顺手抛出的那个"我只用 Office 的 5%，只是每人用的都不是同一个 5%"的老段子，其实藏着一个足以让整个 SaaS 时代动摇的观察：过去 40 年，软件之所以必须"通用化"，是因为分销和开发成本极高，只能靠"最大公约数"回本；而 Agent 让这个经济学假设彻底反转——每个人只写自己那 5% 的成本，第一次低于购买通用软件的成本。

这不是"AI 让我写代码更快"，而是软件从规模化工业品回到手工定制品的相变。就像 3D 打印没有杀死宜家，但让"我需要一个刚好卡在这个墙角、正好这个高度的柜子"从奢侈品变成日常。真正被威胁的不是苹果这个公司，而是"通用软件"这个品类本身存在的合理性。

二、Linux 的"隐形登基":最大威胁从不是同类竞争者

一个几乎没人愿意点破的反常识事实——Linux 早就赢了，只是赢的方式让所有人都没认出来。你的路由器、冰箱、烤面包机、Android、汽车中控、数据中心，全是 Linux。它输掉的只有你桌上那台电脑，而这恰恰是最没意义的那场战役。

这里有一个跨领域的强烈共振：这和电力革命的路径几乎一模一样。爱迪生和特斯拉打得你死我活时，没人意识到最终的胜利者不是"某个电力公司"，而是"电"本身变成了看不见的基础设施，藏在每一面墙里。Linux 对 Apple 的真正威胁，不是有一天你会装 Ubuntu，而是"操作系统"这个概念本身正在像电力一样蒸发成后台。当 Agent 成为你和机器之间的新界面，Windows/macOS/Linux 之争会像"你家用交流电还是直流电"一样无人关心。

三、DHH 自己就是他描述的那艘"超级油轮"——而他成功掉头了

最出人意料的一层，是这段独白的元叙事：DHH 是 Ruby on Rails 的作者，是"用一门语言解决所有 Web 问题"这一整套哲学的教父。而他在这段话里得意地宣布：过去两个月他写了 C++、写了 Qt、成了 polyglot。

翻译一下潜台词——他刚刚亲手告别了自己二十年的身份认同，而且语气轻松得像在换一双鞋。这才是这段视频里最值得警觉的信号：当连"框架布道者"这种最深度锁定于某个技术栈的身份都能在 20 分钟内溶解，那么苹果生态里所有靠"Xcode/Swift/App Store 三件套"筑起职业护城河的开发者、公司、投资逻辑，都在同一片流沙上。

跨领域再连一次：这几乎是新教改革的技术版。路德的关键突破不是"神学更好"，而是印刷术让每个人都能自己读圣经，中间的神职阶层瞬间失去了不可替代性。Agent 就是软件世界的印刷机，而 App Store、认证开发者、平台税，就是那批即将失去解释权的神职阶层。DHH 一边写着自己的 Markdown 编辑器一边说话的样子，就是 1517 年那个把《九十五条论纲》钉在教堂门上的人——表面上在聊工具，实质上在宣告一个中介阶层的黄昏。

📝 转录文本

超级油轮困境：为什么大公司无法转身

This is the classic innovator's dilemma. These companies have gotten so good, so established at the old way, and therefore their entire structure — management layers, processes — are tuned for a time that no longer exists. But you can't pivot that. These are supertankers. It just doesn't happen.

This is why we're finally getting this upset in the technology industry.

移动双寡头的松动

For a while, I was very upset about the duopoly between Apple and Google on mobile, because it felt like mobile was the most important computing platform that we had, and I could not see a path to unseat either Google or Apple sitting on top of that, controlling everything, taking their toll booth money.

But the game has changed. This is no longer the most important platform. Mobile phones are important, but there's also a lot of other form factors coming — whether it's glasses, or it's ear pieces, or whatever else have you. It's all in play now.

But the computing platforms themselves are in play for the first time in probably 40 years.

Linux 的悖论：赢下了一切，除了桌面

If you look at the desktop, Linux has been around since '91. It's not taken off or taken over on the desktop. It's taken over everything else — all the devices you have on your desk, your fridge, your toaster, everything runs Linux, except for your computer.

Now, funnily enough, your Android is actually Linux, but wrapped so sufficiently that you can't really recognize it.

5% 的突破口：Agent 时代的软件重写经济学

But now there's an opening, and the opening is exactly as you say it. If there's a piece of software you depended on that bound you to Windows, it is completely within reach for you personally to start rewriting it. And maybe you won't get to 100% coverage, but this is the old joke about Microsoft Office: "I only use 5%." Yeah, well, we all use a different 5%.

Well, what if we all just built our own 5%? What — [snorts and clears throat] — if I just took the functionality that I need and just did that?

That is a completely different challenge, and one agents are incredibly capable of doing right now, today. And I've done it a lot of times over.

亲身经历：从 Ruby 独尊到多语种程序员

So, one of the amazing things I've found with the latest agent age is I have become a polyglot programmer — something I was absolutely not before. I was a Ruby programmer first and foremost, and then I dabbled a little bit in Bash when I had to.

And in the last 2 months, I've written C++. I've written three applications that have shipped in a Mach Quattro.

案例：20 分钟重写 Typora

I wrote a writing app. I was using this app called Typora, which is a very nice app, which in itself is based on another app called iA Writer, which was my real love on the Mac for a clean, simple markdown writing environment. That's where I write all my essays.

And then I moved to Linux and I couldn't get iA Writer. So I moved over to this other tool called Typora. It was a piece of shareware, and it had a lot of features I just didn't need.

And about 6 weeks, 7 weeks ago, I thought, "Do you know what? I only need 5% of Typora" — which is already a basic app.

I literally told the agent to get going: that I wanted it written in C++ and Qt, because that would fit well with the aesthetic of what I was building with Quattro. And in, I think, about 20 minutes, it had the first version. I started using it, and it wasn't quite right. Within 2 days, I'd given up Typora, and I wrote — and have written all of my essays since that moment — in iA Writer.

item.title: [Dwarkesh Clips] Why Isn’t China Further Behind in AI? - Dylan Patel
item.dc:creator: Dwarkesh Clips
item.content:encoded:
💡 创造性洞见

一、被误读的"算力差距"：真正的瓶颈其实是"研究带宽"

大部分人把中美 AI 竞争理解成一场"电力/芯片军备竞赛"，但 Dylan 在无意间抛出了一个反直觉的拆解：在 Anthropic 手里，5 GW 的算力真正被用在"那一次预训练"上的只有不到 200 MW，占比不到 4%。剩下的 60% 训练算力里，50% 是"研究"——试架构、调数据配比、跑消融实验，10% 才是"开发"（真正的训练执行），另外 40% 是推理。

这意味着：中国头部实验室用 100–200 MW 就能"看起来不落后太多"，并不是因为他们有神秘的效率红利，而是因为当前范式下，前沿的瓶颈不是"能把训练做多大"，而是"能同时跑多少个想法"。中国以 1/25 的电力做出接近的模型，本质上是在打一场"研究带宽"的仗，而不是"训练规模"的仗——这是一个只有拆到二级预算才能看到的隐藏结构。

真正令人不寒而栗的推论在后面：一旦 automated coder / automated researcher 上线，研究和训练的比例会开始反转——研究可以被自动化打薄，训练规模反而重新成为瓶颈。也就是说，中国现在"用小算力打出大模型"的窗口，恰恰会在自动化研究员诞生的那一刻突然关闭。这不是渐进式落后，而是范式转换那一天的悬崖跌落。

二、跨领域连接：中美创新体制是两种"进化策略"

Dylan 顺口说了一句极关键的话：美国金融体系愿意"YOLO"押注初创；中国金融体系一旦选定行业，补贴力度超过全球其他国家半导体补贴的总和。

这其实是生物学里两种截然不同的进化策略： - 美国 = r-策略（大量后代，高变异，高死亡）：一次同时孵化 50 个 AI 实验室、100 个 fabless 芯片公司，跑得快的通吃。 - 中国 = K-策略（少量后代，重投入，高存活）：一旦锁定"半导体"这个生态位，就把整个资源池灌到几个国家队里，压低失败率、拉长存活时间。

推论：如果 takeoff 很快（自动化研究员两年内出现），r-策略压倒性获胜——中国还没来得及"选中赛道"就被拉开。但如果 takeoff 慢一点，K-策略反而更占优——因为 r-策略最怕的就是"资源持续消耗但环境不剧变"。所以出口管制的真正意义不是"封锁"，而是赌一场时钟战：赌自动化研究员会在中国国产芯片 hockey stick（他预测在 2028 年）之前出现。这是一场关于时间差的豪赌，不是关于绝对能力的差距。

三、意外观察：政治正在做一件"角色反转"的事

访谈里有一句极其容易被略过的话："the only thing they're going to do is accelerate it"——中国唯一会做的事就是加速 AI，而美国政客却开始尝试为 AI 踩刹车。

这在冷战叙事框架里是完全反过来的：过去我们习惯认为"威权体制会因为怕失控而减速，自由社会因为分散决策而加速"，但在 AI 这件事上，中国正在扮演历史上"美国"的角色（无脑加速），美国反而在扮演过去"苏联"式的自我审查角色。

再叠加一个隐藏的资本流向：Dylan 的"质量加权 gigawatt"概念——中国 50 GW 国产芯片 ≈ 美国 20 GW 英伟达芯片——本质上是在为算力世界发明一种类似 PPP（购买力平价）的换算单位。这是一个非常重要的思维工具：未来讨论 AI 军备竞赛，我们需要的不是"多少 GW"，而是"多少质量加权 GW"，就像讨论 GDP 需要 PPP 一样。当研究者、政策制定者、投资人还在用裸 GW 争论时，实际的战略地图早已经在另一套坐标系里展开了。

一个可能让你意外的收尾：Dylan 作为公开的自由意志主义者，居然承认出口管制"真的起作用了"——这本身就是一个信号。当一个意识形态上反对干预的人，被数据逼到承认干预有效时，说明这套结构性差距已经大到无法用理论优雅地否认了。

📝 转录文本

全球算力版图：从 2022 到今天

Q: If you think there's 200 gigawatts globally in 2028, how much is in China by that point? And how does Chinese compute continue increasing through this whole trend? Because if the RSI stuff kicks off in the West before China has a large amount of compute, maybe we're living in a different world than when it doesn't.

Dylan: Yeah, so China today — so if we sort of level set back to 2022, the US was adding about 45 to 50% of the world's compute. China was adding about 30 to 35% of the world's compute, and the rest being taken up by the rest of the world.

Since 2022, we've had big regulations against China, and a dramatic increase in America. So today, 70% of watts are being deployed in America. And, you know, China is really a very small number. It's sub-10% of watts being deployed for data center AI compute in China.

And as we step forward, they're still at a very small number. Their domestic production is quite small. Their purchasing from Nvidia is still quite small. And a lot of that ends up in other places as well, right? You know, Malaysia or what have you. So ultimately, China domestically still continues to have sub-10% of incremental new compute.

So in 2028, might start to inflect up, I think. But it's pretty easy to say China will have like 30 gigawatts of AI compute or less.

Q: By 2028?

Dylan: Yeah, in 2028.

走私、晶圆厂与 2028 拐点

Q: Okay. And then how fast does their hockey stick go up?

Dylan: I do think in 2028, they have a big uplift in what compute they're able to deploy. 2026, they're still mostly relying on a lot of the smuggled chips — you know, a lot of the chips that TSMC made for companies that they thought weren't Huawei, but ended up being Huawei, or a lot of HBM that Samsung is shipping.

But in '27, fabs start to go up. In '28 especially, fabs start to go up from SMIC and CXMT and such, where domestic production is actually reaching many millions of units a year. And now they're incrementally adding, you know, 5–10 gigawatts in just 2028 of domestically produced chips.

Those chips are definitely worse than the chips that Nvidia will have in '28, or Google will have in '28, or OpenAI will have in 2028.

质量加权：30 GW 的真实含金量

Q: So even the gigawatt number overstates things, you're saying. Like it's 30 gigawatts but it's really much worse chips. But then — how, yeah, how does it… If you think the world is going to add 100 gigawatts the following year? Or something — you know, I know you said you can't really say that far out. How much is China able to add the subsequent year? Basically, I want to know: did they just hockey stick at the point at which they are able to start shipping large amounts of compute, or is it still going to be less than US plus allies?

Dylan: There's a lot left to — you know, whether or not the US passes the MATCH Act, whether or not ex-tools continue to get export controlled, how fast China can build their new equipment that they're starting to be able to domestically produce.

But ultimately, you know, China is definitely going to hockey stick. If there's anything China's really good at, it's scaling manufacturing really, really quickly. And I imagine China will start to be able to extract more and more purchasing of even foreign chips into domestic China, or at least close the gap in what the US is allowing Nvidia to sell them or what have you.

Q: But do you think China could do adding 50 gigawatts by 2029? Marginal incremental gigawatts in 2029.

Dylan: I think that's completely reasonable. And part of that could also be purchased from foreign.

Q: Yeah.

Dylan: But yeah, I think it's completely reasonable that China in 2029 can do 50 gigs. But if most of those are the domestic chips, there is some factor there where that 50 gigawatts is really worth as much as 20 gigawatts in America — or from American chips.

Q: Right, right. So you're actually projecting a world where maybe the leading lab in 2028 has more compute than China will have in like all of China will have in '29 or even '30 — if you weight gigawatts by their quality. Implying that there's nothing to done to slow down the US labs, but clearly the government is starting — politicians are starting to do that. Whereas China is not going to slow down AI. In fact, the only thing they're going to do is accelerate it.

出口管制：一个自由意志主义者的重新评估

Q: So honestly, when Aaron and I were chatting and asked about export controls — I am a libertarian person, and I wasn't genuinely sure what I thought about this issue. I was steelmanning what is the opposite view that he has, and — because I think it's important to hash out ideas. But I'm like, yeah, maybe there's a world where if we just cooperated with China, it would be better for us, especially since they control so much of the supply chain and the other things that will be needed for robotics and other things.

But I didn't realize the compute situation was as as you're saying. Like actually the export controls do seem to have really — if they ship the amount that you're saying, that's a huge difference. By the time we have automated coder and even getting into automated researcher, China is like way far behind on the compute stock. And so if that ends up being the case, that would have worked. I think that's actually a notable success.

Dylan: I would say the only caveat there is: some of it is export controls, but some of it is also just financial systems, right? American financial systems are more willing to YOLO into startups than Chinese financial systems. But once Chinese financial systems choose an industry to focus on, they'll subsidize it a hell of a lot more.

Q: Yeah.

Dylan: And so the Chinese semiconductor industry has significantly more subsidies than the rest of the world's semiconductor industries combined — which points to, like, if takeoff is not as fast as sort of you're implying, but actually takes longer, then ultimately China will catch up drastically on the semiconductor side, which then is compute at some point.

中国实验室的"效率悖论"

The other aspect of this that I think is noteworthy is: Chinese companies today are not that far behind in AI models, at least perceivably by the public, relative to the amount of compute they have, right? The leading Chinese labs have 100–200 MW total of compute at most. ByteDance — Seed being the one outlier where they have significantly more than that. But, you know, Kimi is not running a gigawatt or anywhere close to it.

Q: Yeah.

Dylan: Whereas Anthropic is nearly 5 GW by the end of the year, right? Or more — sorry.

拆解算力预算：研究 vs 开发 vs 推理

And so the question is sort of: well, does it matter? And I think right now it doesn't matter that much, this difference in compute. Because when we break down the compute ratio or budget of a lab historically, it's been, you know, let's say 60 or so — so far it's been like 60% training, 40% inference.

But that training gets broken down further. And that's actually like: 50% of the compute is research, like 10% of the compute is development, and then 40% is inference.

And what I mean by research and development is: you know, researchers are generating ideas, testing new architectures, testing new data mixes, testing new hyperparameters, whatever it is they're doing — new attention techniques, blah blah blah. But ultimately, when they do the training run, when Anthropic trains Mythos, it's sub-200 MW, right? The pre-train of the whole —

Q: Thing.

Dylan: The pre-train. Yeah. It's sub-200 MW for call it 2 months. And then the RL is even less.

Q: Do you think the RL was less than the compute than the pre-train?

Dylan: At least in terms of single-side inference. I mean, single side of the pre-train, yeah.

Q: But total compute was probably higher, right?

Dylan: Total comp — but it's like sequential, right?

Q: Yeah.

Dylan: So at most, the most they ever used at one point in time was maybe 200 MW. And then in reality, they had multiple gigawatts, so most of their compute was going to the research, not the development of a model.

为什么无法把 2 GW 全部用于训练

And there's reasons for this, right? You can't — it's hard to coordinate all these clusters. It's hard to collocate all of them. It's hard to do multi-site training. It's hard to do RL — you know, generating even more rollouts during RL does not necessarily make it better. There's all sorts of reasons why you may not be able to leverage, you know, all 2 gigawatts that you have for training onto training, right? Actually, I can only leverage 200 megawatts.

As we get closer and as we get further and further down implementate automated coding, automated researcher, I actually expect the percentage of the compute budget that goes to research versus training to start to become a lot more fuzzy, or even higher for training. Also things like continual learning, right? All of these things start to mean that more and more is actually going to training the model.

If you enjoyed this clip, you can watch the full episode here and subscribe for more clips. Thanks.

这意味着：中国头部实验室用 100–200 MW 就能"看起来不落后太多"，并不是因为他们有神秘的效率红利，而是因为**当前范式下，前沿的瓶颈不是"能把训练做多大"，而是"能同时跑多少个想法"**。中国以 1/25 的电力做出接近的模型，本质上是在打一场"研究带宽"的仗，而不是"训练规模"的仗——这是一个只有拆到二级预算才能看到的隐藏结构。
真正令人不寒而栗的推论在后面：**一旦 automated coder / automated researcher 上线，研究和训练的比例会开始反转**——研究可以被自动化打薄，训练规模反而重新成为瓶颈。也就

item.title: [YC Root Access] How Outset Turned AI Interviews Into a New Category
item.dc:creator: YC Root Access
item.content:encoded:
💡 创造性洞见

一、最反直觉的观察：AI 不是"效率工具"，而是"人格解锁器"

大多数人把 Outset 理解为"更便宜、更快的调研工具"——这是表层叙事。真正颠覆性的发现藏在 Aaron 的一句话里："人们对 AI 说的话，比对真人说得更多。"

这才是 Outset 的真正商业底层：它不是在替代"人访谈人"这个动作，而是在利用一种新出现的人类行为模式——人在没有社会评判的情境下，会释放出连焦点小组、连一对一深访都拿不到的"地面真相 (ground truth)"。

这里有个惊人的悖论：调研行业花了 50 年训练访谈员如何"消除偏见、建立信任"，而 AI 一夜之间通过"不是人"这个特征，绕过了整个行业的方法论。 匿名树洞 App、Reddit 的深夜自白、和 ChatGPT 的私密对话——这些都是同一种人类学现象的不同切面。Outset 是第一个把这种"去人格化坦白"制度化、商品化的公司。

二、跨领域连接：Outset 走的是"新品类"的经典博弈论路径，和 Airbnb、Uber、Salesforce 是同一条曲线

Aaron 描述的"没有预算行项目 (line item)"的困境，其实和 Marc Benioff 早期卖 Salesforce 时说服 CFO"云端 CRM 不是 IT 支出而是销售效率支出"是同一个游戏。所有品类创造者都必须完成同一个动作：把自己塞进买方大脑里既有的会计科目，或者创造一个新科目。

但 Outset 有个别人没有的加速器——AI 模型每 6 个月自己变强一次。这意味着它是历史上第一批"产品价值曲线陡度大于市场教育曲线陡度"的创业公司。传统 SaaS 要花 5 年教育市场，等市场懂了产品也没升级。Outset 只需要撑到 GPT-4 出来，市场就自动从"你在说什么"变成"我们必须要"。

这是一种全新的创业物种：赌"共识时刻"的到来，而不是赌自己能造出共识。 Aaron 说 2025 年是拐点，不是巧合——那是市场心智追上模型能力的那一刻。

三、隐藏的系统性真相：Digital Twins 是在偷偷解决一个更大的问题——大公司的"决策贫困"

表面上，Digital Twin 是"随时可用的虚拟客户"。但 Aaron 无意中说漏了一句更重要的话："大公司每天做的绝大多数决策，都是基于直觉，因为没预算和时间去做调研。"

这句话揭示了一个 B 端市场从未被承认的黑洞：大公司不是缺数据，是缺"决策级"的数据消费带宽。研究团队是稀缺资源，只服务于"大项目"。而无数中层决策——一个文案、一个定价、一个功能优先级——全部裸奔。

Outset 实际上在做的事，从"调研工具"变成了"组织级直觉的置换基础设施"。这和企业软件史上一个反复出现的模式一致： - Figma 把设计从"设计师的专属"变成"所有人可参与" - Notion 把知识管理从"IT 项目"变成"个体动作"
- Outset 正在把"客户理解"从"研究团队的季度产出"变成"任何人的日常查询"

真正的护城河不是模型，而是"grounding interviews"——那些一小时的深度真人访谈。 这是 Digital Twin 的"锚点数据"。谁拥有最丰富、最持续更新的锚点，谁的 Twin 就最不会漂移。这意味着 Outset 在悄悄建一个永远不会被基础模型商品化的私有数据资产层。

这才是 Aaron 没说但显然想到的下一步：Outset 最终不是研究公司，是"人类偏好模拟层"的基础设施提供商——一个介于 Palantir 和 Bloomberg Terminal 之间的新物种。

📝 转录文本

开场介绍

[music] I'm excited to be joined here today by Aaron Cannon, co-founder and CEO of Outset. Outset is the leading AI customer research platform used by some of the biggest brands in the world like Google, Microsoft, and Nestle. Uh, thanks so much for being here, Aaron.

Thank you for having me.

Outset 做什么

Cool. Well, why don't we start a little bit by telling us exactly what Outset's product does?

Yeah. So, I find it useful to kind of look at the world of research and like to to put into context what we do. So um when you're trying to listen to your users or talk to them uh usually you've had to use things like surveys which are very very uh uh kind of shallow uh capturing of data or you actually do user interviews and you call them one by one. The problem is that's super expensive slow and timeconuming. And so what we invented back when we started was this idea of AI leading interviews. That means AI is actually leading a conversation with a person with a real person having a back and forth and digging really deep. So you get this kind of the scale and speed of what we would, you know, do with a survey, but you're getting it at the depth of an actual interview. And so that's what we built.

Cool. And can you give a sense of kind of what scale you operate at today?

Yeah. So, so as you mentioned, we work with a lot of the biggest brands in the world. Um, and we've now done millions of customer interviews all led by AI. So it's become a really key way that people are actually learning from their markets and their users.

回到 2023 年：一个还不存在的品类

Cool. So, as I remember it, when you went through YC in winter 2023, uh this whole idea of AI doing customer interviews seemed uh nonobvious. It wasn't like a market that clearly existed. Uh tell us what that felt like back then and what was it like trying to get the first few users and people to believe in this.

Yeah. So, back in 2023, it was like ancient history at this point from the world of AI, the AI timeline. And so, we like had this idea leaning very much on my own background. So, I started my career doing research myself. uh a lot of ethnographic research in people's homes and doing very one-on-one interviews. So, I had a deep kind of care and passion for how we understand human beings. It's like what drives, you know, business forward everywhere. And so, I cared a lot about it. So, I thought, you know, at the time, uh chat GPT was really good at, you know, conversation. And so, we thought, well, what if we put that into the position of a of a interviewer, right? And ultimately, an interview is just using conversation to elicit good insights.

But the problem was like the the market was not there yet, right? Like in summer 23 it was like people were barely absorbing the idea of AI in the first place. And so you know what we put forward was super novel. So like we got lots I think it was like our we launched the first week of the batch. We were the first one in our batch to launch which we thought was like our special hack and a lot we got a ton of demos booked during the batch which is like an incredible position to be in but honestly very few of them converted. And so it's like that's what it feels to be too early to a new category right where it's like everybody wanted to come and learn about what was new and interesting and possible but no one had internalized where exactly how exactly to deploy this kind of thing.

第一版产品长什么样

Do you remember exactly what that's with the first version you launched with um what did it do?

So the first version uh it was it was a uh basically it was taking the GPT models and it just like wrapped around a basically chat interface where it would ask questions and a you know person would answer the synthesis of that data which is the other half of our product. It's like AI leads interviews and then it synthesizes the results. The other half was literally a CSV export. So, so it was like a super super bare bones and so that's all it did, right? Is like you sent it to almost like a survey. You sent it to your users and they would answer questions by AI.

So, it's like an interactive survey.

It was basically a conversational survey was the way to think about it.

为什么早期 demo 转化不了：企业买家的"科目困境"

Why did these demos not convert? What was the resistance you met from buyers?

So, I think we found pretty early on that there's a lot of interest in from enterprises which we loved. It's like should you be so lucky from the beginning to actually work with enterprises. The problem was that like these these teams and buyers were not they did not have budgets for this. They did not have any framework for fitting this into their to their budgets. So it's it's like a when an enterprise buyer like you're talking to them, you you like they already have line items. They're already there. So either something is swapping something else out of a line item or they need to make a case for an entirely new line item. And to make that case, they need enough external validation that their their boss or their boss's boss believes it. So the problem is when we're coming in with something novel um and it does not fit into an existing line item then it's like on is incumbent on us to to kind of will this new category into existence so that line item appears.

What what was sort of the alter like what were they doing as the alternative and maybe where was the budget for that coming from?

So there's a bunch of incumbents in the research world, right? So we're talking about like uh Qualrix and Medallia and these like uh user testing these kind of older school companies and those had line items, right? So but those were like just static research, you know, the idea of hearing from lots of people at once. You just send a survey and it asks very static questions. And this idea of a conversational one, it didn't fit into that bucket because it's not quantitative research in the way that people think about surveys. and that it wasn't qualitative research in the way you think about a focus group or a one-on-one interview. And so there just like wasn't a nice home for it when we started. And so what the the kind of yeah the challenge was how do you convince them that this is the best of both that we've like changed the economics of this thing and put that new line item there.

定价困难还是行为改变困难？

And so was a challenge getting the the teams to understand how to use a tool and adopt the tool because it wasn't clearly qualitative or quantitative or was it um did you have a different pricing model and people didn't know how to think about that and compare the price to like Qualrix?

I think it was more of the former. So it was more about how people uh the hard part was to get them to understand where this fits into what they do, right? Um do they replace a project where they otherwise would have done interviews? Do they replace a survey? And the hard part is like if it is something net new, which it definitely was, then you know sometimes it's not a exact rip and replace. It's actually behavior change.

And so behavior change like especially when they're a prospect is really really hard. And so uh we had to ultimately do a lot of market education. So it's like our our first kind of couple years of existence, it was all about kind of market education, not straight sales, not classic sales, right? It was like we have to help you know bring you on the journey of this thing.

第一个客户：Weight Watchers 与"75 折 case study"策略

So you launch sort of as quickly as you can during YC lots of demos demos don't convert. You realize you have to do more sort of educating the buyers because the cater is not the future isn't quite sort of where you want it to be. Um what does that look like again like tactically like how do you educate buyers? I mean so hard to get their attention just for a sale. So how do you how do you kind of get them around with it?

Our first customer ever was Weight Watchers which was was an amazing logo to get as your first one. I happened to have at the time somebody I knew there which is my advice always for YC founders of like shamelessly use your own network. Um but we had somebody new there and so

were they the buyer for the product or they know someone who was the buyer?

They were call it an influencer but not the buyer.

Yeah.

So it was not it was a door open but it wasn't necessarily like a you know contract closed right so so I I think the best way with enterprises is validation. And so what that looked like for us is getting a case study. And I remember our first contract ever. Uh we uh we pretended we had some, you know, perfectly uh rational pricing, you know, whatever. But we were still trying to figure it out. And we priced them at uh 10K for the year with a 75% discount

just for that case study, which by the way is like a fraction of what we charge now. And now we have seven figure contracts. But at the time it was uh all about the case study. And that was the most valuable thing we could get out of it. And then we brought that case study and and to the next customer and the next customer and that was I think the best way to start educating the market was like through examples.

So getting Weight Watchers to understand the right way to think about the product and and adopt it. How did you overcome that?

I mean I I just there's no replacement for just spending a lot of time with them. And so I think it was a very uh felt pretty forward deployed right we were like spending like a kind of irrational amount of time with that early customer and uh we kind of convinced them to try it in a few instances and once they actually tried it in kind of a particular instance where it was really successful that became the blueprint for them and it became much easier. So that was like boulder rolling downhill for them. Now we had to bring that knowledge to the next one and the next one.

模型变强 = 产品变强：作为"增长故事"来卖

You guys seem to me like the classic case of a startup where it's like as the models have got better, you've benefited from that massively. Um maybe talk us through that like how exactly have the underlying models becoming more powerful and there being more intelligence to build on top of. How has that improved the product you're able to build and how has that maybe changed some of the attitudes to the enterprise buyers you're talking to?

So I think it's actually worth stepping back and like think about the world of customer insights or customer research. Like out in the market there's actually like a uh insatiable demand for it. It's like an uncapped thing. So we're not just automating an existing workflow but rather we're saying hey you can actually get way more insight about your user about your customer which means you can build a much better product which means you can do much better marketing which means you can grow your business. And so the way we sell is actually a growth story right? is like a how how like you can by accelerating your ability to do research you can accelerate your own business. And so because of that there is not like a single kind of beginning and end to a use case that needs to be automated and so hey uh you know second tier model will do it it's like the better the models get the better we can do interviews the better we can synthesize data and pull in other kinds of data the better we can actually drive more insights. And so our first product was on Da Vinci right like forever ago um and now we use all the frontier models in various ways that work together. So we positioned ourselves basically as like the more the models get better, the more insight you are going to get.

最反直觉的洞察：人们对 AI 说得比对真人还多

Have there been particular types of insights, maybe even specific insights some of your customers have gotten where it's it's very clear they would never have been able to get that from a traditional survey or like a focus group. They could only have got it from their customers talking to the outset AI.

Yeah. Okay. So I'll give you one example uh which I'll actually stick with the Weight Watchers example from early days. So I think what you know when we started this product we we we could tell hey there's an opportunity to do something in a more scaled way than we've done before. And so we tested that and Weight Watchers had the first pilot project. They did a study about weight loss and what motivates people. And you could imagine for a company like Weight Watchers, that's actually a really uh kind of strategic question that matters a lot for how they speak to their market and how they advertise, how they do everything, right? And so we did a study uh where a 100 people were interviewed um about what motivates them and about their journey.

And what was so interesting is not only did they get a hundred interviews done in a matter of a couple of hours, which the traditional methods would never have gotten anywhere close to that. A hundred interviews takes months. But also people shared more with AI than they would than they would otherwise with humans. And that's the really like counterintuitive thing here. So like it's not just that this was a kind of better economic decision to run AI interviews, but it's actually that you are getting data that was impossible to to unearth otherwise. And I think it's like a it's the result of like, you know, people like love those anonymous apps where they can say anything and they they feel like they're able to express themselves, but there's no kind of personal judgment and you're not trying to come off a certain way. It's like that that's just transferred to research now, right? Which is like the most kind of uh incredible thing you can get is like people's ground truth. Like what actually matters to them, what do they really think of your idea? All of those things really matter.

AI 不只是效率工具，它创造了新的人类行为

It kind of reminds me when um when chat GPT was first taking off. I remember the people who really were deep in like early power users of it um could understand that this was clearly going to replace Google search. But I think the people sort of at Google or working with search engines felt like oh like people were still want like like the fastest way to find a result and it takes too long to like chat to a thing and wait for it to tell you like which things you should buy or go for. But the like once open AI once the um once the models have all this context on you like because you share so much with them, they can actually get you to the thing that you want really really quickly. Um and it just feels actually more efficient than trying to like browse through it or look through it yourself. And so I imagine you have like the similar thing like early on I bet a lot of incumbents will know like if we're going to do surveys and we need to like go through all of like the um the responses ourselves to understand what's going on or focus groups need to be really um hightouch and done in person but people will like bear their souls to these things. That's like really rich information for you.

Well, I I think about this like even on a more macro level where you just AI can make us more efficient at things we want to do anyways. But then there's like AI, you know, the the the the uh has changed actual human behavior. And so I think what I didn't realize when we started, I thought about it being an efficient way to get a thing done. And the reality was is it was creating a new set of human behaviors that we've really really benefited from. It's funny because like understanding humans is of course what our product does, but it's also like we had to do that to take advantage of what's now possible with AI.

2025 年的拐点：从"我们要不要试"到"我们必须试"

And you guys have hit a real inflection point on growth over the last year. So tell us what's um what's been driving that.

Yeah. Well, I think it goes to the throughine of like we create a new category after YC. uh we continued to push on the market and I know my co-founder and I at the time we were like wanting things to move faster, wanting to hit an inflection point but we kept hitting conversations with people where they were really intrigued but did they have budget yet and were they overcome like were they able to overcome their skepticisms um of the category. And so that's where we pushed on the education we pushed on the awareness we we brought case studies to bear and we kind of scraped and clawed our way through and then really in 2025 I think there's a a big inflection point and what happened is the market like this became went from experimental thing that are you willing to take a bet to consensus. And so this is like a you know if if you're you know if you think about like hitting tailwinds of AI right like this is a you want to be there and already have mind share when the inflection point hits

right and like we had already been there at beating the drum and so the moment you know the conversation shifted from should we explore this to we should explore this we were already synonymous with the category which was like I think in category creation like we just wanted to be associated with that net net new category and that's the position we got. And so the last 18 months have you know been been completely uh have been massive.

下一站：视觉智能、Co-design、以及 Digital Twins

I feel like Ian I feel like going back to the fact that this was such a non-conensus non-obvious idea in 2023 going back in time and explaining to people then that you'd be able to like talk to your agents because voice would have really taken off would have just seemed like crazy talk um if you project out forward sort of what's coming next for you guys like what are some of like the the crazy capab capabilities that you're excited for that will let AI go even deeper into sort of figuring out what people want and and going and probing much further.

Well, it's funny actually. Uh I remember in 2023 during the batch having calls with people where I literally had to educate them on what were LLMs.

Yeah.

Like I actually had calls with people who was like what what what do you mean LLM? And I had to go. So it's like such a different world.

In the last three years now we like AI can do so much. It's talking to your user's voice. And we've actually included a ton of visual intelligence, too. So, now we're using computer vision models to say, let's just say, you know, AI is running an interview and it can watch your screen as you're interacting. It can watch your face. It can watch your environment, probe on those, dig deeper. We even have a way where AI will get feedback from people on a design and then literally change the design in real time and get the person's further feedback. We call that codeesign. So there's like so many ways that AI has now like kind of uh uh uh become his superpower for research.

But um I'm really excited to announce and to launch that we're uh we're shipping outset digital twins this month.

Oh, cool.

And so what that is is we're we're able to start synthesizing actual customers, actual users into what we call digital twins. So the idea here is that when you're doing research, sometimes you're able to and have the time and money and investment to go out and learn from people, but as you do, you're able to put together actual twins that you can interact with as well, which are representations of those people. And so, um, this is part of our new simulations lab that we've stood up at outset and we've developed a methodology where you're actually able to very accurately, uh, simulate what a person would say.

If you think forward, right, businesses um ultimately just want to predict human behavior, right? That is the thing that matters. That's why research exists. Predict will somebody buy a thing? Will somebody use a thing? Right? You're all you're it's always, you know, you're always trying to figure out the future. And so now we have the ability to both gather the data to inform the future and also actually simulate it with real uh digital twins.

Digital Twin 是怎么造出来的？

So that sounds really cool. Could you tell us maybe a little bit about how exactly do you generate these digital twins? like what what inputs are going into creating them and then what's the value to your customers of using the digital twin for feedback versus just going to like the actual cumid customers and asking them.

Yeah, good question. So when we work with a customer, we identify what are the audiences they care most about, right? Maybe it's their own customer base, maybe it's net new prospects they want to get, you know, bring into their to their business. And so we generate these set of twins based on them. We reach out to real people and we actually do hourlong grounding interviews. These are extensive AI run interviews that are digging into all sorts of dimensions about their personality, about what they value, about what they care about. And through that, we're able to develop this persona core that can best represent that person. So, we've now created this digital twin that represents them.

And what's cool is now anybody in your business can interact with that digital twin at any time. Traditional research is great and you you know you want to keep doing it in all sorts of uh uh use cases but it costs money, it takes time. Not everybody can go do this research but um with a digital twin anybody across the business can be tapping into that knowledge can be asking for example maybe your marketer wants to test a new messaging with that kind of digital twin or your finance person is working on new pricing models and wants to simulate what would happen if I change that price. This is this infrastructure that should exist for companies to simulate the future.

解放大公司里被"没预算"憋死的想法

Yeah, it seems like it should unblock like a huge amount of creativity because there have to be lots of good ideas are generated by people in these companies that they talk themselves out of and it's too expensive to go out and get budget or whatever to go and run them like do like a focus group. But now, yeah, if you just have a digital twin, you can like test it out and build the case for it um without talking to anyone and that that should be pretty exciting.

That's right. It's like amazing how many decisions are made at big companies based on someone's gut or instinct. And like yes, they pull on the research team for the big projects, but there's so many decisions day-to-day that don't have that. You can't do that. You don't have the budget or time or or capital to do that. And so being able to just talk to a twin of an actual customer or talk to a hundred twins of an actual customer like that is a really powerful mechanism.

Yeah, that's definitely one of the things I feel founders talk about as the companies grow in scale as they sort of in the sort of YC stage. It's almost so it's so easy in certain ways cuz you just you have an idea and you go out and talk to users and like you just do it yourself and then the company gets bigger and there's all this other like stuff going on. But maybe with outset you actually like help bigger companies be able to come up with new innovative ideas.

That's right. And I think it like comes down to two things. It's like one accelerating the ability to get this input, get the insight, right? Right? It's like we're if we're shipping code at the ridiculous rate that we are now, we're actually blocked on understanding what people actually want, right? That becomes more of a blocker. So, we need to accelerate that too. But the other is like going and understanding humans in a way that we haven't before, right? And whether that's a direct outside interview with a person or a digital twin that's representing the most, you know, impactful audience that you have, both are ways to just capture more insight more quickly.

Aaron 的创始人之路：不要等灵感

Okay. Well, maybe take changing gears here a little bit. A lot of people watching this are hoping to start a company themselves one day. Uh maybe tell us a little bit about um your journey to becoming a founder. Um because I think you worked at some places before. So maybe tell tell us about that story.

It all started I walked I walked into Harsh's office and he No, but but but uh but my actual my background was working uh doing product at a number of startups. So I so I worked uh

Yeah, we worked together. You were our first product hire.

That's right. That's right. Har took a bet on me. Um, and I was the the head of product under under harsh and team at triple bite and and I think like for me working very closely with at existing startups. So if I you know at the time I wasn't ready to go start my own thing and so like being able to work really closely with founders who are in the trenches and understand that experience and start you know pattern matching like out of different phases was a really big way that helped me.

The other the other the other advice I always give of like if if folks are you know thinking about it one day is basically uh life is short and do it now and uh you know I uh decided to uh leave my job and start a company and I hadn't yet figured out exactly how that was going to go or what that was going to be and I was still kind of exploring you know kind of uh I just decided decided to start working with Michael my co-founder just deciding to do it and not sitting around waiting for the right idea to strike me right like walking down the street was the most powerful thing I think that that happened.

结尾

Well, I think that's all we have time for today. Thanks so much for being here, Aaron, and can't wait to see the digital twins launch from Outset. [music]

Thank you for having me. >> [music]

item.description:
## 一、最反直觉的观察：AI 不是"效率工具"，而是"人格解锁器"
大多数人把 Outset 理解为"更便宜、更快的调研工具"——这是表层叙事。真正颠覆性的发现藏在 Aaron 的一句话里：**"人们对 AI 说的话，比对真人说得更多。"**
这才是 Outset 的真正商业底层：它不是在替代"人访谈人"这个动作，而是在**利用一种新出现的人类行为模式**——人在没有社会评判的情境下，会释放出连焦点小组、连一对一深访都拿不到的"地面真相 (ground truth)"。
这里有个惊人的悖论：**调研行业花了 50 年训练访谈员如何"消除偏见、建立信任"，而 AI 一夜之间通过"不是人"这个特征，绕过了整个行业的方法论。** 匿名树洞 App、Reddit 的深夜自白、和 ChatGPT 的私密对话——这些都是同一种人类学现象的不同切面。Outset 是第一个把这种"去人格化坦白"制度化、商品化的公司。
## 二、跨领域连接：Outset 走的是"新品类"的经典博弈论路径，和 Airbnb、Uber、Salesforce 是同一条曲线

item.title: [Lex Clips] Social media is breaking your brain | DHH and Lex Fridman
item.dc:creator: Lex Clips
item.content:encoded:
💡 创造性洞见

一、意外观察：DHH 描述的"戒 X"，本质是一场"神经系统脱毒"，但真正的成瘾物不是内容，而是被算法揭示出来的自己

大多数人谈社交媒体成瘾时，把矛头指向"平台设计"或"多巴胺回路"。但 DHH 说了一句极其精确却容易被忽略的话："算法找到的不是你说你喜欢什么，而是你的 revealed preferences（暴露的偏好）。"

这意味着：你戒不掉的不是 X，而是那个在深夜停留 3 秒多的自己。 算法只是一面镜子——它把荣格所说的"阴影自我"以毫秒精度渲染成一条条推文喂回给你。所以"戒断反应"的真正来源，是不得不承认：我不是我以为的那个我。 这也是为什么单纯的"意志力"总是失败——因为你在对抗的不是产品，而是被高分辨率成像后的自我认知。

二、跨领域连接：斯多葛哲学 × 《第四转折》× Transformer 训练——三者共享同一个"防过拟合"结构

Lex 与 DHH 谈到读斯多葛让人意识到"你并不特殊"，谈到《第四转折》里的历史循环论。听起来像老生常谈的"读点历史吧"，但把它放在机器学习的视角下，会出现一个惊人的同构：

  • 斯多葛的"记忆死亡（memento mori）" = 给个体经验加一个强正则化项，防止你把"当下的焦虑"过拟合成"世界末日"。
  • 《第四转折》的周期论 = 用 80 年一个 epoch 的低频信号，把你从当下的 batch noise 里拉出来。
  • AI 的 dropout / 数据增强 = 强迫模型不要死记某一个样本。

换句话说，人类文明发明宗教、哲学、历史意识的深层功能，就是给"意识"这个模型加正则化，防止过拟合到当下时刻。 而现代社交媒体做的事恰好相反：它给每个人的意识注入极高频、极高维、极局部的即时信号，是一台反正则化机器——让你确信这一瞬的政治撕裂就是人类命运的终局。DHH 需要"cold turkey"三周，本质就是给大脑做一次强制 dropout。

三、隐藏真相：DHH 无意中揭示了"信息节食"和"食物节食"的深层同构，但真正的启示藏在他没说出口的地方

他说得很俏皮："吃两三颗巧克力草莓可以，17 颗就不行了。" 表面上这是节制论，但真正让人惊心的洞察藏在下一层：

当代人正在经历人类历史上第一次"信息营养过剩"，而我们连"信息肥胖症"的诊断标准都还没有。

想想身体的进化：几百万年的食物匮乏，让我们对糖和脂肪有无法关闭的渴求，直到工业化食品把这套回路劫持成了肥胖流行病。信息也一样——几百万年的信息匮乏（谁在骂我？谁是盟友？部落里发生了什么？），让我们对"社会情绪信号"有无法关闭的渴求。X 就是信息界的高果糖玉米糖浆。

但真正被 DHH 的话点出、却没有明说的第三层是："snark 我想要 10%"这个愿望永远无法被算法满足——因为算法只能优化"停留时长"这一个标量，而人类想要的其实是一个多维度、有配比、有节奏的信息饮食结构。这就像跟一家快餐店说"我要 30% 蛋白质、20% 蔬菜、只要一点点糖"——它做不到，因为它的商业模式不是营养师，是老虎机。

所以未来十年真正稀缺的产品，不是更好的推荐算法，而是"信息营养师"——一个愿意为你的长期心智健康优化、而非为停留时长优化的中介层。谁做出这个，谁就是信息时代的"有机食品运动"。

📝 转录文本

一、AI 时代的孩子，与"这次不一样"的错觉

Lex: What do you think about them coming up in this world full of AI? It's a totally different… It feels like maybe I just sound like an old man on a porch, but it feels like a very different world. So I grew up before the internet, but even the internet doesn't feel like as big of a transformation as this.

DHH: No, but there's been bigger transformations. I mean, imagine growing or being born in like 1880. Imagine seeing the first world war and the second world war. Imagine seeing the airplane, the radio, television. I mean the transformation…

I think Peter Thiel makes this argument that basically nothing has happened in the physical world in quite a long time. We've been stagnant. All the development has been in the digital realm. And as important as that is, it's actually not as consequential as we like to believe it is. Maybe AI will be that thing that is more consequential. It does seem to point that way. But there are other humans at other times who have lived through transitions that for them certainly would feel as momentous as what we're living through.

二、斯多葛的解药：你并不特殊

And I think having that sense of history — that you're not that special in your sense of worries, in your anxieties — this was one of the great revelations of discovering the Stoic writings. You have these guys 2,500 years ago dealing with very familiar dilemmas and challenges in their life. And recognizing that we're not so special in that regard, I think is a great liberation. Because then you think, okay, well, we have whatever — 200,000 years of human development before us — and they somehow made it through.

Lex: Yeah. And uh…

DHH: …we will make it through.

Lex: The thing that makes life worthwhile is basically the same today as it was…

DHH: Yes.

Lex: …2,000 years ago.

DHH: Yes. Love, creation, creativity…

Lex: …same challenges.

三、历史是圆，不是直线：《第四转折》

I read this book — The Fourth Turning. You check that out? It talks about this notion of history working in cycles, and there are these phases to history and they name them and so forth. And the specific theory is not as important as just realizing that history is a circle more so than just a straight line. And we are repeating many of the same patterns over and over again. They feel so unique to the moment. And whatever crisis we're dealing with right now, it feels so pressing and important — until we zoom back a little bit in history and realize that the last one also feels so pressing and important to the people who lived through it.

Lex: [sighs and gasps] Yeah. You make me feel better. So, I'm going to travel across the country and spend a lot of time with no access to the internet, alone with my thoughts.

DHH: I think that's healthy. Taking a break.

Lex: It's okay. It's okay.

四、DHH 的三周戒断：X 是信息版的老虎机

DHH: I took — not a big break, a little break — from X this summer. Three weeks.

Lex: Yeah, you disappeared off of…

DHH: I'm surprised you noticed. [laughter]

Lex: I went through withdrawals. No — uh, you disappeared for, I don't know, a few weeks…

DHH: …about 3 weeks.

Lex: Three weeks. What happened?

DHH: Um [clears throat] — this is after…

Lex: After…

DHH: I've done that before. I just sometimes get this sense that X in particular is the most addictive form of information, entertainment, connection that exists in my life. And anyone that follows my Xtreme — as I was on my flight over here — would certainly go like, "that man is deeply addicted."

Lex: Yeah.

DHH: …to the connection. And yes, guilty as charged. Which also means that occasionally I got to cut it cold, because I do think you can break your brain.

And over the summer in particular, for whatever reason, I had somehow managed to steer my feed, my algorithm, towards too much politics and not enough tech and not enough optimism and not enough building. And even if I agreed with the politics and the angles that were being presented, I just didn't need that much of it.

Lex: Yeah.

五、"17 颗巧克力草莓"：算法与欲望的过量供给

DHH: And I think arriving at a place where you just — like, okay, that's enough.

Lex: Mhm.

DHH: Not that it doesn't have to be something bad. I would also say after eating probably two, maybe three chocolate strawberries, I'd go like, "Okay, that's enough." Like it's not that I don't like the chocolate strawberries. It's just like — I don't want to eat 17 of them. And I think X and the modern algorithms are very good at feeding you freaking 17 chocolate-covered strawberries.

Lex: I wish I could control that — because there is… I would like some politics: 5%.

DHH: Yeah.

Lex: I would like — for example, one of the things I don't like about the tech community is the snark, but I like some snark [laughter] cuz it's funny. But I want that to be like 10%.

DHH: Yeah.

Lex: I want to do this right version of the algorithm.

六、算法是镜子：revealed preferences 与荣格的阴影

DHH: Well, the problem is the algorithm finds out what you respond to, not what you say you like. It's all revealed preferences, and unfortunately those revealed preferences are not always pretty. I mean, we have this shadow, as Jung talks about — like all these dark aspects of ourselves — and they are expressed in how long you linger on a tweet and what you like and what you don't like. And the algorithm holds up a mirror, and it's not always pretty. And I just went, you know what, I need a break.

Lex: Mhm. I've gotten to — I started staying off social media, and I've started scraping X. Like, for example, in preparation for this conversation, I've scraped all your tweets.

DHH: That's actually a method I was using for a while. I was using a tool called — I forget. It was an email tool that would summarize every day. And unfortunately freaking X cut off their access. Now, to get access to the feed, you got to pay some exorbitant sum that the startup couldn't pay. So I couldn't get it that way.

And I actually thought, man, that's a miss — because X has and reveals some of the most interesting thoughts, some of the most interesting people all the time. But it's like a damn slot machine. And most of the time, you don't hit the jackpot. You hit like something else. And if I could just get it in sort of snack sizes, not like all of it, it'd be nicer. But that's not the product.

七、"最大化提取"与 AI 的隐忧

And I think this goes for all of social media. It's all optimized towards maximal extraction. And if we're making the parallels here to AI, that is the great fear, right? That once there is a reward function — how much time can I get this human to scroll away? — AI, and machine learning before we called it AI, has become very, very good at delivering just the stuff that you will find most enraging and most addictive.

Lex: I think legitimately, engagement-maximizing social media is a huge harm to society. That's creating this brave new world situation that I hope is a temporary thing that people will just solve. It's a technology problem.

八、反其道而行：主动向"好气场"灌注

So I try to consciously flood the channel in the other direction, and this required a mental shift. I think if you look at my tweets — I don't know — uh, 5, 10 years ago, they tilted far more negative. If you look at my tweets now, I'd hope…

DHH: Well, I guess we can do a sentiment analysis and see if it's actually true.

Lex: But I hope to — it's more positive. It's more good vibes. It's more like: here's a bunch of cool stuff I found. Here's what I'm excited about. Here's what I'm building. Here's some encouragement to other people who are discovering things.

DHH: I also accept that that's just not how human brains are built for maximum engagement. Like there's a — whatever — I literally think you can quantify it, that negative sentiments find, what is it, 50% more traction or something. And eventually that just crowds things out. So that's why so much of the feed is that negative stuff, because we respond to it. But you can make a conscious effort to not do that.

九、TikTok 作为"棉花糖测试"

This is one of the reasons I've liked TikTok so much. I only use TikTok when I travel. And this actually was the first travel where I didn't use TikTok. And part of the reason was that even though the internet had high download, it was kind of crap anyway. It wasn't Starlink, so I couldn't actually use TikTok on the plane. And I was too engrossed with the agents.

But normally when I travel, I watch TikTok.

Lex: Mhm.

DHH: And there it's such a marshmallow test.

Lex: Mhm.

DHH: A video will scroll down and like — it'll activate some sort of primal instincts of rage or lust or whatever. And if you linger on it, you don't get the marshmallow of science, excitement, art, music, all these other things. You have to be disciplined to instantly scroll away such that the algorithm doesn't pick up your revealed preferences.

And I find that just — the metagame of TikTok — to be pretty interesting. And then also just fascinating in itself. Again, as we talked about, there are a lot of really funny, really talented people in the world that you would never ever have heard of if it hadn't been for these platforms.
