item.description:
## 一、被隐藏的"甜甜圈城市"：印度城市不是在成长，而是在**外翻**
Rana 在谈到 Indore 时揭示了一个几乎所有政策讨论都忽略的诡异现象——印度城市正在呈现"donut 形态"：制造业从中心外迁，服务业留在核心，中间层空心化。这不是印度独有的规划失败，这是**土地要素市场扭曲下的一种"病理性去中心化"**。
真正让人意外的是：这与美国 1970-1990 年代的"郊区化"看似相似，实则相反。美国的外翻是**富人主动出走**（车、房、逃税），而印度的外翻是**工业被动流放**——因为市中心的建筑法规、FSI 限制、土地转换难，使制造业根本无法在需要它的地方存在。换言之，**美国郊区是选择的结果，印度的 peri-urban 是禁令的产物**。这意味着相同的空间形态，背后是完全对称相反的因果机制——而如果政策制定者用美国经验（TOD、混合用途）来"治疗"印度的甜甜圈，可能药不对症。
## 二、印度城市治理的真正 bug：**"没有人在思考本地经济发展"**
Rana 提出了一个我几乎没在城市经济学文献中见过如此赤裸的问题：**"如果你问，谁在本地层面思考经济发展？如果

item.title: [Lex Clips] The genius of Linus Torvalds | DHH and Lex Fridman
item.dc:creator: Lex Clips
item.content:encoded:
💡 创造性洞见

1. 一个反直觉的观察：Linux 用 34 年时间在等待"用户的失能"

大家都在讲"Linux 终于要拿下桌面了"，但真正值得注意的不是 Linux 变了，而是用户从"需要懂计算机"退化到了"只需要会说话"——而这恰恰是 Linux 一直等待的历史窗口。

DHH 说了一句非常隐晦但极其锋利的话：Commodore 64 一开机就进 BASIC，那才是"可塑的电脑"，只是需要"象形文字"（hieroglyphs）。Agent 是罗塞塔石碑。

换句话说：过去 40 年 Windows / Mac 的胜利，本质上是"帮不懂符号的人绕开可塑性"的胜利。而 AI 不是让 Linux 变强，是把用户重新变回了"有能力面对可塑系统的人"。Linux 没有等到技术突破，它等到的是用户被 LLM 反向升级。

这就产生了一个诡异的对称：Linux 从 1991 年至今没变多少（还是那个内核、那个哲学），变的是它周围的人类。操作系统不动，人类被重塑，然后适配就自然完成了。

2. 跨领域连接：Linus × Elon × 编辑器 —— "刺"是一种系统性的免疫机制

DHH 顺口把 Linus 和 Elon、Jobs 放在一起，看似是"难搞的天才"套路，但底层其实是一个信息论问题：

在一个 4000 万行代码、上千贡献者、承载全球计算基础设施的系统里，"温和的反馈"本身是信息噪声。因为温和的反馈让边界模糊，让"哪些提交是不可接受的"变成一个模糊分布。而 Linus 的辛辣评论，本质上是给系统提供高信噪比的边界信号——它让"标准"这条线在几万公里之外的贡献者眼里依然清晰可见。

跨领域看，这和三个东西同构： - 免疫系统：靠误伤少量自体细胞维持对入侵者的高敏感度； - 法律的"象征性重罚"：偶尔一个夸张判决维持整体守法预期； - 编辑（editor）在文学里的存在：不是为了让作者舒服，是为了维持标准的位置感。

所以 Linus 的"刺"不是性格问题，是分布式系统的边界维护成本。你要么付出这个成本，要么你的系统边界会随时间熵增到模糊。

3. 更深一层的隐藏真相：DHH 在悄悄描述"个人操作系统"这个即将到来的品类

访谈表面在讨论 Linux 和 AI，但如果你把 DHH 的两段话拼起来—— - "malleable operating system, you can tailor to your desires" - "an operating system shaped in your image"

他其实在预告一个尚未被命名的品类：Personal OS ≠ Personal Computer。

过去 40 年的"个人电脑"只是共用软件的个人硬件——每个人的 macOS 长得几乎一模一样。而"个人操作系统"是每个人的软件形态都不同，因为它是被那个人的语言、习惯、审美实时塑造出来的。

这里有一个几乎没人注意到的哲学翻转： - 工业时代的软件是"产品"（Product）——一对多； - SaaS 时代是"服务"（Service）——多对多，但仍然共享形态； - Agent 时代的软件将是"倒影"（Reflection）——一对一，形态即用户。

这也解释了 DHH 说的"看到截图流泪"的多巴胺现象：那不是"我做出了软件"的成就感，而是人类第一次在屏幕上看到自己的形状。这是一种类似照镜子的原始快感，只是镜子这次是可交互的。

一旦你意识到这一点，Windows 和 macOS 的护城河就消失了——因为它们的护城河建立在"共享形态"上，而下一代用户根本不想要共享形态。Linux 的胜利不是打赢了对手，是对手被战场本身抹掉了。

📝 转录文本

一、开源社区对 AI 的态度，以及 Linus 的定调

If you look at the way a lot of the Linux communities, open source communities have reacted to AI, it is not universal love. I would argue that the majority of them are actually, if not skeptical, then outright hostile to AI.

Now, the saving grace is that the BDFL himself, Linus Torvalds, just wrote a few weeks ago that he actually welcomes AI.

That's right.

He wants to steer it, he wants to make sure it's good and whatever, but the line was something — if you think Linux is an anti-AI project, think again, and you should just do the open source thing and fork it, because we're going to use AI. And you see these graphs of the number of AI contributions going into the kernel and it's a parabolic curve. So, Linux is leaning hard into this.

二、Linux 已经赢下一切，只差桌面

And now it actually — in other ways, it was surprising that it didn't. Linux conquered everything else. All the AI infrastructure that everyone runs off, it's all running on Linux.

Mhm.

All the systems, all the servers, everything is Linux. So, it was kind of a curiosity that the desktop and —

[snorts]

— the personal computers we were using really hadn't been captured, but clearly it was just waiting for this moment. Linux spent the time from '91 to now waiting for agents to fully flourish as an end user operating system.

I — yeah, hope it takes over. I mean, it is perfect. It's perfect for agents, but it's hard for people to switch.

三、为什么 Ubuntu 没成，而 Agentic OS 会成

I think it's hard to people to switch when there's not a compelling reason to do so. This is one of the driving design goals for Mach U. It was not going to be team O Windows or team O Mac. It was not just going to be a cheap copy where we try to make it as familiar as possible and then kind of worse.

I mean, if I was being unkind, I would say that's what Ubuntu has tried to do. And there's something in that — or there was something in that at least — where if you make something really familiar, you can get some people who don't want to learn something new, and then maybe they'll be compelled about your whatever "free as in speech, not as in beer" stuff, and it just didn't pan out that way. People just didn't care. They just wanted whatever was better.

And I think this is why Linux now has the opportunity to win, because as an agentic operating system, as a malleable operating system, you can tailor to your desires. It is unparalleled. And that is so compelling.

四、Product-Market Fit 的信号：多巴胺洪流

And I could see it now. Just since the release of Quattro, the amount of people who have embraced that aspect of it — the malleability — started making their own things, sharing screenshots of it, and being absolute just —

[snorts]

— flooded with positive emotions and dopamine. That's the product market fit signal, right?

Because what a lot of these individuals are experiencing, they're experiencing the very high of what the best of being a programmer is like. You tell the computer these arcane commands, this rigid logical structure, and it produces what you want.

Now suddenly you sit down and in plain English ramble for 20 minutes — "oh, it'd be great if it did that. I actually know that's not right. Let us…" — and out comes software. Out comes an operating system shaped in your image.

Yeah.

I think that is one of those experiences that if you have it, if you feel that power in your hands, it's very difficult to go back.

Yeah, and I think if you get it right, it's one of those things that will seem obvious in retrospect.

五、回到 Commodore 64：可塑性的原初形态

Yes. This is how computers were always meant to be. This is how computers started. The Commodore 64 — you turn it on. First of all, it boots in a second, amazing. Second of all, it boots straight into BASIC.

Yeah.

It was the malleable computer from the get-go. It just so happened that you needed to know hieroglyphs to be able to take advantage of that. Now we've translated it. Agents have given us the Rosetta Stone. And you can simply just speak your desires. And so they are.

Beautifully put.

六、Linus Torvalds 的天才：坚持、汇聚与开放

Since you mentioned Linus Torvalds and since you're working on a Linux distro, you get to have contact with the kernel. What can you say about the genius of this one guy that helped create and grow —

[sighs]

— this ecosystem?

The perseverance and the commitment and the longevity is truly remarkable. Again, Linus started in '91. He hasn't stopped. I don't know, but he's probably taking some breaks along the way — it doesn't seem obvious that there was that many of them.

It seems like he just really likes the flow of doing kernel development. He really likes steering where this 40 million line code base is going. He really likes aggregating the net capacity of hundreds or thousands of contributors. And we as beneficiaries of that must just sit back and marvel.

I mean, at this point Linux is a system. Like if Linus stepped out for a while, it would continue to go. But it's still one of those — protect this man at all cost.

And he's still open-minded enough to be able to evolve and accept AI into this —

Not only AI, they're letting Rust into the kernel, too. I know that was a controversial one, too. He has this capacity to look at new information and arrive at different conclusions.

七、关于"辛辣沟通"：世界需要一点辣味

What do you think about his style of communication that is akin in some ways to your own? Well, he can be sometimes a little spicy.

I think the world has gotten too bland. We need a little spice. I think there's a fine line between being spicy and mean. But it has to be in a good spirit. You can be harsh — let's put it that way. If you're trying to impart a lesson to someone you believe could actually learn it —

Mhm.

— I actually don't think it's always the worst thing in the world to be a little harsh. Sometimes that lesson sticks. And I think if you talk to people who worked for difficult leaders —

Elon, Steve Jobs, maybe even Bill Gates —

— many of them afterwards would go like, "These were some very difficult years, but also some of the very best."

Yeah.

"They got the best out of me."

Now, I don't think it's my style. I mean, maybe people I interact with feel differently, but in —

[snorts]

— personal interactions, I try and get to the outcome and the lesson in a less abrasive way. But I also think we need some spice in this world. We need unreasonable people.

八、使命的重量与"辛辣的比例原则"

And Linus has justification to be unreasonable. In many instances, the weight of the world is literally on that man's shoulders. The Linux kernel runs the entire civilized society. If the Linux kernel suddenly disappeared tomorrow, nothing would work. So, if he's not harsh when that's at stake or at risk, like when ever would you be harsh?

So, I feel sometimes also there's a proportionality to the size of your mission. This is also why I think these stories about Elon sometimes perhaps being a little bit difficult are easier to rationalize. It's not even that you condone. You can separate those two things and go like, "Do you know what? It'd probably be — maybe he would have an even easier time getting to his objectives if Linus or Elon or anyone else in that position was a little nicer."

But also, who am I to judge that? Like, when you have the weight of that on your shoulders — either firing little rockets at Mars and transitioning all of us to electric cars and whatever, or you're responsible for the damn Linux kernel that runs billions of devices — do you know what? It is not my place to call uh sort of code of conduct on you.

Again, is there a line? There's a line for everything. There's something — can't — but like a few harsh words on a mailing list? No. It's actually a beacon in some regards, that like there are standards.

Mhm.

And if you fall below those standards, at when the stakes are as high as the Linux kernel, uh you might get ridiculed in public. That's a liability you should be willing to endure if you participate in this project.

九、卓越 vs. 讨喜，以及多样性的价值

Yeah, for high-impact things like that, it's probably good to prioritize the pursuit of excellence versus the pursuit of niceness.

And even more to the fact, you're just not going to get those kinds of individuals being fully rounded, plush, always perfectly polite people. I mean, Elon has this line: "Did you also think I was going to be a nice — or what is it? — a normal dude. A normal chill dude."

What? No, of course you're not going to be a normal chill dude. What would the world gain if we got one more normal chill dude and we had to trade Elon? Holy [ __ ]

I also like diversity of people. I like — I like nice people. I like [ __ ] I like — I like — or like different ideologies being well represented. And that's why freedom of speech works. They clash and we figure stuff out.

Yes.

item.description:
## 1. 一个反直觉的观察：Linux 用 34 年时间在等待"用户的失能"
大家都在讲"Linux 终于要拿下桌面了"，但真正值得注意的不是 Linux 变了，而是**用户从"需要懂计算机"退化到了"只需要会说话"**——而这恰恰是 Linux 一直等待的历史窗口。
DHH 说了一句非常隐晦但极其锋利的话：Commodore 64 一开机就进 BASIC，那才是"可塑的电脑"，只是需要"象形文字"（hieroglyphs）。Agent 是罗塞塔石碑。
换句话说：**过去 40 年 Windows / Mac 的胜利，本质上是"帮不懂符号的人绕开可塑性"的胜利**。而 AI 不是让 Linux 变强，是把用户重新变回了"有能力面对可塑系统的人"。Linux 没有等到技术突破，它等到的是**用户被 LLM 反向升级**。
这就产生了一个诡异的对称：Linux 从 1991 年至今没变多少（还是那个内核、那个哲学），变的是它周围的人类。**操作系统不动，人类被重塑，然后适配就自然完成了。**
## 2. 跨领域连接：Linus × Elon × 编辑器 —— "刺"是一种系统性

item.title: [No Priors: AI, Machine Learning, Tech, & Startups] Rethinking Legacy Data Infrastructure with Eon Co-Founders Ofir Ehrlich and Gonen Stein
item.dc:creator: No Priors: AI, Machine Learning, Tech, & Startups
item.content:encoded:
💡 创造性洞见

出人意料的观察：破产法庭正在成为AI时代的"数据交易所"

Google花1000万美元从破产的Spirit Airlines手里买的不是飞机，而是数据——而竞标对手是Mercor这样的AI标注公司。这个细节值得反复咀嚼：破产清算程序正在悄悄演变为AI训练数据的一级市场。

传统破产法把资产分为"有形"和"无形"，无形资产里商标、专利被反复拍卖，但"日常运营数据"从未被单独定价过。现在AI改变了估值逻辑——一家航司的内部工单、中层管理者的邮件、客服录音，其价值可能超过它的机队残值。这意味着： - 未来公司的破产清算价值曲线会被重写，"数据完备度"可能成为债权人评估回收率的新指标 - 反向的商业策略会出现：某些企业会被"为了数据而收购"，就像嘉宾提到的Long Lake那样"买公司—AI化—套利" - 一个更隐秘的推论：存活的公司之所以拒绝出售数据，可能反而使它们成为收购标的——因为收购整个公司是获取这批数据的唯一路径

跨领域连接：Enron数据集与"合成殖民地"的悖论

嘉宾提到一个几乎被忽视的细节——Enron的邮件数据集（因造假案被法院公开）至今仍是训练"企业内部沟通"AI最重要的原始素材。这形成了一个跨越法律、伦理、机器学习的深层悖论：

我们正在用一家欺诈公司的行为模式，训练下一代企业AI的"沟通常识"。

这与生物学中的"奠基者效应"（founder effect）惊人地相似：一小群偶然存活的个体，其基因缺陷会被放大成整个后代种群的普遍特征。Enron是"数据基因池"里的一个奠基者，它的组织病理（层级模糊、信息隐匿、道德漂移）可能已经悄悄编码进无数商业AI的推理默认值里。

再往前推一步——这也解释了为什么"合成数据"始终无法完全替代真实数据：真实企业数据里包含大量"非理性但正确"的模式（拖延、政治博弈、模棱两可的授权链），而这些恰恰是agent在真实企业环境里活下来所必需的"生存本能"。合成数据太干净了，训出来的agent像温室里的植物。

隐藏的系统性真相：安全的定义正在从"边界"迁移到"意图"

访谈里最微妙的一句话是——"agent拥有合法权限，但在极短时间内做了破坏性动作"。传统安全建立在边界模型上（防火墙、身份验证、最小权限），核心假设是"非法进入者=威胁"。但agent颠覆了这一切：威胁来自持有合法钥匙的执行者。

这实际上把安全问题从计算机科学问题变成了组织行为学问题： - CISO需要学习的不再是"如何阻止入侵"，而是"如何理解意图漂移"——这更接近内部审计和心理学 - 传统的RBAC（基于角色的访问控制）会失效，因为agent的"角色"是流动的、被临时组合的 - 更颠覆的推论：下一代身份系统不会围绕"你是谁"设计，而是围绕"你现在正在完成什么任务"设计——权限会像水一样，随任务上下文实时凝聚和消散

这里有一个跨领域的映射值得思考：这与免疫学里的"自我—非我"识别危机高度同构。自身免疫疾病的本质是免疫系统无法区分"合法细胞"和"叛变细胞"。企业AI基础设施正在遭遇同样的问题——它需要一套"免疫系统式"的能力，识别"权限合法但行为异常"的实体。而现有安全工具，都还停留在"皮肤+防御工事"阶段。

一个更大的模式：所有人都在"活成数据基础设施"

嘉宾提到"每个人都变成了builder"——社媒经理、法务、财务都在用lovable之类的工具搭东西。表面看是民主化，但更深的一层是：每个员工都在无意识中变成一个数据管道，把公司数据搬进他们控制不了的系统。

这与20世纪初福特流水线诞生时的场景形成有趣的镜像——那时工人被"变成"了机器的一部分；现在，员工被"变成"了数据的一部分。区别在于：福特时代的工人清楚自己在装配什么；今天的builder，往往不知道自己正在训练谁的模型。

📝 转录文本

开场：非人类威胁的浮现

Up until now, the concerns came from human threats. What we're seeing now on steroids is that the same type of threat is coming from non-human actors, agents that essentially have legitimate access to the environment with legitimate permissions. Fortunately for us, it's a very similar methodology in terms of detecting that and protecting against that. But the velocity of that happening is extreme.

Think of the non-technical people. They're not even aware for things like security or compliance or who is going to use this data. Maybe their agent that they are building are using other agents and they're not technical to even understand what it means. It creates complete set of actors inside the organization not bound by the rules of the organization and not necessarily running within the premises of the organization but handling sensitive data. It's a good thing and bad thing that everyone inside organization can become builders. We live in very interesting times.

嘉宾介绍

Today on No Priors we're joined by Ofir Erlich and Gonen Stein, the co-founders of Eon. Eon is a cloud backup disaster recovery centric services designed for the AI era. In this discussion we talk about data, AI, why Google bought out the data of Spirit Airlines out of bankruptcy, and what it means to really manage and use data infrastructure in the AI era.

Ofir, Gonen, thank you so much for joining me on No Priors today. It's great to see you.

Absolutely. Thanks for having us.

Eon 是什么

Yeah. So, one thing that you guys are doing at Eon is — or actually why don't you give a quick overview of Eon and what it does really quickly, because I think that'll set the context for how we think about AI and data and models and fine-tuning models. I think there's a whole stack that's built on top of different types of data sets. And so, maybe we can start with what you all do and then I think we'll kind of walk through like how the world is shifting relative to the enterprise data stack.

Yeah, sure. So what we do at a high level is we've created a new data foundation that runs in the cloud, and we provide multiple capabilities that allow customers to first map and classify their data across their environment, across multiple hyperscalers, and identify what they have, where they have it, what's sensitive, not sensitive, and so on and so forth.

Then we provide an ability to easily ingest that data from all these different sources — structured, unstructured data — into this data foundation. And the data foundation then provides a very cost effective way of both maintaining the data for protection and recovery, but also makes sense of the data. So it allows customers to very easily access it, query it, search through it and apply their AI models and LLMs on top of that data that's ingested from a variety of sources.

从备份服务到 AI 数据底座

Yeah. And my sense is — I mean your starting point was really as sort of backup and data recovery and protection service — and I think along the way you kind of realize if you have all this data from a backup perspective, and you have all their customer history over all time, you can start using that for interesting application areas. What are some of those directions where you're seeing customers take this full history of data that you all have or represent?

So as you mentioned, when we started, I said, "I'm this crazy person starting a non-AI company in an AI world," and the AI tailwind became absolutely insane and made sure that data becomes the most important thing that an organization has.

When you can think about it — models, compute, everything is relatively ephemeral, almost zero switching cost, and those are important part of the infrastructure for the industry. But if you are a company — whether you're a hotel chain or you are a food chain, technology company, doesn't matter — the most valuable thing that you have is actually your data.

案例：Google 收购破产 Spirit Airlines 的数据

And you see more and more companies finding this out. You know, just two days ago, you saw Google buy something from the bankrupt Spirit Airlines. They didn't buy airplanes. They bought the data. They bought the data for $10 million because they think it's very important in that perspective. They're using that to train models.

I think the rumor too is that the other bidder on that data set was Mercor, right, in terms of the bankruptcy bid process. And so it's interesting. You had multiple different companies in the AI world bidding on a bankrupt airlines enterprise data set, which is fascinating.

Yes.

Do you think we'll be seeing a lot more of that in the future? Like, do you think we're going to basically be seeing these out-of-bankruptcy data buys?

So we've seen it for multiple use cases. That's what's really cool about it. And you see Mercor, see other companies are continually trying to already trying to buy data. If you're a tech data CEO today, I can tell you that you constantly get questions: "Are you willing to sell your data?" I hear it all over, and it seems that's going to be a significant trend as you go.

I'm hearing about, you know, labs going through Wall Street and trying to buy data from hedge funds and try to understand how to map and analyze companies. So you see data that was accrued throughout the years by companies which was usually like tapes. It was usually sitting on a shelf collecting dust, and all of a sudden this becomes very important.

数据成为护城河

And you see companies now realize that what I have today that differentiates me than anyone else is my data, and this data is gold — and actually I can leverage it to get more value for my company and to continue building my business when AI is actually coming and flatten the playing grounds.

It seems that everyone can start — even large and small companies basically have the same playing field — and the only real advantage that companies have today is of course their people but also the data that they've approved, because everyone has access to all of those cool new tools.

Yeah, it's become a moat. I guess — I mean, people have been saying data is the new oil for a long time and I was always a little bit skeptical of that statement. But I feel like now what's happening is because of post-training and reinforcement learning, and, you know, there's companies like Applied Compute and others that are starting to provide these sorts of services where you can fine-tune models or open source models against specific data sets — like, it seems like people are trying to optimize these things for their own use cases.

Spirit Airlines 数据的可能用途

I guess in the case of something like Spirit Airlines, is it customer support for building like an airline app? Like, what do you think they're actually going to do with this information? Is it something else? Is it the internal documents? Like, I'm just sort of curious — what is the reinforcement learning, or is it like a customer support agent?

Yeah. But think, if you're trying to build agents today, you can't just build them in a lab. You need to train them on new data, on some training data. And it's very hard to find very good data sets.

You see that Harvard just released a legal data set just a few days ago, but you don't find too many good data sets that don't look like real — synthetic data that can actually be used to really look like the real world. And I think that Spirit Airlines can be used both as an airline company but also as a large enterprise, as a place where lots of people work — a lot of, you know, the hierarchy, middle management, top management, and workers working together.

And if you're looking at what other public data sets do you have out there, there aren't a lot of those. There's the — seriously, I'm speaking with companies asking what kind of data do you have, what you train on real fine stuff. For example, the Enron data is out there in public and people are actually using that as real data from a company — how a company works. And the reason is it's very hard to find data that will help you to work like in the real world.

智能体训练与合成数据

Anytime you see someone building an agent or building a new application, you know, most of them don't really work. You have to go to the world, you have to actually interact with real world companies in order to really build something significant. Now, you can do that when you go to customers. So, you know, buy data and train in house. So when you first release your products, every new product that you have, you don't have to first interact with customers at your initial interaction.

So I think you're going to see more and more of that — both by creating new synthetic data in new innovative ways, in addition to getting existing data, whether it's the real data, whether it's somehow masked — think about it, contains sensitive information like PII, financial information, so on so forth — and actually be able to build real world stuff on top of that.

Yeah, and Google obviously — they're in this travel space for a while, right? They want this type of data. They're already monetizing it. This allows them to understand, train it, understand it, monetize it even further. And it's a unique situation, right, that obviously people want to take advantage of. And I think we're going to see more and more of that in such situations. And regardless of that, customers who have existing data want to be able to unlock that existing data as well.

为什么还需要新的数据工具

What sort of tooling are you all building at Eon to allow people to make use of their data for AI applications? Like, how are you thinking about this problem yourselves, or what sort of tools are your customers asking for?

So let's go back to the problem statement and why there are so many tools for data and processing. Why do you need new tools? Isn't it — sold already so many great companies throughout the years and everyone understands data is important?

So to put it this way: back in the days every data team could find their own data, decide what project do they have, and, you know, get data, do something with that — very tactical. They were using — I don't know — some great companies: Fivetran, dbt, Monte Carlo, all the data tools that exist in order to fulfill their tasks. And for some of the data, they didn't even know exist. It was — this was locked. Why was it locked? Because there are multiple business unit owners across the same company.

一个思想实验：数据团队 vs 业务单元

And let's say you're a data team leader in some company and you are based in San Francisco, or we're now here in New York, and both of us — different business unit leaders — and now there's this thing called AI. And even the boss is playing with ChatGPT — so the CEO and the board and the shareholders — they understand that AI is real.

So they're coming to you and they tell you, "Look, we have a lot of data in the organization. We now realize data is the new oil. We can actually activate it with the new tools that we have today. We couldn't before do something with the data, make it useful, and use AI for that, because it's valuable for us and because it's cool. What can you do?"

So you say, "Great, I've done this thing before. I know all of those new cool things that are coming out every day in Silicon Valley. I can just leverage them." The problem is — where's the data?

And so you come to us, and we are business unit leaders. If you even know us, maybe you don't, but let's say that you somehow got to me. I'm a leader of a business unit. I have data, probably, and somehow you convinced me to give you access to my data.

遗留数据的黑箱

Now I don't know what data do I have. I have a lot of people working for me. They have data in multiple systems for the last 20 years. Some of them systems that no one really understands — where they contain production data, sensitive information — there's always this server that no one knows what it's doing, but connected to the power, whether virtual or physically, that everyone's afraid to turn off because we don't know what's in there.

So we had all of that. And let's say that somehow I know what's in there. Now I need to bring engineers and compromise maybe security and compliance and production uptime and to extract the data just to give it to you and store it in a very inefficient manner. It's very hard.

Eon 的差异化解法

We understood that there's a problem with how this works because we have different incentives. You were tasked with doing that. I'm tasked with making sure my systems work, and I'm tasked with making sure that data is intact — no data is running away, I don't accidentally have the salary of the CEO inside my data and it's actually going to be trained to be used for training or post training by you.

So we at Eon solve it in a very different way. We can help you — not me, you, the data team leader — find all the data that's in the organization in a very simple way, understand what it is, classify it, map it, understand context, layer on top of that as build a semantic layer, and then be able to continuously bring all the data from me that is relevant without compromising production, without compromising security, compliance. We're actually keeping audit and, because data is classified, I know that I'm not accidentally going to share with you sensitive information that you shouldn't have eventually in your data. We can do it in a very cost-efficient and performant way. So you can actually do it from all over the place, bring it to you and actually use it.

三到四层能力总结

So it sounds like there's three or four things that you're solving for. One is you're aggregating lots of historical and current data for people. Number two is you're able to then mask personally identified information or other fields that they don't want necessarily shared, or set permissions on top of that. And then third, it sounds like all this can then be exposed into AI models for sort of their uses or applications.

Yeah, and the key point to that is that customers already have this data. That's kind of the ironic thing. Customers today already have this data. It's kept in their environment in different forms, but it's locked. It's not accessible and usually it's very very expensive. Right? So we're able to take what customers already have, convert it into this new data foundation format that's much more efficiently stored and provide the mapping, classification, access control, and connect it into the AI workflows.

AI 时代的安全：从人类威胁到非人类威胁

How do you think about security? So there's been a lot of news recently about the labs where they'll have agents escape sandboxes and do all sorts of things. And, you know, there may be broader things afoot in terms of why that's happening beyond just the agent capabilities. Like, who knows how these things are set up or configured — sometimes it's a little bit uncertain how people are approaching these things. But, you know, fundamentally there's a lot of discussion of AI security. How do you think about that in the context of the enterprise stack — what people should do or not do, how CISOs should be thinking about all this?

Yeah. So, up until now, the concerns came from human threats, right? So this is not new where customers would come to us and say, "Hey, we were exposed by this ransomware attack." So during our time at AWS, it was a very large customer that was impacted by ransomware. We thought that they were completely protected using our technology — the disaster recovery service that we managed there. And we learned unfortunately that the customer thought that they were protected. They weren't protected because they didn't map and classify and tag their resources properly. So it wasn't protected. And so 60% of the environment was exposed by ransomware.

And that's one of the reasons why we decided to launch Eon and solve that pain point around human threats such as ransomware — so being able to detect when that happens, look for irregular write patterns and entropy changes and things like that, protect against it, and then also allow customers to recover in a granular fashion and very quickly.

Agent 带来的"合法权限威胁"

What we're seeing now on steroids is that the same type of threat is coming from non-human actors, from AI agents that essentially have legitimate access to the environment with legitimate permissions into such-and-such databases. And all of a sudden — and this now happens very rapidly — a table is all of a sudden dropped. Fortunately for us, it's a very similar methodology in terms of detecting that and protecting against that and allowing to recover, but the velocity of that happening is extreme.

Yeah, something I noted is that like six months ago, no one would even discuss this with me. But a few months ago, pretty much every person I meet, every leader in a company, tells me either they are afraid of that happening to them or it personally happened to that person who's speaking with me — which is crazy. You see it all over the place. You see real fear from — "I no longer decide what's really running on my data. I no longer understand. I need to be prepared for both external threats because all the new MCPs make it much easier for attackers to come to me and attack me, but also from the inside with agents I actually approved running in my environment."

So it's a very very tricky time. We need to assume breach whether it's malicious or not, and need to be able to handle it and act accordingly. It's a very weird situation today.

Agent 时代的企业数据栈是否颠覆？

Yeah. How do you think about the broader enterprise stack and agents? So, you know, the current stack really evolved around people or humans asking very defined analytical questions. So we have warehouses, we have dashboards, we have the ETL pipelines, we have BI. And agents may behave differently and more dynamically. They may be able to reason over much larger sets of data. They may have access to SAP, SaaS apps, and historical data and a variety of other things and then act. So what do you think changes in terms of how you store, access, interact with data in the context of the agentic world? Or what else do you think needs to change? Do dashboards go away? Like, what shifts?

I actually think we'll see more dashboards because this will be the only way to kind of figure out what they have going on in the world. Because first, coding agents have started to write most of the code that's running in the world — so that's indirectly. But also, agents activating other agents that would activate other agents, and trying to keep track of the non-human identity — it becomes almost impossible task.

So many actors inside the organization — when it's very hard for a human to understand the chain of responsibility. And this is part of what you're seeing in proliferation of cybersecurity companies. How many cybersecurity companies you see in NHI, in non-human identity right now — an infinite amount. And there's a reason for that. It became the number one, number two problem right now.

端点安全与"人人是 builder"

In addition to that, the second thing is endpoint. You see endpoint security which looked like it solved — there so many great companies around it — and just a few years ago when endpoint was a completely different problem with the AVRs. Now everything that's happening — you see people are running agents today on their laptops, and the agents sometimes connected to other networks. They are connected to, think, an open Claude connected to your WhatsApp but also to your internal network and also to other applications.

And you see it's very hard for the VP of IT, for the CIOs to understand what should they do. On the one hand, they want to — they are being pushed by the board, by the CEO: "enable AI in my organization now, don't block me, you can't block me." On the other hand, it's so scary.

I mean, every person — don't even think of technical people, think of the non-technical people building something with, you know, let's say a Lovable or any other software that you — for themselves, putting company data there. They're not even aware for things like security or compliance or who is going to use this data. And they're all using all of those new cool things. So maybe their agent that they are building are using other agents, and they're not technical to even understand what it means.

So it creates a complete set of actors inside an organization not bound by the rules of the organization and not necessarily running within the premises of the organization but handling sensitive data — which is the property of the organization, could be exposed to the world, it could be incorrect, could be incorrectly used, and becomes a big problem.

It's a good thing and bad thing that everyone inside organization can become builders. Whether you're a social media manager, whether you're a finance person, whether you're in legal or finance.

Mhm.

So, it's amazing, but it's also — we live in very interesting times in that perspective.

现有数据基础设施还剩多少？

How much of the existing data infrastructure do you think survives all this? So, you know, there's all the ETL data engineering infrastructure that you know people have been building and deploying over the last decade. Does that stick around? Does that shift? Does that change? Like how quickly does all this upend?

So you see there's a strong compelling event to pretty much change everything, because what's called the plumbing today is very limited and everyone built a solution to their set of problems.

So think about what happens now. Gonen goes downstairs after recording this podcast and he really wants coffee. So goes to the store and buys coffee, and he puts it on his credit card.

Now there's a transaction and this is written in some database somewhere.

Okay. Right.

So someone needs to — today what they're doing, they're extracting the data, putting it somewhere, and that's it. Someone else at some point takes this data and processes it in some other way, and that's it. So there's no connection with all of those stuff, and every person is very different. They don't have the context of what happened before.

单一目的到全域上下文

And the reason is very simple. It wasn't so important before to have all the context, all the data of the organization, because you could only do with the data things you really intended to do to begin with. So you had a single purpose in your mind when acting on the data.

Mhm.

Today it's very different. Today you understand that if you're able to smartly collect and clean all your data and make sure you store it in efficient manner, and if you can activate that efficiently, you can let a team go wild with all the data that they have. And the more data that they have, and the more high quality data that they have, and the more context on that data that they have, the team handling that can create wonders and think of things which were unimaginable.

汉堡与披萨：跨库连接的思想实验

Let's say that there's one person in the organization who have all the list of all the people in New York who love burgers, and another person in the organization has a database of all the people in New York who love pizza. They don't know they can find a list of all the people in New York who love burgers and pizza because they didn't work together. Now if you use it for post-training and use it for the new capabilities, you can actually do wonders with that. You can actually start asking your data intelligent questions. You can start using that for your own purposes — just something that you couldn't do before.

数据的爆炸与噪声

So you're seeing companies — first they're collecting tons more data than before. The amount of data being ingested is absolutely insane, especially comparing to earlier. We see trends continuously, both us and other companies that we're seeing in data. You see data is growing out of proportions. So much of it — and so much of it being generated by those new agents. So there's a lot of noise in the data. There's a lot of value and noise as well. So you need tools that are able to both understand data from multiple locations, clean the noise, and make sure all of these data that's been created is actually usable.

Mhm.

And it doesn't apply with the old tools that were very — some of them were incredible. Fivetran was an incredible company, dbt and so on so forth — but very specific tools for that purpose.

Databricks 与"打不过就加入"

So this creates a very interesting brave new world. You've seen companies like Databricks, you know, one of the most incredible companies on the planet in my opinion, looking at "I have more and more data coming in. I don't necessarily know where it is. I'll help you catalog the data and make use of that." But it's an after-effect. You already have the data. Now you need to process that.

But they are reinventing themselves all the time because they understand that more and more data has been generated by agents. And they thought — the way I see it — if you can't beat them, join them. "We'll build our own agents. We'll build our own databases." They want to take charge of how data is being used, data is being created. And it's completely different than how any other people used that just three or five years ago.

为 builder 与 agent 文化赋能

Yeah. So the goal is really to enable this culture of builders and the culture of agents with the ability to automatically help them understand what's there, automatically help them ingest the data without having to build manual pipelines for each and every application that is being built, and then also help them maintain control on top of the data that's created.

Makes sense.

And you see with every data that you have, there's another problem right now that lots of data is amazing but it's scattered — which is a sort of problem. But then you need to access that, you need to pay for that for storage, and of course tokens. And we're not in the time of token maxing anymore — trying to go to actually getting value for every token that we have, because it becomes more and more expensive. So you want to be very wise. I don't want to say "not paying millions" — pay millions and even more than that if you need to, but get the value that you can from actually doing so. So it's very expensive, very lucrative — let's make it relatively as least expensive as you can have it.

从云迁移到 AI 迁移：CloudEndure 时代的对照

So I guess, you know, the other thing that you guys have really lived through is the cloud transition. So prior to Eon, you started a company called CloudEndure that was acquired by AWS. And at AWS, you really saw that migration from on-prem to the cloud at like a huge scale in terms of that big sort of generational shift that had happened before this. How would you compare this infrastructure change to what's happening with AI right now? Like, what do you view as sort of the cloud era versus the AI era, and what are takeaways or lessons that you can apply across them?

Yeah, I think it's like that but on steroids. And even before we sold our last company CloudEndure to AWS, we supported similar large scale enterprise migrations with other hyperscalers — with Azure and with GCP — where our product was integrated OEM into the console. So very large enterprises that were moving thousands, tens of thousands, or hundreds of thousands of servers, and then we saw those modernized further in the cloud. And after we sold to AWS, we did that as part of the Application Migration Service. But that's kind of where it ended, and it required a lot of work, a lot of effort — both from a technology side as well as from the human side.

What we're seeing now in this crazy world of AI and agents is that those transformations are happening way faster, and customers are losing control to a point where that's becoming an inhibitor, right? Not an enabler. They're stopping, they're pausing because they're afraid that things might break, that data might leak, that IP might break out. And so they're looking desperately for this level of understanding of what's happening and control.

云 vs AI：抽象 vs 直觉

So it became so insane and so fast. And one of the reasons is that cloud, in my opinion, cloud is somewhat abstract because it's very hard to explain what it means. Cloud is basically just someone else's computer, but who knows what it is. It's hard to explain to my grandmother about the cloud.

AI — everyone understands AI. Everyone lived from the ChatGPT moment when we all felt what AI could do. "Oh my god, this is incredible." So they're getting pushed by C-levels, by CEO, by the board, by the shareholders — "use AI for the business, otherwise we're irrelevant." So you see people doing it both for the value that you get from AI but also from the fear that you get from AI.

软件消费方式的重塑：Forward-Deployed Engineers 与 PLG

And you see new trends of — for the first time in many years, you see how companies consume software in a brand new way. What's happening with forward deployed engineers — used to be something that looked like services. Palantir were doing that. No one really understood what it means. And now everyone's doing that.

Now it seems that you come into a large legacy enterprise, they really want to adopt AI because they have to. The problem is they don't know how to do it. They understand that their processes are very long. Some takes a year or two or more, but they need to have it now. And the only way they can actually get it deployed and become AI much faster is by letting strong engineers who understand what they're doing and coming with the tools that they've created in top Silicon Valley startups and sometimes larger companies to come and transform those organizations. And you see them shrinking sales cycles, and you see companies growing really fast because of that.

You also see companies buying really fast — especially the new companies — buying using product-led growth really really fast AI infrastructure which actually helps to build agents, because everyone now wants to build agents.

Now, in the past I was arguing that for the majority of things PLG doesn't work, especially for dev tools, because the world is very fragmented, people don't want to move so fast, so forth. Now it became super hot — looking at companies like Cognition for example, which is, you know, an incredible company, that were able to first go through a PLG (we used that way in Eon) and then through the FDE motion, telling — going to banks and then will replace engineering that you don't want to do with our engineers, making you focus with the things that you do want to do. So leveraging on all fronts, so it became super super super interesting.

收购套利：把公司变成 AI 公司

The world is changing so much. And one other really interesting way that companies are leveraging AI is — they are very slow to adopt AI, but there are really great companies, for example Long Lake, that say, "Instead of you adopting AI, I know how to do it more efficiently. If I can buy the company and transform that into an AI company, we can all win. We can extract arbitrage, make higher margin more efficiently." And this is a really radical new way for those companies to actually start using AI, become more efficient.

结语：革命才刚刚开始

And we speak about this as a revolution, but I think we just started. Most companies still don't use AI. Most companies still are at the beginning of this journey. They all understand that something is happening, they understand that data is important, they understand that their existing processes are somewhat mundane and they have to do something about it, but it's scary — but you have to do it. So it's a fascinating thing to see.

It's a fascinating evolution on what's going on right now in how companies consume AI software, how companies transform into being more modern, how much we're being pushed to do that. And I think that eventually — I know it's a very wild ride — but I think everyone is going to — the world in my opinion is going to be better because of that.

Amazing. Well, thank you so much for joining me today. Very interesting wide-ranging conversation on data and AI. Really appreciate it.

Thank you. Our pleasure.

It was a pleasure.

All right.

Thank you.

Thank you.

节目尾注

Find us on Twitter at @NoPriorsPod. Subscribe to our YouTube channel if you want to see our faces. Follow the show on Apple Podcasts, Spotify, or wherever you listen. That way, you get a new episode every week. And sign up for emails or find transcripts for every episode at no-priors.com.

## 出人意料的观察：破产法庭正在成为AI时代的"数据交易所"
Google花1000万美元从破产的Spirit Airlines手里买的不是飞机，而是数据——而竞标对手是Mercor这样的AI标注公司。这个细节值得反复咀嚼：**破产清算程序正在悄悄演变为AI训练数据的一级市场**。
传统破产法把资产分为"有形"和"无形"，无形资产里商标、专利被反复拍卖，但"日常运营数据"从未被单独定价过。现在AI改变了估值逻辑——一家航司的内部工单、中层管理者的邮件、客服录音，其价值可能超过它的机队残值。这意味着： - 未来公司的**破产清算价值曲线会被重写**，"数据完备度"可能成为债权人评估回收率的新指标 - **反向的商业策略**会出现：某些企业会被"为了数据而收购"，就像嘉宾提到的Long Lake那样"买公司—AI化—套利" - 一个更隐秘的推论：**存活的公司之所以拒绝出售数据，可能反而使它们成为收购标的**——因为收购整个公司是获取这批数据的唯一路径

item.content:encoded:
💡 创造性洞见

一、老黄在做一件"反博弈论"的事——他正在扮演AI时代的私人MITI

传统博弈论告诉我们：垄断者应当藏信息。信息不对称是垄断利润的护城河。但Jensen这次做了一件让所有商学院教科书需要重写的事——他把未来六个季度的需求可见性免费送给了整个供应链、竞争对手、甚至股东。

这不是一次财报电话会，这是一次私人产业协调会议。它的历史原型不是苹果或英特尔，而是日本1960年代的MITI（通产省）——政府用"行政指导"让整个产业链同步扩产。区别只是：这一次，指挥棒不在东京官僚手里，而在一个穿皮衣的黄仁勋手里。

意外的观察：当一个垄断者的"边际成本"变成"供应链协同成本"时，他会自动从博弈论行为切换到计划经济行为。老黄不是在做营销，他是在做私人版的五年计划。这也解释了为什么70%其实是被供给"锁住"的天花板——一个不受约束的垄断者，此刻反而在自我限速。

二、NVIDIA正在悄悄从"硬件公司"变成"垂直整合的金融保险公司"

CoreWeave那个"最低收入担保+超额分成"的结构，本质上是保险合约。NVIDIA承担了残值风险和空置风险，收取的"保费"是未来算力销售的分成。

这个模型的历史原型是GMAC（通用汽车金融公司）——1919年通用汽车创立GMAC，用消费金融解决了"车买得起但客户没现金"的问题，从此垄断美国汽车业半个世纪。同样的模式还包括：波音资本为航空公司做的飞机融资、卡特彼勒金融、Xerox当年的复印机租赁。

跨领域连接：所有从"制造业冠军"进化到"生态系统霸主"的公司，都经历过同一个阶段——当产品价格高到客户无法一次性买断时，制造商必须变成金融机构。NVIDIA现在处于这个进化的临界点。而更值得注意的是：非超大规模客户增速25%季环比vs超大规模的14-15%，这说明NVIDIA正在逃离对四大云的路径依赖，用"金融杠杆"扶植一批新型客户（Neocloud）来分散议价权。这不是技术故事，这是权力再平衡。

三、Salesforce-Anthropic合作揭示了软件行业最恐怖的隐喻：媒体行业2010年的重演

Marc Benioff亲口承认Claude可能成为B端的"入口"——注意这个词。上一次一整个行业的公司集体承认自己不再控制"入口"是什么时候？

是2010年前后的传统媒体。当报纸和电视台开始把内容"分发"到Facebook和Google时，他们最初以为这是渠道拓展。五年后他们才发现：当读者的注意力入口不在你手里时，你和读者的"信任关系"就已经被中介抽走了。这就是"脱媒"（disintermediation）——媒体行业用了整整十年才理解这个词的血腥。

令人不安的观察：CRM把这个动作命名为ClaudeForce并宣传37个"skills"，语气像是征服，但结构上是投降。他们承认了在Agent时代，客户的第一触点可能不再是Salesforce UI。所谓"零数据保留"（Zero Data Retention）承诺听起来像是对客户的隐私保证，但从产业组织角度看，它其实是Salesforce在向Anthropic抵押数据主权换取入口地位——就像当年报纸把内容开放给Google爬虫换取流量。

短期是双赢，五年后可能是"Wintel时刻"（Windows吃掉Intel的定价权）的翻版——只是这次AI是Windows，SaaS公司是Intel。

四、隐藏的元观察：市场对软件的2.5年错判，揭示了"预期定价"作为市场机制的根本缺陷

Xiao Tao无意间说了一句极重要的话："市场对AI利好软件的判断，方向对了，但时间错了两年半。"

这不是一次普通的错判——这是效率市场假说与有限理性之间的裂缝。市场对了方向（AI最终利好软件），但把"三年后的兑现"提前折现到"零年"，然后在两年半的"验证真空期"里被反向情绪反复鞭打。

跨领域连接：这与生物进化中的"寒武纪大爆发"高度对称。寒武纪之前有5亿年"信号发射"（基因工具箱早已就绪），但真正的物种大爆发只发生在环境窗口打开的那一刻。软件公司的AI能力储备也已经就绪三年了，但只有当客户愿意为AI功能实际付出60-80%溢价的那个季度（也就是本季度），"进化爆发"才真正启动。市场提前定价了3年，等来一次爆发，中间被折磨了两年半。

这对投资者最深的启示是：在AI这种平台性技术面前，"方向正确"和"时间正确"是两个几乎无关的变量。买错时间点的方向正确，会让你亏损两年半再回本。这也解释了为什么Xiao Tao说"这需要情绪的层层积累+基本面的层层积累"——他其实在说：范式转变从来不是一次财报能完成的，它是一次连续的相位跃迁。

📝 转录文本

开场

Welcome everyone to a professional US stock channel that goes beyond just reporting the news. I am your market analyst, Xiao Tao. Even though the earnings season is behind us, I don't know why I still feel incredibly busy. It was already midnight when I finished listening to the earnings reports of these two companies to record this video for you, so given this level of passion, I feel a great sense of responsibility, right? To come here and put together this episode for you all today. And because of that, shouldn't everyone start by hitting like, leaving a comment, and sharing?

Alright, I won't waste any more time; let's get straight into it. Today I will only discuss company earnings; I won't cover other things or general market trends, including certain data points. I believe macro data isn't as important as the wealth of information revealed behind these two companies' earnings reports.

一、NVIDIA 财报解读

1. 超大规模客户 RPO 与资本开支节奏

Let's start by looking at Nvidia's earnings. Let's break it down point by point. First, in Nvidia's report, they mentioned hyperscalers, with an RPO of 2 trillion—that is, the combined orders for all hyperscalers to be fulfilled in the future amount to 2 trillion. Capital expenditure for '26 is 800 billion, with '27 capital expenditure projected to reach 1.3 trillion.

Looking at the year-over-year growth rate, the year-over-year growth in capital expenditure for '27 will actually be slower compared to '26. '26 is nearly doubling, but if you calculate the year-over-year growth for '27 by dividing 1.3 trillion by 800 billion and comparing it to '26, you will see a slowdown in the year-over-year growth rate.

2. 非超大规模客户成为增长主引擎

Furthermore, in Nvidia's earnings report, they have now separated their AI orders, categorizing them into hyperscalers and non-hyperscalers. Let's take a look: non-hyperscaler revenue growth is 4 billion, with a quarter-over-quarter growth of 25% and a year-over-year growth of 138%, while the growth for hyperscalers is around 14% to 15% quarter-over-quarter.

So, clearly, the quarter-over-quarter growth of non-hyperscalers has surpassed that of hyperscalers. What does this indicate? It indicates that moving forward, Nvidia's customer revenue growth will primarily come from non-hyperscaler companies.

This is also how everything connects, and why Nvidia recently joined forces with six major fund companies to provide loans, with Nvidia acting as a guarantor for the residual value of GPUs for these emerging cloud companies—why is that? It is because they want to support these new companies from a financing perspective, as these companies will become the main driver of their revenue growth in the future.

3. 炸裂指引：FY2028 收入增长 70%

Then, the third point from this earnings call might be considered a bombshell news or guidance: the revenue growth forecast for fiscal year 2028 is 70%, while the market expectation was only... so why would he do that?

Looking at the first point in the Q&A, Jensen indeed mentioned—when asked by an analyst—that they had never provided guidance for a year and a half out before. We have just entered their second quarter of fiscal year 2027. Their fiscal year differs from the calendar year, so there are two quarters left in FY27, yet they are already providing guidance for FY28. Normally, you would provide guidance for FY28 in the final quarter of FY27, but they are essentially doing it half a year in advance.

Why would they choose to do that? Jensen said he wanted their customers, supply chain, and investors to all have the same information, because it is extremely important. Why? Because many people across the entire supply chain are currently committing a significant amount of resources.

My thought is that the market expected 40%, but Jensen provided 70%. In reality, he could have easily followed the market expectations and delivered even higher results. But why did he choose to give this 70% guidance directly now?

It is first because, as he noted, demand is massive. He mentioned that this 70% guidance is still constrained by supply-side factors, because our demand will exceed this supply capacity. If there were no supply-side constraints whatsoever, their growth rate could easily reach over 100%.

4. 老黄的"供应链共同扩产"逻辑

The reason he is doing this is because he wants the entire supply chain to keep up, which is exactly what Jensen has been working on for the past two years. In this earnings call, he mentioned that if he hadn't brought Micron along to expand production back then, at this current stage, there would definitely be an even greater shortage of memory, and the price increases we've seen would be even higher than what we've experienced recently.

So, he is very glad that he led the entire supply chain to move forward together at that time. The same logic applies now; since NVIDIA is the leader in GPUs, he wants to signal to the entire industry what the projected growth rate is for fiscal year 2028, hoping the whole supply chain and industry will expand alongside them.

This point is crucial and quite rare, because since 2023, Jensen usually only provides guidance for the next six to nine months—two to three quarters—because their visibility on order demand typically only extends about half a year to three quarters. Yet this time, how much did he reveal? He's looking a year and a half out, revealing he already knows the demand for the next six quarters.

So, this is indeed a very important signal, a bombshell that has left the market very surprised. Because market expectations for revenue growth are currently at 45%; for fiscal year 2026, which just ended, revenue growth was over 60%, and this year, growth is expected to be over 80%. You'll notice that despite such massive scale, their revenue growth is actually accelerating; although 2028 might show a slight dip compared to 2027, the reason for that decrease is solely due to supply-side constraints.

If one had to pick a key highlight, it would be the 2028 revenue guidance, which is truly incredible—70% revenue growth at that scale; which other company in the world could achieve that? No one, only Jensen, and the reverse is also true. If he weren't leading the entire supply chain forward, Jensen himself could not achieve 70% revenue growth; it would be absolutely impossible.

5. Blackwell：史上最快产品爬坡

Moving on, the fifth point: Blackwell will become the fastest product ramp in history, which also alleviates some market concerns, as essentially all revenue for the coming quarters will come from Blackwell, the new generation of GPUs.

6. NVIDIA 与 CoreWeave 的合作细节：数据中心"保险合约"

Next, the sixth point regarding the cooperation details between NVIDIA and CoreWeave has also been disclosed this time. They stated that they guarantee a minimum revenue for the data center; for you, CoreWeave, if you build a data center, we can guarantee a minimum total revenue for that data center.

For example, if we guarantee this data center will generate 3 billion in lifetime revenue. Then, if the revenue ultimately exceeds those 3 billion, we will share the excess with CoreWeave based on a certain ratio. So, from NVIDIA's perspective, if the data center is profitable or meets the minimum revenue requirement, it can actually collect two streams of income: the first is the money from selling the hardware, and the second is the money from CoreWeave. For all the computing power that CoreWeave sells, NVIDIA gets a cut.

So, the entire cooperation detail can be understood as what? It can be understood as NVIDIA providing insurance for the data center's total revenue, offering this minimum revenue guarantee, so what is the premium? The premium is that CoreWeave needs to pay a portion of the excess revenue to NVIDIA, and for CoreWeave, this is still a positive, why? Because with NVIDIA's guarantee, CoreWeave's cost of building data centers will be reduced.

7. 毛利率的短期承压：存储涨价传导

Moving to the seventh point, which is also something the market might be concerned about. To be honest, if NVIDIA hadn't released the revenue guidance for fiscal year 2028, the market might have fallen after this quarterly earnings report was released. Of course, right after the earnings report or the data came out, the stock did drop, but then the decline was erased, and now it has risen back.

The initial decline was because the gross margin for the fourth quarter, the fiscal year 2027 fourth quarter, will see a decrease. Why would it decrease? It is because of the rise in storage prices, as the magnitude of this increase exceeded expectations. Since it exceeded expectations and their shipment volumes and prices for this year are already set, they are unable to fully pass on the storage price increases to their customers.

That is also why the gross margin in the fourth quarter will reach a low point of 71%, while for the full year, the market expectation is around 74%, and last year it was around 75%, so the gross margin shows a certain degree of decline. Then the company expects gross margins to stabilize between 72% and 73% in fiscal year 2028. Why? It is because starting from the first quarter of fiscal year 2028, their new GPU pricing will be reflected in their revenue reports.

So, after their explanation, I think this short-term dip in gross margin is acceptable. It's actually the same as Apple; if you look at Apple, their gross margins will also decline soon. Why? Because they simply cannot—it's not just about passing the memory costs onto consumers; if you want to maintain the original gross margin, what must you do? You would have to make a profit on top of the memory cost itself. In other words, even though you didn't produce the memory, you would be treating it as your own product and selling it at a premium. That isn't reasonable, and it's not ethical, right?

So that is why for both companies, whether it's Nvidia or Apple, they can pass the rise in memory costs entirely to their customers, but they cannot earn higher premiums while these costs are rising. Therefore, once the memory costs are added to their own product costs, a short-term dip in gross margin will occur, okay?

8. 行业数据更新：1GW 数据中心成本

And the last point is some industry data that we can update, as Jensen just provided some new figures. Five years ago, a one-gigawatt data center cost about 30 billion. Now, after they launched Blackwell, the cost for a one-gigawatt data center is about 60 billion. So, a while ago I heard JPMorgan say a one-gigawatt data center now costs 100 billion; that figure is too high. Jensen just gave the latest data, which is around 60 billion, or 60 billion dollars.

9. 估值更新：NVIDIA 变得更"便宜"

After this revenue guidance was provided, let's update the valuation. In yesterday's video, I talked about the title of my video, which was that Nvidia's valuation is cheap. Now, if you look at the fiscal year 2028 revenue guidance provided, you will find that if you look at its P/E ratio, Nvidia's valuation has become even cheaper, it has become even more affordable.

Based on market expectations, just like the EPS growth I mentioned earlier, the revenue and EPS growth are actually the same. The market assumption for fiscal year 2028 is a 45% revenue growth and 46% EPS growth, assuming no gains in operational efficiency—meaning profit and EPS grow in line with revenue. Thus, the market projects 46% EPS growth for FY28.

Now, if we factor in that 70% growth rate, the original FY28 P/E ratio was around 16 times, or 15.9 times to be exact. If we plug that 70% growth rate in, what does the FY28 P/E become? 13.7 times. 14 times, what does that imply? It means if we assume that over the next year and a half the stock price remains flat and the earnings reports perfectly match market expectations, its static P/E ratio is 14.

What kind of growth rate does a 14x static P/E match? A 14x static P/E matches a future EPS growth rate of around 10%. If that growth stays around 10% in the long term, you could argue that a 14x static P/E is reasonable. Otherwise, for any EPS growth rate above 20%, a 14x static P/E is an undervaluation, or looking at it now, a 14x P/E is significantly undervalued.

二、Salesforce (CRM) 财报解读

1. 与 Anthropic 的合作：软件末日论被打破

Okay, now let's talk about the recent CRM earnings report. First, a rather important piece of news from their earnings call was the partnership with Anthropic. This collaboration marks a new model for the future of AI and software companies: AI won't completely disrupt software companies; instead, software will become part of the AI ecosystem. The AI will handle the "brain" layer, and software will handle the "tool" layer, where the brain calls upon these tools. This is the direction we previously envisioned for AI agents and their underlying tools.

This is also why, after checking the news regarding the CRM and Anthropic partnership, I believe it's reasonable that the stock price of WEN dropped. The reason is that from CRM's perspective, they believe Anthropic will become the orchestration layer for future AI agents—it will become a "brain" that sits on top of the software, controlling the software below. So, if Anthropic can achieve that position, it will certainly pose a certain level of threat to Microsoft. I think it is reasonable that Microsoft's stock price saw some decline after hours. Of course, as to whether this will ultimately cause massive disruption or impact for Microsoft, I don't think it will, because Microsoft will also have its own AI agents.

2. ClaudeForce 与 37 项技能：入口之争

Let's get back to the CRM side of things. Regarding the partnership between CRM and Anthropic, they have launched a new product called ClaudeForce, and they have developed 37 skills. How should we interpret this? It means that within Anthropic's Claude, they have developed 37 CRM products, meaning if you enter Claude now, you can fully utilize CRM products through Claude.

So, as I mentioned earlier, CRM believes that the future gateway for the B-end market is very likely to be Claude. So, who is the gateway right now? The current gateway is CRM's own user interface. The partnership between CRM and Anthropic stems from their belief that a portion of future B-end traffic will directly come through Claude, which is why they chose to collaborate with them.

Therefore, these two companies will have a division of labor going forward: CRM will be responsible for sales and distribution, leveraging their many salespeople to promote this product. CRM and Anthropic will then enter a state of coexistence, with Anthropic serving as the brain and the gateway, and CRM acting as the tool and distribution channel—for now, it appears to be a partnership based on supply.

However, as I said, there is a risk that in the future, CRM might lose this UI and lose this gateway. If they lose the gateway, there is a certain risk, considering that the trust currently built between CRM and their clients exists because they have a direct connection. But if they lose that gateway in the future, it essentially means the clients themselves will form an interdependent relationship with Anthropic.

3. 双重视角：短中期利好 vs 长期脱媒风险

So, I think this partnership between CRM and Anthropic can be viewed from two angles; one perspective is that internally, AI itself is not solely reliant on their partnership with Anthropic. It's because we know their internal view, Mark's consistent belief, is that models are commodities and are interchangeable.

So, their internal products offer a choice; whether their customers want to use open-source models, Claude, or OpenAI, Salesforce provides these options. You can choose the underlying model; this is on the product side, within their own user interface. Within their existing products, you can select different models to perform different tasks.

Building on this, they chose another approach: they believe Claude could become a gateway for enterprise endpoints. They don't want a situation where, if a client's primary entry point is Claude, they can't access Salesforce products—so they must ensure the client can still choose Salesforce. Do you understand? They view Claude as a distribution channel. If Claude becomes a gateway in the future, they want to ensure that Salesforce products are available on that platform.

There is a risk here: currently, customers rely on Salesforce products, but in the era of AI agents, customers might rely on the agents themselves rather than the Salesforce product, right? So, if that happens, it might not necessarily be a long-term benefit for Salesforce. While this partnership is definitely a positive in the short to medium term, it's not necessarily a win from a long-term perspective.

Of course, this could also be seen as a defensive move for Salesforce rather than an offensive one, because they need to defend. Defend against what? Defending against the possibility that Anthropic could become a giant in the future.

4. 数据隐私：Zero Data Retention

Next, let's look at the second point, which wasn't asked during the earnings call, but Mark brought it up himself. In their partnership with Anthropic, there is a crucial issue that has been widely discussed recently: data privacy in AI. Are customers willing to share their data with Claude? Mark touched on this, which is why I'm asking: why do customers feel safe using it? Why are they confident enough to use it? Aren't they afraid that their data might be taken by Anthropic?

So, Mark himself mentioned it. He asked, what does zero data retention mean? Zero data retention means that any internal company data you run through their large models will absolutely not be retained by the model. The model won't keep any of our customer data, which is why it's called Zero Data Retention. CRM ensures that data won't leak.

5. 高端版本渗透率仅 5%：巨大升级空间

And lastly, the second point in the Q&A where their management mentioned that currently, only 5% of customers have upgraded to the latest version, called the Premium tier. This version of the product has a 60% to 80% price premium, so they believe there is huge room to help existing customers upgrade, as they are very bullish on the current version—that is, the version upgraded with AI integration.

三、软件行业的宏观拐点

1. 本季度是软件公司 AI 变现的"元年首季"

So, in fact, up until now, we have already looked at this quarter, we have already looked at the earnings reports of many software companies. By now, I am slowly realizing this issue, and I hope everyone realizes it too: it's only starting from this quarter that we are gradually discovering the integration between AI and these software companies' products, and we have already seen it land—we are actually seeing customers willing to pay for these AI software products.

Therefore, I believe this quarter is truly the first quarter where software companies are monetizing their integration with AI. It can be considered the first quarter of the inaugural year, just getting started.

2. 市场错判了两年半

To some extent, the market actually thought back in late 2023 and early 2024 that 2024 would be the year of software, because software would benefit from AI, given that AI's implementation is centered on software. As a result, software kept falling from 2024, falling for two and a half years, until roughly the middle of this year—from the beginning of 2024 all the way down to June 2026.

So, throughout these two and a half years, the market clearly misjudged, anticipating the benefits of AI for software too early. In reality, it is only this quarter that we are truly seeing that AI seems not to be a headwind for software companies, but a tailwind.

3. AI 的真实红利：试错成本骤降 + 产品周期缩短

Of course, this benefit is predicated on the company's ability to effectively integrate AI into its own products and then upsell them to customers at a higher price. This entirely depends on the company's execution and its capability to seamlessly merge its existing products with AI and successfully bring them to market.

Therefore, the cost of trial and error has also dropped significantly. You'll notice that every software company now launches new products much faster; what used to be two or three features a year is now a dozen features per quarter. Through this continuous trial-and-error process, once they hit on a blockbuster product, they push it out aggressively. With their existing distribution, sales teams, and FDE, the deployment speed is incredibly fast, leading to rapid revenue growth for these software companies.

This is the true benefit that AI brings to these software companies: trial-and-error costs are drastically reduced, and what we call the product cycle—the time to launch new products—has shortened significantly.

4. Salesforce 的经营数据与估值

For example, Salesforce is a great case. I've plotted their adjusted margins below; look at their profit margins over the past five quarters: 32, 27, 34, 35, 34, 34.8, 34. They have remained completely unaffected.

As for their revenue growth, they have been making acquisitions, so as a relatively traditional company, CRM's revenue growth is largely driven by those acquisitions. Now, in this past quarter, the revenue growth rate was 11%, which is a slight slowdown compared to the previous quarter, but their RPO is more important because RPO represents future revenue growth. RPO saw a 14% year-over-year growth, up from 13% in the previous quarter, so we are seeing a re-acceleration in RPO. So, my expectation after listening to this earnings call is that their RPO growth will continue to trend upward.

With these perspectives in mind, let's finally take a look at their valuation. The market currently expects their revenue growth for the next two and a half years to be 11%, 9%, and 10%, which is very much in line with CRM's typical revenue profile. Their revenue basically stays around 10%, and whenever growth slows down, they just make an acquisition, right? But things are different now; it's about the integration between products and AI to drive upsells. By selling these AI products, the bottom-line growth is projected at 13%, 11%, and 17%.

Well, one of my expectations is that their revenue growth will see an acceleration. Revenue growth is currently averaging about 10%, exactly 10% over the last two and a half years, and I expect that growth to re-accelerate. Because the integration of AI with their existing products will lead to upsells and a premium on the product side, which aligns with their revenue and EPS growth—EPS averages about 13% to 14%, and with a trailing P/E of 13, the PEG ratio is around 1. It is considered to be on the low side.

If you look at the price-to-cash flow, it's 1.7 times, and for the next three years, it's roughly 11, 10, and 8.8 times; most software companies currently have a price-to-cash flow ratio around 10. Basically, if everything remains unchanged, the cash they earn over 10 years would be enough to buy back their entire company.

5. 结论：软件板块估值终将修复

My expectation is that I still believe software companies are currently undervalued in terms of their valuations. I expect that companies like CRM, along with many other software firms, can at least see their valuations return to former levels—not necessarily 25 or 30 times, but at least back to the 18 to 20 times range, which I consider a reasonable zone. Building on that, since their fundamentals continue to change, if they keep improving, I don't think it's impossible for them to return to previous valuation levels or former P/E ratios.

I said half a year ago that the reason the market was selling off software was the belief that these companies' terminal values were affected—specifically, that their revenue growth five or 10 years down the line would suffer—but that view itself is something you cannot prove or verify. Over the past two years, we've seen that for many software companies, their revenue hasn't been impacted at all, and their margins remain unaffected, so on what grounds do you assume your assessment is correct?

That's why I say as long as companies continue to execute, the story Wall Street is currently selling will eventually be proven wrong. You can't keep running this kind of narrative for three or four years. It's impossible for software companies to keep executing, where their revenue shows no slowdown, shows no disruption from AI, and margins aren't hit by AI, and then expect this story to keep running for three or four years.

Therefore, I think this quarter, starting with Microsoft releasing their earnings first, followed by many other software companies, you can see that the market's feedback has been relatively positive. Why? First, the primary reason is a lack of positioning, and second, the market is slowly realizing that it seems not all software companies are being affected or disrupted by AI. As I said, this requires a layering of sentiment and a layering of fundamentals; it won't be just one company's earnings report that immediately brings the software sector back to life. That won't happen.

It's the same with hardware. The reason hardware has performed so well is due to a continuous layering of market sentiment and earnings results. So, I think most software companies have reported decent earnings this quarter, and I hope this continues into the next quarter, as I believe valuations in the software sector will gradually recover.

四、结尾与直播预告

Alright? That's all for today's sharing. A quick heads-up: this Thursday at 9:30 PM, I will be hosting a livestream exclusively for members within the APB app. We did a public livestream this past Monday, and one the week before that, but this Thursday will be for members.

The main reason is that I can dive deeper into that interview, and address any questions you might have, including the MVEL earnings after the bell on Thursday. If I have time, I'll listen to the MVEL earnings call and share my thoughts with everyone during tomorrow's livestream, along with other macro topics and questions you may want to ask during the member stream, okay?

The QR code on the screen is the download link, and even if you don't join tomorrow's livestream, that's perfectly fine. I encourage everyone to download it first. Once downloaded, you'll find that many of the features inside are actually very useful and completely free. After you've downloaded it and given it a try, then you can consider joining as a member. Alright? That's it for today's content.
